Which report was concurred in, and the brethren therein named were
admitted to seats.
The Grand Master then delivered his Annual Address, as follows: BRETHREN OF THE GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA: We are again met in Annual Assembly, as it was ordained of old that Masons
Hhould meet,
" To amend the defaults if any were found
Among the Craft within the land ;"
and "seriously to communicate and consider, to transact and settle all matters that
concern the prosperity of the Craft" within our jurisdiction-met with a fuller rep re·
sentation of Lodges than ever before, and under most favorable auspices. The year
has been to us one of peace, of plenty, and abundant prosperity. Scarce a ripple of
the terrible tide of war, that has been, and is, sweeping over and devastating our
sister States, has reached our distant and peaceful shores.
We are met for the first time in our own Grund Lodge Hall-in the Masonic
Temple which our San Francisco brethren, three years ago, promised to build for
our accommodation and their own convenience. Then, they showed us a picture of
a magnificent structure, as perfect in the simplicity and beauty of its architecture,
and in its adaptation to the uses for which it was designed, as cunning artists could
make it-a beautiful picture. The amendment to our Constitution, changing the
place of meeting from Sacramento to this city, was then under consideration, and
many thought and said the picture was all we should ever see of the Temple. But the
Grand Lodge, knowing the ability and the determined perseverance of those wlw
had promised to build a home for us and themselves, trusted to their good faith. On
the twenty-fourth day of June, 1860, Grand Master Cum'IB, assisted by the Grand
Lodge, laid the corner stone, with imposing ceremonies, in presence of the largest
assemblage of Masons ever gathered together on this coast. Then the Temple was
to cost $100,000. Already our brethren have expended upon it more than $150,000,
and it is not yet completed. Even now they are proud of their work, und we too arc
proud of it. It is the finest and most perfect building on the Pacific coast, and when
finished will be the most beautiful, if not the most expensive, Masonic Temple in
America. It is a noble monument of the energy and liberality of our brethren of
San Francisco, and we will not complain though, as in the case of that of old, seven
full years should be occupied in its building.
My duties have been, for the most part, of the pleasantest and most agreeable
character; and few of my official acts have be~n of sufficient moment to be reported
here. We have tested our Constitution, und know that it is good~ our brother NEILJ,
of Texas said" as perfect as any instrument of the kind can be made." Experience,
however, has shown us that slight amendments were necessary, and, doubtless, will
ehow us that others are necessary. 'l'wo amendments will come before you at this
Communication for adoption or rejection-one proposing to change the time of our
annual meetings from May to Octa ber, the other providing that commissioners for
trials shall be appointed by the Master, instead of being elected by the Lodge, as
now. But a single voice opposed the adoption of the first last year, and I trust it
will this year be unanimously adopted. May is one of the busiest seasons of the
year in the mountains and in the vallies -the month, of all others, when it is most
inconvenient for miners, farmers, mechanics, and business men of all classes to leave
• their homes; October is, perhaps, the most convenient.

Proceedings of the

[May '12,

During the year I have several times been called upon to decide questions arising
under Sec. 5, Art. Ill, Part Ill, of the Constitution, and to give construction to every
clause of it. Early in August, lVoodbridge J,odge, No.131, sent me for approval an
amendment to itsBy-Laws, requiring a separate ballot for each degree. I was of
opinion that the prohibition in the first clause of that section was absolute as to all
J,odges, except such as, at the time our present Constitution was adopted, had a pro'
vision in their By-Laws fonieparate ballots. The Grand Secretary, and others whom
I consulted in regard to the matter, and in whose judgments I placed great reliance,
advised me that it had been otherwise construed by my predecessors-that it had
been construed to mean not only those Lodges which, at the time of the adoption of
theConstitution, had provided for separate ballots, but all which should thereafter make
such provision. To give the Lodge the benefit of all doubts in the matter, I approved
the amendment, and it will come before you for final sanction at this Communication.
In February, I received for approval a like amendment to the By-I,aws of
Saint James Lodge, No. 54, and refused to approve, but recommended to the
Lodge to present the amendment to the Grand Lodge for its action. The law is, that
"no Lodge, unless it be otherwise provided in its By-Laws, shall have more than one
ballot for the three degrees;" and, as I understand it, it means absolute prohibition,
or else it means nothing; for to say that no Lodge shall have more than one ballot
for the three degrees, unless it provide otherwise in its By·Laws, is no prohibition.
If the Constitution had made no provision in regard to ballots, that would have been
the rule. I think there should be but one ballot for the three degrees, and if, by a
fair construction, the law, as it is, does not prohibit absolutely the use of more than
one, J advise that it be so amended that it will. I learn from the Grand Secretary
that only seven or eight of our Lodges use more than one ballot. Such as do, have
the right to continue to use three. We can not be too careful in our precautions
against the admission of improper persons to a participation in our mysteries, but it
seems to me that our precautions should be taken in the first instance--that we should
guard with greater vigilance the entrance to the ground floor of our temple. As Ma·
sonry is at present constituted, it is idle to say that one is good enough to be an En·
tered Apprentice, or a Fellow Craft, but is not worthy to be received among Masters.
If he is worthy to be a Mason at all, he is worthy to enter the innermost sanctuary
of our temple-to know all its mysteries. If he is not worthy to enter and be re·
ceived as a brother there, he is not worthy to enter the outermost gates, and having
entered he is not worthy to stay. The time to make diligent inquiry of a man's fitness
is before we admit him to the outer door of the Lodge. We have surely stationed
guards enough to protect a.JI the appr~aches to the temp.le, if they ~o their ~uty. We
require 11 residence of twelve months m the State, and six months m the midst of the
particular communityof which the candidate seeks to become a member, before hi!l
petition can be received. The petitioner must be recommended to the Lodge by two
of its own members, who, by their recommendation, vouch for his standing and char·
acter as a man. A committee of investigation is appointed, who should " diligent
enquiry and true report make" of the mental, moral, and physical character of the
applicant- of the fact that he is a good man.- of his fitness to become and be a
good Mason. In addition to nll this, we require a. ~animous ballot. It wo~Id be
diillcult to devise surer and better means of determmmg the fitness of the applicant,
if all do their duty. Yet, with all our precautions, unworthy men do, from time to
time, seek and obtain admission to our Lodges. The fault most frequently lies with
the committees of investigation. They neglect their duty, and present false reports
to cover their neglect. Whenever such a committee reports favorably, no matter in
what form of words their report may be couched, they say to the Lodge: "We have
carefully investigated the character of that man, and we know him to be sober, in·
dustrious, a good citizen, a good man in all the relations of life-one whom we may
safely receive into our society, and welcome as an equal and a brother-one who will

do honor to us as a Mason; and when they report favorably or unfavorably, without
.
due enquiry and reliable information, their report is false.
The second clause of Section 5, Art. III, Part III, above alluded to, provides that
if objection be made by a member of the Lodge, before initiation, the ap?licant
shall not receive the degree until the objection be withdrawn. The question has
been suggested, whether or not an objection may not, in that way, close our doors
to the applicant forever. That question I have had no occasion to decide, but I pre·
sent it now, that the clause may be so amended as to ei;::press, beyond _a doubt, our
meaning. We have provided that an applicant, rejected, may apply agam after a full
year of probation ; and a once unanimous election to receive the degrees should not
surely place him in a worse position than a rejection would.
Under the next clause, several questions have been presented to me for decision.
1st. When an objection has been made, and a committee appointed to investigate
the causes of objection, what is the duty of the committee, and may they advise the
candidate of the objection, and hear his defense?
2d. When a member of the Lodge has interposed an objection, stating the cause,
and the Lodge, upon the report of its committee, has decided that it is not" a valid
and Masonic one," has the same member, or another, the right to interpose the same
objection a second time, or any objection for the same cause?
3d. When an objection has been decided by the Lodge not to be " a valid and
Masonic one," is it the duty of the Master to proceed to confer the remaining degree
or degrees whenever the candidate exhibits suitable proficiency?
I report to you my decisions upon these questions, that you may take such action
upon them as shall seem just, and in accordance with the spirit of the law; so that the
Craft may be advised of the rights of all parties interested in like cases which may
arise hereafter.
1st. The committee is appointed to hear the testimony that may be adduced, and
to inquire into, determine, and report the facts to the Lodge for its advisement, that
it may wisely determine whether or not the objection is well founded; or, in the Jan·
guage of the clause, whether or not the cause is a valid and Masonic one. That the
committee may arrive at the facts, it must hear all the testimony, as well for the de·
fense as the prosecution. The candidate is a Mason, and, before conviction, should
be heard- should have his day in court. In many cases he should therefore be in·
formed of the objection made against him, and should be heard in his defense.
2d. When a member of a Lodge has objected to the advancement of a candi·
date stating the cause of objection, and the cause of objection has been inquired
into' and decided by the Lodge not to be "a valid and Masonic one," it is not com·
pete'nt for the same, or another member, to interpose a second objection for the
same cause, except on the ground of newly-discovered and material evidence, or for
acts su bseque!ltly committed. In the first instance, it is the right of every member to object, without stating the cause, if he so choose; but if he, or another, tle·
aires to interpose a second objection, he must state the grounds on which it is based,
and it is for the Lodge to determine whether it will or should consider the second
objection.
3d. When the Lodge has decided that the objection is not sustained, or that the
cause is not a valid and Masonic one, and the candidate has attained suitable proft·
ciency, it is his right to ask to receive the remaining degrees, and it is the duty
of the Master to confer them. He has promised "to submit to the awards of
his brethren, when convened, in every case consistent with the constitutions of
the Order." Wben the Lodge has decided that the candidate is worthy, and he
presents himself, ready to approve his proficiency, the Master may not refuse to con·
fer the remaining degrees, and thus overrule the action of his Lodge.
The Representative Fund will demand your attention. That fund wa.s created to
equalize the burdens of representation, and to secure a fu!l attendance at our annuat

Communication.~. The resolution creating the fund was adopted in 1861,and proposed
to pay only the necessary traveling expenses of one representative from each Lodge
in the jurisdiction, in coming to and returning from the place of meeting. Thus far
it has secured the end proposed. Last year, out of one hundred and thirty-five
Lodges, one hundred and eight were represented on the first day of the session ; this
year, out of one hundrea and forty-four Lodges upon our roll, the representatives
of one hundred and twenty-three have to-day answered to their names. The weakest
and most distant Lodges are placed, a& nearly as may be, upon an equality with the
strongest and nearest. Before the creation of this fund, many of the more distant
Lodges could not alford to be represented. The expenses of a representative would
have exhausted nearly, or quite, all theii: annual revenue. Shall we say to them, if
they can not afford the expense, let them stay at home ? I think not. The law requires that they shall be represented, and it is certainly important that they should
be. The business that we have in hand seriously affects and concerns the whole
Craft, and it is titting that all should participate in it. We all feel that it is good for
us to be here, and if for us, it is good for them. It is objected that the burden of
raising the fund falls very unequally, and that those who contribute most towards it,
receive the least from it. That is very true, and is as it should be. The strong
should help the weak. It is true that the Lodges of this city contribute largely and
receive nothlng from the fund, and that the Lodges located near the city pay more
than they receive ; but I am fully persuaded that they pay it cheerfully- that they
count the location of the Grand Lodge in this city of such worth that they can well
afford to pay their proportion of tl1e fund which places a Lodge in Siskiyou, or San
Diego, on an equality with thelll!!elvesin the matter of representation. It is something
worth to be able to attend the meetings of this Grand Body, and still to be at home.
For myself, I like the object of the fund, and I trust we shall give it a fair trial. That
we may do so, we should so perfect the plan adopted, by judicious legislation, that
all disputes and contentions in regard to the amount to which each Lodge is enti·
tied, may be avoided..,. That amount should be fixed. That being done, we can
determine very closely the amount to, be raised. Our object is to pay the expenses
which are necessarily incurred in coming to and returning from our meetings; and
if the person representing a Lodge receives those expenses from any other source, it
is not just that he should be paid them again out of this fund.
The subject of uniformity of work will be brought specially to your attention by
the Committee on Jurisprudence, to whom was referred last year a resolution, looking to the appointment of a committee with authority to agree upon, adopt, and
promulgate a uniform system. In 1854 such a committee was appointed and invest·
ed with like power. That committee did meet and adopt the system of work and
lectures since exemplified by Bro. JsAAOD.A.v1s. Bro. DAVIS was appointed Grand Lecturer ,and a considerable number of Deputy Grand Lecturers were appointed under him;
and through the Lecturers the work then adopted was taught, and received in nearly
all the Lodges in the State. Since then the same work has been several times exemplified before, and approved by the Grand Lodge, and all its subordinates have been di·
rected to receive and use it. The language of approval and adoption is clear and unequivocal; and I cannot understand how any one, who has read our proceedings, can
doubt that it was adopted, and is now the only authorized work in this jurisdiction.
Yet many of our brethren seem to doubt whether the Grand Lodge has ever taken
any such action in this matter as shall preclude them from using and teaching in
their own Lodges any peculiar system of work for which they feel a predilection.
To me, it seems of comparatively little moment whether we adopt and use the work
more generally used among us, or the work and lectures as taught and practiced in
New York, or New England, or Pennsylvania, or Illinois. There are differences, but
they are slight, and unimportant. All conform to the ancient landmarks and constitutions; all are good; all teach the same great doctrines of Love and Charity. But

1863.]

Grand Lodge of Oalifornia.

15

I do think it important that all the Lodges of this jurisdiction shall use the same
system; and I have no doubt that It is competent and proper for this Grand Lodge to
adopt a system, and to enforce conformity to it by all its subordinates. I trust the
report of the committee, which has the matter in hand, will inform us whether or
not we have adopted a work; and that tbe Grand Lodge will take such decisive and
distinct action at this time upon the subject, that there may be no longer any room
for doubt. If we have not adopted a system, it is surely time that we should adopt
one; and in order to secure and preserve uniformity in the work of our Lodges, we
must have well qualified and duly authorized teachers. We should have a Grand
Lecturer, and should make provision that he may receive a reasonable compensation
for his services. We must furnish facilities for acquiring the work correctly, else we
can not expect, or require, that all shall know and use it. I commend the subject to
your careful consideration.
Nearly all the Lodges of this jurisdiction have adopted the uniform code of ByI,aws, approved and recommended by this Grand Lodge in 1856, and amended in
1860 ; and the testimony of all who have tried them is that they exactly suit theit
purposes, and furnish all the law that they have any occasion to adopt or use for
their own government. The code was prepared with great care ; it is simple, con·
cise, and complete, and I think so much superior to any code that is likely to be
prepared by the members of any new Lodge, that I recommend that all Lodges,
hereafter organized, be required to adopt and use that code. Such a requirement
will save them and us much trouble and annoyance.
During the year, nine dispensations have been issused for the formation of new
Lodges-three of them in Nevada Territory; and I have denied the petitions for
three others. The petitions and papers accompanying them will be presented to you
by the Grand Secretary, and the new Lodges will doubtless come before you to
approve their work and ask for charters. Two applications were made for military
Lodges in California regiments on service out of the State. I declined to consider
the applications, for the reason that our Constitution leaves the Grand Master no
discretion in granting such dispensations ; and, if it did, the establishment of such
Lodgesseems to me of very doubtful utility, and I should have been unwilling to have
assumed the responsibility of granting such dispensations without direct action of
the Grand Lodge upon the subject.
Two Lodges have, with my approval, changed their place of meeting- Gold Hill,
No. 32, from Virginia to Lincoln, and Owen, No. 108, from Johnson's Bar to Scott's
Bar. Nearly all the members of Gold Ilul Lodge, No. 32, had removed to Lincoln, a
thriving village about five miles distant, at the terminus of the railroad, and it was
necessary that the Lodge should change its place of meeting', or give up its charter.
In the case of Owen Lodge, it was a case of convenience. All, or nearly all, the
members resided at Scott's Bar, and had been obliged to walk two miles to Johnson's
Bar to attend their Lodge meetings. In both cases suitable halls had been provided.
At our last Annual Communication the election of Bro. L. C. OwKN, as Master of
Golden Gaf,e Lodge, No. SO, was contested. The case was fully considered, and decided against the contestants. It was apparent, then, that a strong and bitter partizan feeling existed among a portion of the members of the Lodge, but it was
supposed that all would- as good Masons ever should-yield a cheerful submission
to the decision of the Grand Lodge, and that their difficulties would be soon settled and
forgotten. In November I learned, however, from the representations of Bro. OWEN
and other members of the J.,odge, confirmed by the Masters of nearly all the Lodges in
San Francisco, that our hopes had been disappointed, and that their disagreements
had assumed so violent and disreputable a character as not only to destroy, for the
time, the usefulness of the Lodge, but to bring the good name of the Craft into disrepute. J therefore arrested ..the charter of the Lodge by an order dated November
twenty-sixth. In March, having received satisfactory assurances that a complete

In April, 1850, the representatives of three chartered I.odges and two under dispensation met in convention, formed and adopted a Constitution, and under it organized our Grand Lodge. The M.·. W.·. CRAB:LES GILMAN, a Past Grand Master of
Maryland, presided over, and, by his great learning and experience, directed the
deliberations of that convention, and installed our first Grand Master. Since our last
Annual Communication we have learned that he died at Baltimore, the home of his
adoption, on the ninth day of September, 1861, after a long illness, in the sL..:ty-ninth
year of his age. It is fitting that this Grand Lodge should notice his death. He was
for some years a resident of this State, and ever manifested a kindly and zealous
interest in the establishment and prosperity of the Craft here. He was eminently a
good Mason, and perhaps no man was ever more honored by Masons. He was a
native of New Hampshire, and in 1832--3 was Grand Master of that State. Afterwards
removing to Baltimore, he was for six years, from 1842 to 1848, Grand Master of
Maryland. He was, besides, Grand High Priest of the Grand Chapter of Maryland,
and for many years General Grand Secretary, and for three years General Grand
High Priest of the General Grand Chapter of the United States.
We are also called to mourn the loss of an honored member of this Grand BodyBro. HUMPHRY GRIFFITH-who died in this city on the twenty-third day of March, 1863
Last year Bro. GRIFFITH was our Grand Orator, and delighted us by the learned and
eloquent oration he then delivered before this Grand Body. He also rendered us
most efficient service as chairman of the Committee on Grievances.. That committee
being made one of the standing committees, Bro. GRIFFITH was again appointed its
chairman. Re was, also, at the time of his death, Master of Washington Lodge,
No. 20. Bro. GRIFFITH was a lawyer, and had gained a high reputation for eloquence
and learning in his profe~ion. He has gone from us to that bourne whence no traveler returns. We may well mourn, for a good man has gone, cut down in the beauty
and prime of manhood-in the fullness and maturity of int<;llectual strength, when
he had just come to know what it is to live. May we profit by the solemn lesson,
and while we mourn for the honored dead, may we remember that our lives but hang
by a brittle thread, which, sooner or later, and we know not how soon, must snap
asunder. The dead say to us who survive," be ye also ready."
Sometime in March last I received from Bro. J. N. McJILTON, M.'. W.·. Grand
Master of Maryland, a communication, asking that the Masons of California should
contribute the sum of fifty dollars towards procuring the services of a Masonic Chap·
lain for the sick and wounded of our brethren in the hospitals in and around Washington. Immediately upon its receipt I replied, pledging, on behalf of the brethren
of California, the sum required, whenever we should be advised that' a Chaplain had
been or would be employed. The citizens of California had given most liberally for
the relief of the sick and wounded soldiers, and I felt well assured that the Masons of
this jurisdiction would gladly give not only fifty dollars, but many times fifty, if need
were, to send relief and minister consolation to their sick and dying brethren; though
I could not understand why it was essential or especially desirable that the spiritual
adviser in sl\Qh cases should be a Mason. The truest life of Masonry is in the exer·
cise of charities, and nevQr was there such 11 time and such need for the exercise of
true Masonic charities, as.'sinee the terrible war, which is now desolating our country,
began; and never has there been exhibited nobler examples of it, on the battle field,
in the camp, in the hospital, in the homes of widows and orphans, every where.
What truer or nobler aet has been done than was done by Bro. J. Q. A. FELLOWS,
Grand Master of Louisiana, and a few of the Masons of New Orleans, who, when

1863.]

Grand Lodge of Oalifornia.

17

Federal prisoners were first taken to that city, early in the war, in the midst of the
most intense popular excitement, and in spite of the clamors and threats of the infuriate
populace, fearlessly did their duty as Masons-sought out their brethren in distress,
and did, in very deed, visit those that were sick and in prison - did feed the hungry,
clothe the naked, watch over the sick, and speak kindly words of comfort and consolation to the dying. Such deeds are worthy of perpetual record. They tell us of
true manhood and incite us to be true men.
On the seventh of July, the anniversary of the day when the American flag was
first unfurled to the breeze in California, and proclaimed that here freedom should
henceforth make her home, the Grand Lodge, by invitation, convened in this city,
a.nd assisted in laying the corner·stone of the beautiful new Hall of the Society of
California Pioneers. Such occasions are always pleasant. That was peculiarly so.
All the elective Grand officers were present, and a goodly number of brethren, and
when our labors were concluded we joined most heartily with our friends, the Pion·
eers, in commemorating their festal day-the birthday of California independence.
My official duties have been very light, and very pleasant. The Craft has been
and is prosperous and harmonious throughout the jurisdiction. Our laws are so
plain and their commands so just and reasonable that almost all under~tand and
willingly obey them; and so it comes that the Grand Master has little occasion for
the exercise of authority, and finds so very little business to propose for yonr consideration. May He to whom belong wisdom and understanding guide and direct om·
counsels that we may do aright the things we have to do.

Bro. WILLIA.II: .A. D.a.vxs, from the Committee on Jurisprudence, presented the following report in regard to the affairs of Unity Lodge,
No.130:-

\

To the M,., W.·. Grand Lodge of California : Your committee, to whom, at the last Annual Communication, was referred the
papers relative to the arrest of the oharter of Unity Lodge, No. 130, located at San
Bernardino, in San Bernardino county, beg leave to report as follows:The information in regard to the affairs of that Lodge obtained by Past Master
JAMES H. LANDER, who was appointed a commissioner by the Grand Master to inquire into its alleged irregularities, appears to be full and conclusive as to tlie violation by said Lodge of the regulations of this Grand Lodge and of the general regu·
lations of Masonry. From this source your committee find the following:That Unity Lodge has conferred the degrees of Fellow Craft and Master Mason
upon an Entered Apprentice hailing from another jurisdiction, without a ballot being
had- the brother being declared elected by a viva vooe vote, and such vote being
t11ken within less than twelve months from the date of the same brother's rejection
by Unity Lodge :
That, when a petition was received and referred to a committee of investigation,
the record shows that, at the next stated meeting subsequent to its appointment,
two members of the committee being absent, they were discharged and a new com·
mittee was appointed, who, without investigation, reported instanter upon the peti·
tlon referred :
That, after a petition had been duly rejected by the Lodge, and a notice of such
rejection had been forwarded to the Grand Secretary, at the first subsequent stated
meeting after such rejection, the Master, Bro. H. C. RUSSELL, eaused said petitioner

28

Proceedings of the

[May 1~,

to be elected, closed the Master's Lodge, opened in the first degree, and initiated
said petitioner :
That very .little regard has been paid by Unity Lodge to the Constitution of this
Grand Lodge. On the contrary, persons believed to be clandestine Masons have
been admitted to visit the Lodge; and that too when the Master "was not satisfied
fully " (his own language) that the visitor was a legitimate Mason :
That the officers of the Lodge are totally unqualified for the position of teachers
of Masonry- not alone from a want of skill and knowledge in conferring degrees
and generally performing the duties of their respective stations, but also from a lack
of appreciation of the first principles of our order; for it is found from the record that
members were permitted to attend Lodge meetings fully armed with deadly weapons
for any emergency that might arise among such discordant materials:
That smoking during the working hours of the Lodge was a privilege enjoyed by
its members :
.And, as if the evils above enumerated were not enough, that brethren even appeared in the Lodge room, assisting in the work, who were so far intoxicated as to
be unable to keep their feet during the performance of their role.
Your committee cannot better express their views upon the affairs of Unity Lodge,
than by quoting the following language of Bro. J. H. LANDER, in closing his report
concerning its officers and members:"They have generally no conception of the purposes and dignity of the Order no sense of Masonic duty to check and allay personal differences; but all seem to
indulge their personal spites and piques -slandering, back-biting, and recriminating
as though Masonry had never been.''
In consideration of the foregoing, and in accordance with instructions from the
Grand Lodge, at its last .Annnual Commumcation, (See page 368, proceedings of
1862), your committee beg leave to present the following charges against Unity
Lodge, No. 130, located at San Bernardino, in San Bernardino County, and repre·
sented by Bros. H. C. RussELL, Master, BENJ. BARTON, Senior Warden, and l<'RANCIS
Mo KINNEY, Junior Warden ; such charges being for repeated violation of the Constitution of this Grand Lodge, and of the general regulations of Masonry:1st. In admitting to membership, by conferring the degrees of Fellow Craft and
Master Mason on Bro. M. KATZ, an Entered Apprentice Mason, hailing from San Diego
Lodge, No. 35, in this jurisdiction, no ballot being had, but he declared elected to
receive the degrees by a vive vooe vote, and such vote being taken within less than
one year from the date of his rejection by the same Lodge.
2d. In advising a committee to report upon a petition, without taking the time for
examination required by law; and in fact without any examination whatever.
3d. In conferring the degrees of Masonry upon ELI M. SMITH, after he had been
duly rejected by the Lodge, and notice of such rejection forwarded to the Grand
Secretary; one of said degrees having been conferred at the first subsequent stated
meeting after his rejection.
4th. In admitting clandestine Masons to yisit the Lodge.
5th. In permitting intemperance in the Lodge - the carrying of deadly weapons the use of threatening language between members- and a general disregard of the
,regulations and land marks of Masonry.
.All which is respectfully submitted.
WILLI.AM A. D.AVIES, Chairman.

roem bers being furnished with printed copies thereof:To the M.·. W.-. f}rand Lodge of Oalifornia : -

We have, to the best of our ability, endeavored to gather and present to the
Grand Lodge, for the instruction of the brethren, all the current useful information
which has come within our reach since the last Communication. We have sought, at
the same time, to continue the pleasant intercourse which our jurisdiction has enjoyed with the sister Grand Lodges in correspondence with ns; to acknowledge their
· courtesies, reciprocate kindly, and to greet them all with the earnest heart of soldiers
enlisted in the same good cause. If, in reviewing the various proceedings which
came before us, we have expressed opinions concerning usages and laws, it has been,
we trust, in strict deference and respect to opinioaq which according to our observation prevail in this jurisdiction, in reliance upon the Constitution, Regulations, and
the interpretation and construction given In reports of committees concurred in or
adopted. If, tempted, we have rashly allowed ourselves to venture upon a wider
•ea, it has been in dependence upon the old-fashioned Charges and Regulations, ap·
proved by time, and the light which shines upon us from that source, as our chart
and compass.
We acknowledge the receipt, and submit a report upon, the published transactions of the several Grand Lodges mentioned in the following list, which includes all
that were received at the time we finished our work.

CANADA.
This Grand Lodge has no permanent place of meeting. The seventh Annual
Communication commenced on the ninth day of ,July, 1862, at the town of St. Catharines, and continued at labor three days,-tl1e M.·. W.·. T. DouoLASS HARRINGTON,
Grand Master, presiding, and the R.·. W.·. THOMAS BIRD HARRIS acting as Grand

Secretary. Montreal is sele.cted as the place of meeting for the year 1863. One hundred and six chartered Lodges were represented : there are one hundred and fiftyfive on the roll.
The Grand Master expresses his loyal sympathy with his Most Gracious Sovereign,
the widowed Queen, in her sorrow, and with his nation, for the death of the " silent
father of our Kings to be,"-the Prince Consort. The Queen of England is the
danghter and niece of Grand Masters, KENT and SussEx. It is fresh in our memory
that in the midst of her grief the fearful and terrible catastrophe at the Hartley Coal
Mines took place. He recurs to 1ibis, and gracefully associates with the occasion the
sympathy of his craftsmen and their admiration of her deeds. He tells us that, "forgetful of her own sorrow, even at the time when it must have been most poignant,
she identifies herself with the widows of those humble, hard-working miners, who
had been cut off by a terrible visitation, and in her own misery remembered and
soothed theirs." The fraternity have reason to be proud of her affinity when she
nobly illustrates the principles of the Order which honored her father and uncle, and
we record the act in our annals with pleasure. He announces in words of fraternal
grief, the death of the of the M. ·• W.-. THOMAS Gnrns Rrnoi:;T, Past Grand Master of
Canada, whose memory and virtues they affectionately cherish; reports that the Order is pursuing its course of quiet, unobtrusive usefulness; granted two dispensations for new Lodges; chides certain Masters who have shown culpable carelessness
in conducting the ballot by allowing unworthy feeling to prevail among members on
such occasions and enter the ballot-box. He specifies that members have forgotten
themselves so far as to declare, beforehand, that because the proceedings of the
Lodge did not suit them they would stop the admission of candidates. He says that
it was the Master's duty to deprive such members for a time of their privileges, and
report them to higher authority. Such unmasonic spirit, evincing a determination
to destroy the harmony of the Lodge, would readily suggest to the Junior Warden,
or some other brother, in our jurisdiction, the great propriety of preferring charges;
and if proven, a.few months wandering in the cold would remind the offender of the
necessity of cultivating the use of that valuable instrument which teaches a lesson
so important and honest in regard to the management of onr infirmities of temper.
The secrecy and sanctity of the ballot is as the tomb; but if a member declares the
intention to perpetrate, or avows the commission of such an ill-spirited act, the more
prompt and stern the discipline is, the sooner be will be tanght to know what is right,
and that there is wholesome law and just judgment for snch offenses. He regrets
that the Grand Lodges of England and Ireland insist upon the good standing of the
insubordinates within his jurisdiction declared to be irregular, and that the former
shows an unjnst and unfriendly spirit in accusing the Grand Body over which be presides, of studious hostility and aggression. We fear that our noble brother, the Earl
of Zetland, who governs the Grand Lodge of England, is growing old and testy, and
commend our Canadian brother for sympathy to Grand Master DRUMMOND, who pre·
sides over the Grand Lodge of Maine.
The names and title of these Lodges will be found in this report, under the hea(l
of" Indiana," and the committee respectfully direct attention to the subject a~ a
matter for consideration.
Ten District Deputies show faithful and active attention to the duties assigned
them, and the reports present an interesting insight of the working of the jurisdic:
tion. We have read them with general satisfaction and pleasure, but observe in that of
the Deputy of Toronto District an opinion expre~sed which will find favor in the Grand
Lodge of Hamburg, but in regard to which we entertain entirely adverse and antagonistic views. It is, however, a subject which we have no occasion, happily, to di~­
cn~s here, and we hope never shall have, and therefore will not present it before our
Grand Lodge.

We will correct what may appear as an error in this favorable notice. While in 1861
we had one hundred and forty-eight charter numbers, and one Lodge under dispensa·

He takes "great pleasure in noticing the operations of that best of institutions
for doing good, the Masonic Board of Relief of the City of San Francisco ; " bnt the
most unacceptable thing is the announcement by the venerable chairman that his
last report is completed-his last record is closed up ; he goes into dignified retirement. Having held the office of Grand Secretary twenty-seven years, he declined reelection. We would like to quote all the language of his valedictory as he writes it,
but even now, benefited by his wisdom, we are trying to follow his example in using
our best endeavors to make our report" as brief as possible."
The Grand Lodge parted reluctantly with the veteran Grand Secretary ; passed a
feeling and kindly resolution in recognition of his worth and services, which absorbs
our sympathies.

DIST.RIOT OF COLUMBIA.
The Semi-annual Communication of this Grand Lodge for the year 18tll, was held
on the seventh day of May; the Aunual Communication on the fifth of November;
and that for installation on the twenty-seventh of December, at the City of Washington.
At the first-mentioned meeting, the M:. w.·. GEORGE c. WmTING presided, and a
vacancy having occurred in the of!ice of the Grand Secretary by the removal of the
R.-. W:·. G. A. SCHWARZMAN from the District, the R.-. W:. Josm;A T. TAYI,01< 1 who
was appointed in his stead, acted as Grand Secretary. The Grand Master read a correspondence which had taken place between himself and the Grand Secretary of
Rhode Island, in which he was informed that the Grand Master of that jurisdiction
ha.d issued a dispensation authorizing certain brethren serving in a regiment from hiK,
State at the Capital to meet from time to time, while serving in defence of Government, not for work, but for social intercourse and mutual instruction ; and the notifi·
cation is given, as is statetl, in order thathe may not be suspected of trespass. Grand
Master WmTING replies, very fraternally,saying that when they shall have organized,
if they desire to make Masons from their own ranks, he will, upon proper application, authorize them to do so, if the Grand Master of Rhode Island does not object;
and further states to his Grand Lodge, that he has been applied to by brethren, members of regiments from other States, for the privilege of holding occasional or camp
Lodges during their term of service for the purpose of mutual instruction and social
intercourse. This led to the adoption of the following resolution: "Resolved, That the Grand Lodge of the District of Columbia advise that the ;l/.'.
W:. Grand Master grant special dispensation.~ to guch regiments or corps of volunteers of the several States now in the service of the United States, in this jurisdiction, as he may deem proper, to hold occasional or camp_ Lodges;_ provi~ed, that
such dispensations shall only extend to the members of their respective regiments or
corps."
The Grand Lodge of Virginia did the same thing which our brethren of the District now propose; and Grand Master FELLOWE, of Louisiana, protested against the
act as an invasion of his jurisdiction. We have expressed an opinion agreeing with
the latter in this report. Our Grand Lodge holds to the doctrine that her sisters can
not use material from her qua1Ties without permission ; that is, citizens who claim

From the Address read by the acting Grand Master, we can easily learn the con·

pressed upon the Brethren, and, devoting more space to the consideration of that

his Grand Lodge. He condemns the facile disposition with which some of the snhor·
dinates set aside their by-laws and accept applications for membership and d~grees
as cases of emergency. In Indiana, the power which resides in a Grand M8.ster, to
judge of cases of emergency, is divided with the subordinate Lodges, and hy the
nnanimons vote of its members present a case of emergency can be made at any
time, and a ballot immediately proceeded with, either for initiation or membership.
The only traveling, or military Lodge, as they are called, from which they publish a
report, did not fail to consider every application presented to it a case of emergency.
Is not this a dangerous authority to entrust subordinates with?
Grand Master l<'RAVEL, when speaking of applicants entered, passed and raised
on the same evening, uses in his address, language, the force of which every committee-man who has had experience in the examination of visitors, will feel. Of such
an one, suddenly seized with an appreciative sense of its value, when about to travel
abroad among strangers, and who has thus received the degrees, he says : " he goes
into the world deceived and disappointed, deprived of his means without adequate
compensation. 'fhe facts are that this man has deceived himself, and Masonry has
been dishonored by the act." Has not the Lodge, Jet us ask, made itself the instrn·
ment by which the deception has been completed? 'fheir committee on Jnrispru<ience think that subordinates are safe judges, however, of cases of emergency, but at
the same time innocently say that if members would make themselves better acquainted with the Jaws as they stand, the Grand Master won!<} be relieved from much
onerous duty.
Dispensations to organize twenty-seven new Lodges were issued during the year,

From the reports of committees we select some items which may prove of inter·
est to our Craft._ A Lodge dispensed charity to the family of a brother, a member
of a neighboring Lodge, who had gone to the war, and then demanded to be reim·
bt1rsed hy the Lodge of which the brother was a memher ; but the hrother'A Lodge
declined to reimburse the Lodge which had assisted his family, and thereupon complaint was made to the Grand Lodge. The following resolution was reported by the
committee on Grievances, and adopted:" Resolv.ed, That a Grand Lodge has not the power of controlling the charity of
any subordmate Lodge, and the charity fund of each and every Lodge is under it•
own control."
In another case, the circumstances of which are not given, the same committee
affirm the principle more strongly in the following resolution, which was also en·
dorsed by the Grand Lodge :"Resolved, That this Grand Lodge has no power to interfere with or encumber tile
property of any subordinate Lodge in good standing."
As a general rule of action, we think these decisions are accepted as good ]\fa.
sonic law in our jurisdiction.
Our brethren of Indiana are determined to strictly obey the moral law, and we
find a subordinate sustained in its effort to discipline members engaged in retailing
spirituous liquors. We pity a brother who has been forced by circumstances into
such an occupation, for no true Mason at heart will select it from choice, but we can
not regard him as subject to discipline. It is contrary to the spirit of our institution,
which, besides being moral, contains an element of charity and liberality, that a

pressive instruction to regard and practice our policy of close scrutiny, he adds:"I trust it will not be inferred from the foregoing suggestions that I am opposed
to the extension of the principles of Masonry. From the exalted conceptions 1 have
of its noble designs, universal benevolence, and enlarged philanthropy, I could not
for a moment entertain such a sentiment. On the contrary, I have been ready to
put forth every laudable and legitimate effort to deepen its foundations and widen its
sphere of usefulness. My favorite maxim ever has been, and still is, let us open our
doors to the worthy and well qualified, who voluntarily knock for admission, but
close and hermetically seal them against the approach of the venal and treacherous."
The subject of non-affiliation and non-payment of dues, so nearly allied, concern·
ing whic'lt we will further on present the action of the Grand Lodge, is treated of in
both Addresses. It is one .which has given all the jurisdictions trouble, and we feel
pleasure that our brethren of Iowa have at last nearly perfected a system. The
Grand Master's declaration that he will hail the definite settlement of the question,
and the institution of more efficient regulations for enforcing payment of dues, as
an infallible indication of permanent prosperity of the Order, will find an echo in all
well regulated Lodges.
Uniformity of work claims his serious attention, and although he says in the first
Address that twelve months prior he entered upon his duties a novice in Masonry,
unacquainted alike with its ritual and jurisprudence, he has evidently studied closely
and grasped matters with a vigorous hand, showing much determination to place this
in process of final settlement. For this end we find him consulting the testimonies
of the past, from PREsTON to TUCKER, and, as politicians frame it, "sleeping" with
the venerable Grand Lecturer of Vermont, the R.·. w.·. SAMUEL WILSON, one of the
remaining links which connect the present and past, and hobnobbing with our active
Kentucky Bro. MORRIS. We wish him success in his undertaking, pleasant slumbers
and antique dreams with our venerable brother, and lively hours with the Kentuckian. We also congratulate the craftsmen that they have found one possessing will
and ability to pursue earnestly such a desirable end.
Without contenting ourselves, we turn reluctantly from the Addresses, not with·
out making an extract to show how deeply he feels, and how wisely he cautions
against an evil which, wherever it occurs, is the pouring forth of vitriol, and the
Lodge and its Master will lose their reputation when they fail to rebuke and punish.

The Grand Lodge of Kansas held its sixth Annual Communication in Topeka,
commencing on the fifteenth day of October, 1861, and was in session two days. Tile
1~r... W.·. RICHARD R. RHEES, Past Grand Master, was called to the Chair, and the R:.

The Address of the M.·. W.·. GEo. H. F;.rnoH1LD, was presented by the acting
Grand Secretary, and read. In it he states that urgent circumstances beyond his
control, requiring his presence in the East, render it impossible to be present at the
Communication, leaving him only time to report his official action for the year past.
He states that he had diyided the jurisdiction into two districts, making the Kansas
river the dividing line, and had appointed a District Deputy Grand Master for each;
that owing to important duties he had not been able, during the past year, to further
carry out the spirit of the letter of the recommendations adopted by the last Grand
Lodge, in reference to securing uniformity of work ; had granted dispensations for
the formation of two new Lodges-one in Nevada City, Colorado Territory-and ac·
knowledges receipt of $100,Masonic charity, sent by Masters' Lodge, No. 5, New
York, which he had dispensed to the poor and destitute when the State was suffering
from the effects of drouth.
The report of the Grand Secretary, the R.·. W.·. CHARLES MuNDEE, appears on
record, but unlike the Grand Master's, contains no explanation for his non-appearance. From it we learn, with sorrow, of the suffering which has afflicted ouryonnger
sister. He tells his Grand Lodge that the apology by the subordinates for non-pay·
ment of annual dues is, universally, that the drouth of the. past year has so impoverished the people that they are destitute of the means to pay with, and hence
the thoughtful and kindly charity of the Lodge at Albany. One Master returns the

He surrenders the property, "consisting of a letter G of magnificent proportions,

A series of resolutions was offered favoring the adoption of the custom of a sin·
gle ballot for the three degrees; but after discussion, they. were laid over nntil the
next Annual Communication. Our Constitution leaves it optional with the subordi·
nates whether to ballot for each degree separately, or all at one time. We decidedly prefer a separate ballot, and are as much in favor of it now as if, as in old time,
the first two degrees were conferred in the subordinate Lodges and the sublime de·
gree in the Grand Lodge. A majority of our Lodges, however, practice the single
ballot, and some of our most promlnent brethren are advocates of the custom.
A resolution was offered, and referred to a commlttee, which declares that where
a Lodge is reduced in numbers," by dimisslon or other casualties," to Jess than seven
members, it should not work a forfeiture of its charter, provided they pay dues.
The resolution was begotten by a case in point, where a Lodge unfortunately was
only four tin:les better off than the razor-strop man : it had four more left. We think
the Senior Warden working on the ground floor will be nonplused if the resolution is
adopted. Our Grand Lodge, by an established regulation, prohibits the subordinates
under its jurisdiction from transacting business, other than conferring degrees, with
a Jess nnmber than seven members present.

granting them full power to confer degrees. He very justly observes, if permanent
Lodges, with all their facilities for obtaining correct knowledge of applicants, fail
many times in their efforts to select none but the good and worthy, how can a Lodge
in a community where each is a stranger to the other, comparatively, expect to
succeed?

KENTUCKY.
In the month of October, 1862, commencing on the twentieth day, this Grand
Lodge commenced its Annual Communication for the sixty-third time. It was organized with difficulty, many of the subordinates having failed to pay their dues for two
or three years, neglected to send representatives, and disobeyed notifications. A
committee was appointed to confer with the Grand Master upon the question, What
constitutes a constitutional number of Lodges? The committee reported the total
number of Lodges t-0 be three hundred and sixt.een; that the number laboring under
disability was one hundred and forty; and the. number in good standing, one hundred and seventy-six. Of those in good standing, there were in attendance eightyfour; and in order to organize, th" committee recommended that the Grand Master
suspend the labors of one hundred and thirty-eight Lodges, which was done. The
roll being then called, it appeared that more than one third of the active Lodges
were represented, and the Grand Lodge was opened,-the M:. W.·. HIRAM BASSETT,
Grand Master, presiding, and the R.'. W.·. JoHN M. Tonn, Assistant Grand Secretary,
acting as Grand Secretary.
In his Address, the Grand Master alludes to the progress of Masonry since the
year 1800, when there were five Lodges west of the Alleghanies, and less than two
hundred Masons in all Mississippi Valley, -while now there are more than three
thousand Lodges and one hundred thousand Masons. Two applications to form new
Lodges were made during the year, but they were denied upon constitutional
grounds. Many applications for dispensations to confer degrees were made, but all
declined for want of authority. He announces the death of two Past Grand Masters,
--the M.·. w.·. THOMAS WARE, and the M:. w... HENRY WINGATE; urges economy,
points out the causes of unnecessary expense, and advises that the publication of
names of members of subordinates be dispensed with. The Grand Lodge did not
take his advice, for which we think the other jurisdictions will be thankful, because
these lists have proved a valuable and safe source of reference. Re also recommends the condensation of the reports of the committee on Correspondence, which
was concnrred in ; but they did not vote to the committee the finer faculties required
to make a short report. He says, in view of the difficulties they labor under, lenien·
oy ought to be shown to the Lodges, and all possible encouragement given to them
to keep their charters. The Masonic University, for a while closed through the influences of war, has been reopened under the auspices of Bro. RoBERT MORRIS. The subject of uniformity of work is referred to as an important matter of consideration; he
claims that the :Masons of Kentucky can boast of having once had the old Prestonian
lectures, their rituals came from Virginia as far back as 1785; that when T:a:OMAS
SMITH WEBB was in the State, thirty years later, he is known to have endorsed their
ceremonies then practiced, as coincident with his teaching, and JEREMY L. CRoss,
who was there about the same time, assisted in impressing the system," almost nni·
versally admitted to be the old and genuine one." In this connection he suggests the
annual exemplification of Degrees, and rehearsal of lectures in Grand Lodge as
due to "the young and intelligent class with which our Lodges are largely filled."
He cantions the Craft against interference with politics and religion, grieves to find
that Brethren in his jurisdiction have conceived the idea that what they deem political of!ences--crimes against State or civil government-are breaches of M:asonic obligations, and finally directing their attention to the ancient charge concerning civil
magistrates, concludes with much good advice and an expression of the opinion that
it is not the province of Masonry to protect or punish her votaries who may be offenders again.it the State, but leaves them where they belong, to the civil authorities.

"On the fourteenth of June, 1858, a majority of Polar Star Lodge, N?. 1, formed

" The principles decided in these cases are, that though ~nl'. of the members of
the Lodge may withdraw at pleasure, yet, even though a ma.ionty should do so, or
should even vote to dissolve the Lodge, the vote would be of no avail; nor would
the Lodge be dissolved, if a sufficient number should remain to carry on its func·
tious · that a vote of the Lodge can not dissolve it; and that the only way a Lodge,
being' a chartered institution, could be dissolved, would be by the action of the
founder, the Grand Lodge, the State, or courts of justice ~eclarm~ the charter_ ~or­
feited: that all the rights and franchises of the I,odge continued with the remainmg
members who, in fact, would constitute the corporation: that the very attemp~ at
dissolving the Lodge, declaring its charter canceled, and forming themselves mto
another corporation of the same name, was as e!l:ectual a withdrawal as could be,
and required no further act on their part, or of a motion on the part of others, to
bring about a complete severance of their connection with the Lodge.
" The decision of our highest judicial tribunal in these cases has forever fixed the
status of the Grand Lodge and its constituents, as well as the rights ef property h_eld
by them and all other similar corporations, and will have a great infiuence m setthng
all ou't Masonic difficulties."

Grand Master MELLEN, of :Mississippi, who was shocked at reading an account in
the papers of a Masonic Baptism held in the City of New Orleans, now some three
years since, that he is mistaken in supposing the ceremony alluded to was a part of
Masonry, or ever supposed to be such, in Louisiana ; and further add that it was only
a ceremony performed by Masons for, in their view, laudable purposes.
We can not help sharing the feelings of Grand Master MELLEN when Masons pub·
licly engage in a ceremony which i• not "a part of Masonry," and therefore in an
unmasonic act. Masons, as such, have no right to engage publicly or privately in
ceremonies which are not Masonic. 'In our jurisdiction we believe that Grand Master
BELCHER would interpose his authority to prevent such proceedings. Without disrespect to the religious sentiment of our He brew brethren, we might ask if a Mason·
ic circumcision would not be a queer ceremony, as well as an act disrespectful to
Jewish customs? and may not the faithful and devoted Christian, who loves his sac·
raments witb the same fervor, feel as Grand Master MELLEN has expressed it, that
it was" a sort of travestie of the Christian ordinance," and witl1 such feeling will
not his respect for onr fraternity diminish ?

Little outside of the regular order of business was transacted. An opinion as to
the nature, powers, and privileges of a Lodge under dispensation, was submitted by
the Grand Master. Under the dispensation, the brethren who are empowered can
form and open a Lodge after the manner of, if not as, Masons and can then make
M_asons according to ancient usage. This he conceives to be the full extent of their
power. Their presiding officers are not entitled to rank as Past Masters, nor are
they privileged to vote in Grand Lodge ; they can not elect officers or perpetuate
themselves; they can not add to the number of their members, nor fill vacancies ;
their initiates are not returned to the Grand Lodge as members, but only as initiates; dues can not accrue against them. This is the estimate which he places upon
these inchoate bodies in his jurisdiction. Our organic law differs from the ruling iu
Maryland. Such a Lodge here is not constituted with the formality of a chartered
Lodge ; its officers are not installed ; the governing officer obtains no rank as a Past
Master; it can, however, send delegates to the Grand Lodge, who may be admitted
to seats and be permitted to speak, but not vote ; it can make Masons and receive
members l1y affiliation ; it can adopt its own rules, which become by-laws when approved by its creator; it is subject to the will of the Grand Master when the Grand
Lodge is not in commuuication, and he can, as the chief executor of the constitutional power of the jurisdiction, at will take away the breath of its feeble existence.
It is his creature. We are aware that within the borders of our sister of Maryland a
Kentiment exists which places the Grand Master beside the Holy Father of Rome in
his infallible character, and therefore we receive his opinion with great respect as
nnt~ority th~re ; but with us many matters of domestic concern, this among them,
which remam unsettled and undefined elsewhere, have been prescribed in a written
!1onstitution as the basis of our local government.

An interesting case was decided, and we notice it becanse_the question is consid.
ered, whether a Grand Lodge should, upon reversing or setting aside a judgment of
expulsion or suspension of a member of a Lodge, on account of its illegality or injustice, order his restoration to membership in tJ1e Lodge which disciplined him? A
member rendered himself obnoxious to his Lodge by acts so unfriendly to its bar.
mony and prosperity that a continuation of his membership was considered incon·
8istent with its interest. 'l'he Lodge " terminated " his membership by proceedingR
which satisfied the Grand Lodge, the effect of which seemed designed simply to con·
elude his membership in the Lodge which di;;cip!ined him, without effecting his stand·
ing elsewhere,- divesting him only of the privilege of voting and speaking in the
Lodge of which he had been a member. Upon appeal, the committee to whom the
case was referred, decided that the Grand Lodge had no jurisdiction over member·
ship of members in subordinate J,odges, and cite their Constitution in proof, which
declares that" when the Grand Lodge shall reverse or abrogate the decision of a
subordinate I,odge suspending or expelling a brother from the privileges of Masonry,
he shall not thereby be re~tored to membership within the body from which he was
suspended or expelled without its unanimous consent." The propriety of conceding
to a subordinate the right to be the sole and exclnslve judge of the qualification of
its members we have never doubted, and we willingly strengthen the position by
adding a precedent. We allude to the trouble between Antiquity Lodge and the
Grand Lodge of England, which occurred over eighty years ago, and which, unhap,

1863.J

Grand Lodge of Oalifornia.

53

pily, was not reconciled for ten years afterwards. That venerable Lodge expelled
three memhers; the Grand Lodge interfered and ordered them to be restored ; it refused to comply," the members conceiving themselves ·competent and sole judges
in the choice of their own members." It is true that in the long discussion which
then arose, the original question was soon lost sight of, and more important ones
were raised, and finally the difficulty was healed by curing a complaint which was
the result and not the original cause of controversy. This shows that the claim of
a subordinate to be the sole j\ldge of its conditions of membership is not of very re·
cent origin, but was discussed early in the fourth quarter of the last century. As far
as the decision of the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts goes on the point of leaving
subordinates to judge of the qualifications of members, it is sustained by precedent
tind usage, and is an admitted necessity by which a Lodge preserves harmony, and
protects itself from the imposition of unacceptable and uncongenial members. But
suppose a Grand J,odge, upon considering an appeal," reverses and abrogates the
decision of a subordinate suspending or expelling a brother," on account of illegality, informality, or injustice of the proceedings. The case then would stand as if no·
thing bad occurred, but the brother who had been dealt with under the Constitution
of Massachusetts could not again appear in the subordinate Lodge as a member with·
out its unanimous consent, and if he failed to get that, it appears to us under their
law he would be wronged without a remedy, and deprived of his standing in the
Lodge where the complaint and proceeding against him had been "reversed and
abrogated" by supreme authority. If he wishes to withdraw, he is told unanimous
eonsent has not restored him to membership, and of course he can not withdraw if
he is not a member. He is not suspended or expelled, because the Grand Lodge
has "reversed and abrogated the decision'' against him, and yet he can not present
the proof to another Lodge he may desire to affiliate with to show that he is in good
standing. Where then shall he apply for justice? In order to deprive a brother or
a member of any right or privilege, it must of course be done legally, and if a Grand
(,odge" reverses or abrogates'' the proceedings on account of illegality, informali·
ty, or injustice, the brother complained of ought to stand exactly where he did be·
fore. In our jurisdiction the organic law provides that the Grand Lodge may at any
Annual Communication, if good cause therefor be shown, restore a Mason ,wh~ has
been suspended or expelled witllin its jurisdiction, but such restoration shall not i:e·
store him to membership in the Lodge by which he was suspended or expelled. This
pre-supposes that the accused brother has admitted the regularity of the proceedings against him, or that upon appeal the Grand Lodge has afllnned the decision of
the subordinate. The restoration is a pardon, but it does not re-possess him of his
offices. He is again an accepted member of Masonic society ; he may be permitted
to visit the same family; but he is not now entitled to counsel and advise with the
members concerning their domestic matters, without their unanimous consent. He
must win the privilege of membership again, which it is now his duty and should lie
his pride to do, by evidences of obedience, subordinution, and regard for the principles of the Order violated by him. Our subordinates are only permitted to restore
their suspended Masons. We think the doctrine correctly laid down by Grand Mas·
ter 8IMONS, of New York, in a decision recently made: that when the Grand Lodge
reverses the finding of a Lodge for irregularity or want of proof, the defendant there·
by becomes entitled to all the rights and privileges he enjoyed before charges were
preferred against him.

NEBRASKA.
The fifth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Nebraska Territory was
held at Omaha on the third day of June, 1862,-the M.'. w... GEORGE ARMSTRONG
presiding as Grand Master, and the R.·. w.·. R. c. JORDAN acting as Gra·nd Secretary
pro tempore. We have never received a copy of their proceedings for 1861.
Every chartered Lodge but one was represented. From the Address of the Grand
Master, we have tidings that harmony prevails, and the Lodges are flourishing in a
greater degree than could have been anticipated in the present distracted state of
the country. He announces the issue of dispensations to form two new Lodges ;
presents for the consideration of the Grand Lodge, "Proceedings of the Masonic
Convention to organize the Grand Lodge of Colorado Territory," and suggests in
connection therewith the natural withdrawal from the jurisdiction of two of their
snbordinates located in Colorado,-Bummit, No. 7, and Bock:y Mountain, No. 8,and the propriety of recognizing and welcoming the new organization into the fami·
ly of Grand Lodges. He granted a dispensation authorizing the second and third
degrees to be conferred on several persons who were moving westward, and who
had not sufficient time to comply with the local regulations. Acknowledging his reluctance, and giving good reasons why it should not be done, h~ nevertheless granted the dispensations, with the condition that the novitiates should be well instructed
before commencing their travel. In our experience as a Mason, we have seen so
much of the evil effects of dispensations in such cases, that we have grown almost
unmasonlcally stern and uncompromising in our opposition to all easy methods of
making Masons, and we recognize in these sudden applications and new-born aspi·
rations to be listed upon the roll of our ancient and honorable Order, only that mercenary spirit which, looking clear-sighted for the benefits, totally disqualifies a man
from ever becoming a real Mason, even though he should have received the degre-es.
Passing shabbily from the quarries to the presence chamber, storing the memory by
rote with the ritual, without comprehending the spirit or ever discovering the grand,
the noble, and the beautiful, which underlies, no more makes a Mason, than memorizing the signs of the zodiac, and the Chaldee and Syriac characters, would have made
a. mague for Belshazzar; hence, while acknowledging the existence of the high pre·

The Report on Correspondence is from the familiar pen of Bro. JosEPll H. Hoi;oH,
Grand Secretary, reviewing proceedings of twenty-seven Grand Bodies in an inter·
esting manner. Ours is very fully noticed. He takes occasion, in considering the
report of Rhode Island for the year ending June, 1861. to express an opinion con·
cerning traveling Lodges in connection with the army now in the field; and as there
is already developed a difference of opinion, we p1·esent his view of the subject. He
says:" The Address of the Grand Master (i. e. of Rhode Island) reports having granted
an application for a dispensation for a traveli
e to be attached to the Rhode
Island Regiment, to be styled 'American
e'; having authorized the applicants to hold such a Lodge, and to do all~
usiness except the making of
Masons, and to make returns of their meetings to the Grand Lod/le with their rec·
ords. He states that the action has met the unqualified approbat10u of the Grand
Master of the District of Columbia. This is a subject of some considerable moment.
The regiment with their, traveling Lodge may go or be ordered to Virginia, or some
other State. To hold a Lodge in the territory or jurisdiction of another State, we
believe to be unmasonic ; as between Masons there are no difficulties in this Union,
and we as such must treat them as brothers, by not doing what they would not do
under similar circumstances. Have we not all acknowledged that State lines are the
territory exclusively belonging to the Grand Lodge of the States? and do we not expect that they on their part will be true to their vows? But if we encroach upon
them by founding Lodges, traveling or otherwise, we violate a principle which has
never been questioned. The &"\-and Lodge of Ham burg granted a warrant to Py·
thagoras Lodge, located in the City of New York, which has been universally condemned by all the American Grand Lodges, and very properly so; and we can not
but see that this matter of making traveling Lodges to meet on the territory of another is of very doubtful propriety."
The Grand Lodge concurred in the opinion of the Grand Master and the commit·
tee, for we find that it refused to adopt the report of the committee on .Turisprndence
and Charity, to whom had been referred that portion of the Grand Master's Address,
in which the latter committee recommended that dispensations be granted upon con·
ditions, to wit: that the application be made in proper roim, and proof to the satis·
faction of the Grand Master that the granting of the warrants will not tend to dam·
age the interest of the Grand Lodge.
We ehoose to express an opinion concerning tile propriety, rather than· the legality, at this time. Sad experience in the past has taught us that" Masonry hath al·
ways been injured by war, blood-shed, and confusion," and we believe that any act
o!' a Grand Lodge which can be construed by another as au evidence of unkind feeling, will now inflict a corroding wound which years of nursing will not heal if we
should commJt an error. The history of our Order on this continent will never prob·
ably present an occasion which will require a greater exercise of wisdom to preserve harmony than the present; and as we have been in our intercourse honest and
true in respect for the jurisdictional rights of others, we will not be consistent, at
least, if we do not agree that there is impolicy-saying nothing of the legality~
in permitting brethren, by the authority of our seal, to hold a Lodge within the recognized limits of a sister jurisdiction of an American State. We believe that such
an act would damage the interest and reputation of our Grand Lodge, and accom•
plish no good which can not be done by individual Masons who are lovers of our
whole Fraternity wheresoever dispersed. In expressing our opinion we do so tolerantly, especially when there is such contrariety of sentiment, finding ourselves dif·
fering from some of the ablest and most distinguished Grand Lodges in America :
we may mention New York and Massaclrnsetts.

The complaint by New Jersey of the invasion of her jurisdiction seems to have
caused some embarrassment iu the absence of any regulatiou defining what is a residence. If the Grand Lodges of the country would do as we have done, incorporate
in their several Constitutions the provision that" no Lodge in this State shall receive
an application for the degrees of Masonry, unless the applicant shall have been a
resident within the State during twelve months, and within the jurisdiction of the
Lodge during six months next preceding the date of his application," the gre.at
wheels of our noble machinery would revolve with regularity that would not be disturbed by one ill-shapen cog. We take the liberty of making a broad-cast suggestion here, at the risk of being again called "a good big girl"; because while th_e
question is agitated and discussed, and so fresh in the mind of the Grand Lodges, it.
is most likely to receive the attention its importance deserves. The Grand Lodge ?f
New York at this Communication adopted a regulation which establishes the rule m
its-jurisdiction.
From the various decisions made by the Grand Master, and approved by the committee to whose consideration they were referred, we present the following: an E.
A. must be tried before a commission of Master Masons; when charges are preferred through the Junior Warden, a brother on trial has a righ,t to kno~ ~he name of
his real accuser ; when bias is charged against one or more comm1ss10ners, they
should resi""n. and others be named in their place, or triers appointed to test it, and
the defend:nt given an opportunity to show cause ; (it has been held in our jurisdiction that it is too late to challenge for bias after the commissioners have assembled
for trial : it is the duty of the members to attend and see that no biased commissioner is elected:) that a Mason may be tried for fraud in procuring admission to the
Order purposely withholding knowledge of an offense committed prior to his application· a certified copy of the record of a conviction of felony is sufficient evidence
for pr;secution; when the Grand Lodge reverses the finding of a subordin~te for irregularity or want of proof, the defendant there by beco~es en~itled to all rights and
privileges he enjoyed before charges were preferred agamst him; that the ballot for
each degree separately is an undeuiable right when demanded, but where the ballot
for the first degree has already been taken, the right to demand applies only to the
remaining degrees unless cause be shown; that in the absence of the Master and
Wardens of a Lodge, authority does not revert to a Past Master, nor can the Lodge
supply the place; that any Master of a Lodge, or other ~ason ent~ring '.nto.a combination, secret or otherwise, for the purpose of teachmg and d1ssemmatmg any
other system of work than that approved by the Grand Lodge, and taught _by the
Grand Lecturer and his assistants, is guilty of violating his covenant and subJect to
<:liscipline ;-a just rebuke to the "Conservators of Masonry." He expresses himself
very fully on the subject of physical qualifications of applicants, and is in favor of a
strict construction of the Old Regulations, and leaving the matter to the judgment
and discretion of the Grand Master. The committee so fully agreed with him in this,
that they declared that no Grand Officer or Grand Lodge can change the rule, and
applications to the former for construction are only in vain; in other words, " Remove not the ancient landmarks." He reprehends the disposition manifested for

The Report on Correspondence, prepared by the R.-. W:. E1,LICOTT Ev ANS, reviews the proceedings of forty-two Grand Bodies, including ours. In it is gathered
11nd presented, with discrimination and perspieuity, whatever of interest has taken
place in other jurisdictions worthy of the attention of his brethren. Declining to
"nter into discussion of the decree of non-intercourse promulgated by the Grand
Louge of Virginia against the New York brethren on account of the Union of 1858,
he says, with force and justice : " it does, however, seem singular, and a little hard
that one Grand Lodge-Pennsylvania-should have refused to recognize our brethren
11H Masons, while a split existed in our Grand Lodge, and that another should ndopt
I.he same rule because that division is healed"; nn illustration of the dangerous reMponsibility incurred in passing judgment upon 'the domestic mntters of a body supreme in itself.
We lean toward the Grand Lodge of Virginia in our opinion, which is based upon
I.he statement and history of the matter so far as the Grand Lodge of New York has
chosen to publish it, regarding the mode by which the schismatics were healed ;
nrivertheless, our confidence in the ability and learning of the Grand Lodge of New
York, and the known purity of character of many whose names grace its roll of
c:rand Officers, convinces us that they have ncted with a better appreciation of all
the circumstances than any other body could possibly have, and with a full sense of
I.lie dignity and nobility of our Order.
We do not, however, in this connection, admit that a Grand Lodge should not
1.l1ke cognizance of gross and violent departure from Masonic usage, tampering wit-h
I.he land-marks, or the prostitution of its uses for unhallowed purposes, if such things
Hhould be attempted by another Grand Body; for there is somewhere a line of denrnrcation to show when eomity ceases and the duty of self-preservation commences,
which we can not now undertake fully to define. Can it be supposed, however, for
llTI instant, that if a WEISHAUPT or a KNIGGE, with insidious genius, should attain
power in the East, and infuse his subtle influence throughout his jurisdiction, that
1•atholic Masonry would not seal that body, even as the bee encloses the obnoxious
Intruder into her hive with a waxen tomb, that the pestilential exhalations might not
Infect the pure atmosphere of our consecrated temples? The present condition of
M11Honry in Prance indicates that there is danger of its abuse, and the time may come
.vet when the Grand Lodges of the world will be called on to express disapproval,
or even go farther: we pray that it may be forever averted.

"The facts in discussion may be definitely stated. In the year 1851 the Grand

Lodges in the State of New York solely consisting of German Masons, and working in

in June next,' that bein'g the first meeting of the Grand Lodge of N cw York after
the receipt of the .M.·.W.·. Bro. BUEK's letter, at which action upon'the proposition. under our Constitution, could be taken. Another letter was written by the Grand Master of New York to tl1e Grand Master of Hamburg, in the month of January, 1851, containing views similar t-0 the above, and saying: 'I do most earnestly, then, dear brethren, beg of you to pause. Lodges.'
