"We may here as well reply to the evasion of Hamburg, of the charRe of encour·
aging negro Masonry in the United States. We think that when a Grand Lodge
claims a right to establish subordinate Lodges in a foreign country without the consent of the Grand Lodges of that country-When it calls attention to the wrongs ol'
negro Masons-when it claims that Masonry is not limited to the free-born, and when
it takes upon itself to legitimatize and assume Grand Lodge relations over a clandes·
tine Lodge in Brazil, and gives as an excuse that the Grand Lodge of Brazil has not
been cordial to her-that it is worse than ridiculous to charge us with slander and
falsehood in assuming that she threatens to adopt negro Lodges in t11is cou11try. lt
is a mere subterfuge to pretend that all she wishes is to know whether the negro
Lodges now in existence are legitimate when she claims the right to make Masons of
liberated negro slaves and to establish Lodges within our jurisdiction.
"In reference to the latter right the Grand Lodge of Hamburg gives us a si11gular
reading of the golden rule in saying that she is ready to grant us the same privilege.
Her version would be something thus: 'Whatever you have done to others, claim
that from them.' If another has a riglit to what you covet, grant him that same right
which he don't want, and the right you covet becomes lawfully yours.
"We thought we had settled the question two years ago of the New York Grand
Lodge being a party to the treaty which Hamburg so constantly quotes as her authority, but it seems she can't understand that the Supreme Council of the 33d is not
the same body as the Grand Lodge. She seems just now to think she can evade that
argument by assuming that the Supreme Council she alluded to is defunct, and that
the Grand Lodge is her successor and thus bound by her acts as by those of her legitimate predecessor. But lt is not worth while to waste any more words where
there is a determination to misconstrue. We have contradicted what, under the circumstances, was a slander npon 11'1.·. w. .. Bro. Knm, and that was our 8ole object in
allowing this matter again to come before the Grand Lodge."
Our jucisdiction, as will be seen by reference to its 6th Regulation, long since
promptly acted in the matter, and we not only have no misgiving in sustaining our
brethren of New York on the main question, and all the issues, but we admire and
commend their able and intelligent defence, and in the papers we have had access
to, discover nothing but what we should have been proud to have done so well as a
duty to the true interests of the Order, except the use of some bitter words; and
even in that is shown the high influence of our tenets which teach us to keep our
passions within due bounds, for the feeling betrayed is honest and virtuous indignation, rather than malignant temper.

In his Address, the Grand Master announces the death of the W.·. Brothers PELEG
CLARK, TULLY DORRANCE, PELEG RlIODES, SULLIVAN BALLOU, JOSEPH J. T!LL!NGIIAST.
and CALEB KELTON, who were members of the Grand Lodge. In the matter of the
Convention proposed at one time" to be held at Louisville, Kentucky, to consult on the
state of the country, after giving the proposition careful consideration he came to the
deliberate conviction that it was extra Masonic in its character, that it would be
through political action lllo.ne that they could hope or expect to influence the public
mind, and such interference would place the Order in a false position. He deemed
it his duty to pass the circular unnoticed, and his Yiews were concurred in by the
Grand Lodge. He directs their attention to a matter of grave importance, affecting
the rights of Masons in a manner new to him: the subordinates of a neighborng ju·
risdiction suspended, without notice, five brethren members of a Lodge under his
care, two of whom were members of the Grand Lodge. He adds, if these proceed·
ings shall be sustained, the practical effect will be to limit the rights and privileges
of Masons to the jurisdiction in which they were initiated. As the facts are not
clearly before Grand Master BALLOi:, we confide the subject to our successors, who
will doubtless furnish our Grand Lodge with further information when received. A
healthy increase, characterized by more watchful care to exclude unworthy persons,
is acknowledged.
One of the traveling Lodges connected with the army returns its dispensation.
The Master is commendably jealous of the integrity of the Order, and states as the
reason for giving it up that time was lacking to attend creditably to the work, and
that no place sufficiently easy of access, and secluded from intercourse, could be secured.
The Grand Lodge of Instruction for the purpose of obtaining, preserving, and
promulgating the work and lectures of Masonry, mentioned by our predecessors in
their report last year, !ms been chartered, and was organized on the twenty-seventh
January, 1862, at Providence. It will meet quarterly, and the work adopted, when
approved by the Grand Lodge, becomes official. A very stringent "regulation was
adopted at the time that this new organization was granted a charter, to the effect
that any Lodge neglecting or refusing to obtain and conform to such work and lectures may be suspended by the Grand Master. In a small jurisdiction, like that of
our Rhode Island sister, so strict a rule may succeed; but where subordinates are
established several hundred miles from the place of meeting of the Grand Lodge,
we fear the Grand Master would suspend some of them on account of non-conformity growing ont of inability rather than wilful neglect or refusal to obtain the work.
A resolution on this subject was referred at our last Annual Communication to the
committee on Jurisprudence, with instruction to report to the same meeting for which
we prepare this report.
A resolution was passed prohibiting dual membership, a practice imperatively
forbidden with ns. ·The several propositions to amend their Constitution, reducing
the number of meetings of the Grand Lodge, admitting the exchange of representatives with sister Grand Lodges; printing their early records, a copy of which our
Bro. Grand Secretary would highly appreciate, and for it heartily reciprocate, were
referred to the quarterly meeting in August.

The W.· · Bro. 'fnmus A. DOYLE again presents the Report of the committee on
Correspondence, reviewing the proceedings of twenty-four Grand Lodges. Ours receives favorable notice. They continue to oppose in decided terms the general
measures adopted in other jurisdictions in reference to the non·payment of dues,
nnd declare the opinion that the evil sought to be remedied is not so great as the
HVil created by the infliction of penalties to cure it. We feel and appreciate the danger which the alarming increase of suspended and expelled Masons threatens, but
•lo not attribute it to the disciplinary measures. Jt is to the recklessness with which
petitions for initiation have been granted of late years, and the indiscriminate issue
of dispensat.ions of all kinds, and for all purposes. These are prominent among the
potent causes which have operated, we believe, upon the Grand LodgeM, and urged
t.hem. to the adoption of sucl1 necessary acts. If every brother who undertakes the
responsibility of recommending 11 friend as worthy to be trusted with the mysteries
of our Order, will first honestly and justly, as it is his duty to do, measure him by
the intellectual, physical, moral, and social standard required, we believe there would
he fewer expelled or suspended Masons, or members of Lodges stricken from the
roll for non-payment of dues. Bro. GEORGE L. BARRY, of the Georgia committee,
who probably has not as much respect for antiquities as we have, has drawn a picture of our Rhode Island brethren, and says they are "old fogies who have for year8
maintained the even tenor of' their way," yet wise and instructive in their words.
There may be something more than persiflage in this, for we suspect that our good
Hister has dwelt so long under the parental roof, and the family has been taught ~o
many " wise and instructive " lessons, that they have grown confirmed in the kimlhearted man's sentiment, that men are radically good. If they bad shared some of
the experience of our young jurisdiction, upon which we have yet to keep a curll,
and had dealt as we were compelled to do in former year~, with hordes of M11sonic
peddlers, mendicants, and Masons made for our market like the gourd vine of the son
of Amittai,-the work of a night,-- and imposed upon us by the old fogies across
the mountains, we think that they would entertain more favorable ideas of the corrective legislation so generally pursued. We agree fully with the committee that too
many Lodges are permitted to be established ; that they have their origin too fre·
quently in the desire of a few who are anxious to wear the jewels of office, an<l
heartily endorse their words magnifying the great importance and dignity which at1.aches to the office of Master; we take them upon our own lips : " Greater scrutiny should be exercised in the selection of the material for the
work ; none but the most worthy should be placed in the oriental chair, and tlte East
should be treated according to its design, as the source of light illuminating the
Lodge, so that thereby the members, realizing its power, may be drawn within its
inllt1ence, and thus the principles of Masonry will become implanted in their hearts,
111Hl in due time the fruit thereof will ·be apparent in their daily walk and conversation ; the fraternal bond, instead of snapping asunder at the slightest shock, will
withstand the rudest assaults, and growing stronger day by day and year by year, it
will be found that such Masons will need no edict of a Grand Lodge to compel their
11Uention to duty."

We feel, too, that the fraternal bond is now being subjected to very heavy tension, but our faith in the continued ability of our Order to stand, as it ever has, true
to its ancient professions, is unabated and unfaltering; especially when from the temples comes up one unanimous voice, pledged devotedly to Ijlaintain, support, and
practice the tenets which bind us together, eschewing all profane matters with which
ae Masons we have no concern. But these very edicts impressing the importance of
"attention to dnty ," constitute the check-rein upon the thoughtless and heedless who
m:i.y err; and the idea of existing without them sounds very supernatural to us.
When the necessity ceases, we will accept it as a fact that men are radically good-that Utopia is no mythical realm-that the millennial day has come
By gilled minds foretold,
When men shall live by reason,
And not alone by gold ;
When man to man united,
And every wrong thing righted,
The whole world shall be lighted
As Eden was of old ;
- but, respectfully, not till then.

VERMONT·
Green sprigs of cypress and acacia are interwoven with the proceedings. of the
Grand Lodge of this State for the year 1862. A mourning page too sadly remmds us
of one preeminent, whose mortal part rests beneath the dull cold marble, and whose

A committee appointed to purchase aprons and sashes to complete the "regalia"
of the Grand Lodge, made a verbal report, which was adopted. Somewhere we saw
this expression roughly handled by a Masonic writer, and we wish that he had so
disabled it that it might never again have made its appearance in such respectable
company as we now find it. We think in no sense is it correctly a Masonic term, and
the definition by the lexicographer shows it to be inapposite ; it denotes the ensign
of royalty, the apparatus of a coronation, as the crown, sceptre, &c., and by no
means conveys the modest and pure idea which the symbol of the lambskin teaches.
'l'he regulations in olden times required that" every new brother at his making is
decently to clothe the Lodge," and such old-fashioned, honest Masonic English ought
not to be forgotten or surrendered for phrases belonging to modern fraternities. We
do not remember but one instance in ou,r limited observation where we thought it
was properly used, and then only in a facetious connection. At our last Annual
<:ommunication an invitation was sent from Bro. DANIEL N ORCRoss, of San Francisco,
who is noted for his taste in the manufacture of "regalia," as well as Masonic
clothing and jewels, requesting the brethren of the Grand Lodge to be present at the
opening of his new store under our Temple. When the Grand Secretary delivered
it, a witty brother, associating the invitation with ideas of refreshment, desired to
know sotto 'Voce if we were to be regaled. It may be palatable when applied to
such internal qualifications for a man, but in its external application we are unfriendly to its use.

WASHINGTON.
The fourth Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge was held at Olympia, commencing-second September, 1861, closing fifth idem. The M.·. W.·. BELUCIUS GAR·
FIELDE, Grand Master, presided, the W.·. R:. THOMAS M. REED being Grand Beere
tary.
The proceedings show that this is a well governed and disciplined jurisdiction,
and though young in years, with a short roll of members, its transactions and regu·
lations evince order and discipline, and manifest determination to guard and preserve the temple from evil infiueftces which surround it.
The Grand Master, in his Alldress, pays a truthful tribute to the disinterested and
lofty aims of our Order, and defining with clearness its true mission, reminds his
craftsmen that
- - "these high ends are attainable only through a well-digested system of de·
tails, each and all of which must be kept properly arranged and in harmonious play
with each other. These details require constant attention from those having jurisdiction, in order to keep the entire machinery in motion and to work out the grand
ends and aims of our Order."
His leading object in visiting the Lodges has been to encourage the study of the
laws of Masonry and teach their application, thus warding off evil by removing the
cause. We do not underrate the great importance of uniformity of work when we
entirely concur with him, that " while uniformity of work is an end to be attained
very desirable in itself, the instruction of the Lodges upon questions of Masonic law
involved in cases of almost daily occurrence is infinitely more important." Is it not
the experience of every member of a Grand Lodge who has served on committees,
that the larger proportion of work submitted originates in ignorance of the simplest
principles of Masonic Jurisprudence, neglect to consult the most accessible and well
known sources of light, and, too frequently, the very Constitution, Regulations, and
By-Laws of the jurisdiction in which they live? While it is in the nature and is the
pleasure of every Mason, who has the honor and interest of the Order at heart, to
impart cheerfully to a brother any knowledge he may possess, it is none the less be·
coming to the members of -the subordinates who care for the reputation of their
Lodges for intelligence, that each should endeavor to inform himself of the simple
lawil by which he is to be wisely governed in his Masonic relations, and the principles and maxims which establish a standard of upright brotherhood. He granted
four dispensations to confer degrees; three to confer the degree of Master Mason,

and one to permit a petitioner to receive the degrees in a neighboring jurisdiction,

The Grand Lodge adopted the following plan to secure uniformity of work. A
Grand Lecturer is to be annually elected, with power to appoint deputies known to
be proficient in the work approved by the Grand Lodge, with authority to the Grand
Lecturer to call together schools of instruction at such times and places as in his dis·
cretion he may deem expedient, with right to tax applicants for instruction such reasonable sums as may be necessary to defray expenses. We suspect that the conservators have their paws on this jurisdiction, and with all of the stern old English moralists' prejudice against play on words, we hope that they will pause and. reflect be·
fore they find themselves entangled into any alliance or association beyond their
borders. The reason for our suspicion is that a resolution authorizes the Grand Mas·
ter to permit some well-informed brother of his jurisdiction to attend a Masonic
School of Instruction in the Atlantic States for the purpose of learning the Webb·
Preston work as taught by the Chief Conservator.
Strong resolutions were adopted condemnatory of the Masons who openly live in
violation of established social and domestic laws governing the marriage relations.
Informal relations with the aborigines ! Is it not painful to find a record of the existence of such a condition of society among Masons? If the whole spirit of Masonry did not loudly denounce such infamies, and the plainly written law in the ancient charges was not sufficient to try and punish the offenders, then we would see
reason for such resolutions. As it is, they sound like our old regulation about the
practicability of the stern morality of Masonry, for which we were good-humoredly
laughed at ; but we disclaim any intention of treating lightly the opinions of our
Washingtonian brethren concerning stern morality: the case is too serious.
The Grand Secretary, who shows regard for system, and a disposition to preserve
records and build up a library, says in his report that the chairman of the committee
on Correspondence has informed him that a "concatenation of circumstances" prevented him from discharging his duty on that committee; that is the same thing
which has impelled us to do ours.
From the Treasurer's Report, we find that the receipts for the last year, including

WISCONSIN.
The eighteenth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of this State commenced at Milwaukee on the tenth June, 1862. The M.·. W.·. ALVIN B. ALDEN,
Grand Master, and the R:. W.·. WILJ,IAM T. PALMER, Grand Secretary, filled their
respective stations.
The Grand Master in his Address says that at no period of the Order in the State
have the evidences of healthy growth and permanent prosperity been so striking ;
he announces the death of Past Grand Master HENRY M. BILLINGS, and Senior Grand
Deacon EP. G. OGDEN, the latter having filled his place since the organization of the
Grand Lodge; he refused to grant dispensations to Lodges to enable them to ballot
for, and, if elected, confer .degrees "upon those of our patriotic citizens who had

11

78

Proceedings of the

[May12,

enrolled themselves in the army of our country;" he says, however ungracious the
refusal may seem, a sense of duty compelled him to deny the application. His rea·
sons are of that class which formed convictions in our minds since the time when first
we seriously devoted a thought to the prosperity of our Order, and which have
aroused in us a cautious jealousy of the indiscriminate and lavish use of the right of
granting dispensations. The fact which he recites that such applicants had neglected
to make application until they were about to be placed in positions of unusual dan·
ger, did not furnish conclusive evidence to his mind that they were wholly uninfin·
enced by unworthy motives in offering themselves, and having neglected to take the
proper steps prior to enlistment, they are alone chargeable with neglect, and have
no right to complain because the necessary safeguards which we have deemed proper to throw around our institution were not set aside for their benefit. As to the
right to complain, that is the natural privilege of every mortal, and we pity him who
can enjoy it; but we acknowledge no right, no claim, no privilege which the profane
can set up iu proof that he is inherently entitled to our honors, which must always
be sought unsolicited and are denied by us to those whom we think unworthy, with·
out condescending to render a reason. This practice does not spring from haughty
pride or unwise desire to e:x:ercise power and influence, whichis said to have provoked
the jealousy of a monarch and caused the suppression of the Order of Knights Templar
in the beginning of the fourteenth century, but it grows out of a profound knowledge
of human nature which our wise teachers have taught us, and the clear light of ex:perience has confirmed. It is one of the chief barricades which, when overcome, the
penetralia is threatened with profanation. We accord the Grand Master, in our hum·
ble opinion, the right to deny a petition for a dispensation without giving his reason
unless he chooses to do so; and we believe it is as inherent in him as it is improper
and unmasonic to seek to know the reason which directs a black ball in the Lodge.
Grand Master Earl of Zetland, in the controversy between the Maine and New Bruns·
wick jurisdictions, suggested the idea of the rights of individuals who are not Free·
masons: we were surprised at such an ochlocratic idea, a word which means more
than democratic, from that quarter; and since enjoying the great pleasure of read·
ing the Address of the lU;-. w.·. CHARLES F. STANSBURY, of the District of Columbia,
delivered in November, 1861, our impressions have formed themselves into reasons
and opinions. Grand Master ALDEN chooses to give us a farther reason for refusing
to grant dispensations, which we consider by no means of secondary importance
that the Lodge, in consenting to confer degrees, enters into an engagement to afford
information, and receives a fee in consideration, and unless necessary instruction is
imparted it fails in its duty,-that unless the candidate becomes thoroughly conversant with the lectures he would be unable to make himself known, and would thus
be deprived of those benefits which he should be entitled to. In our e:x:perience it
is notoriously true that Masons made by virtue of dispensations are proyerbially ignorant, and most eminently distinguished for their non-affiliating proclivities; for
which they are really not so blameworthy as the Lodges which do the shabby work.
In the position taken by the Grand Master, gladly sustained by us, we recognize a
purpose not to add to that class of brethren, ignorant of their obligations, who so
perple:x: our maturest counselors. He granted four dispensations to form new Lodges •
during the year. His Address is a practical and sensible document, devoted to the
affairs of his jurisdiction, evincing watchful care for its prosperity.
A proposition to amend their Constitution so as to reduce the dues paid by subor·
dinates from one dollar on each initiation to twenty-five cents, and on each member
from fifty to ten cents, was reported against by a committee, who advise that there
is rather necessity for considering the question of increasing the same. In 1860 the
dues to the Grand Lodge from the subordinates were reduced to the present standard,
and the committee say now that after deducting that portion of their annual revenue
reserved under their Constitution and appropriated to their Grand Charity Fund,

NORTH AMERICAN MASONIC CONGRESS AND THE GRAND
LODGE OF PENNSYLVANIA.

We have received a pamphlet containing the correspondence between Bro. CYRIL
Pl!ARL, Chairman, and Secretary ad interim, of the so-called North American Masonic Congress, and Bro. RICHARD VAcx, Chairman of the committee of Correspondence
of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania. The former invites the officers and members
of the Grand Lodge mentioned, with others, to meet the Congress in the City of New
York on the fifth day of September, A. D. 1862, to deliberate upon the duty, mode,
and means of applying the balm of Freemasonry to the healing of the country's
rankling wounds.
The latter, in reply, refers to the opinion entertained by his jurisdiction in oppO·
sition to the formation of the Congress; states that no reasons have been since sug·
gested which change that opinion, and declines the invitation on behalf of his Grand
Lodge. He doubts the success of the effort proposed, and is apprehensive that the
result will prove an injury to the Fraternity, rather than good to the country: he
fears that the still small voice of Masonic faith and practice has not power enough to
rise above the din of arms and roar of battle in order that it may be heard, and con·
eiders that the principles and teachings of Masonry are circumscribed to those who
understandingly embrace them, -the outside world, even under the most favorable
condition of its social and political systems, being, as he believes, unprepared to
obey the one, or listen with willing hearts and minds to the other.
In like connection similar sentiments were concurred in by our Grand Lodge last
year, and we especially commend the views so well e:x:pressed by Bro. VAux, doing
possibly some injustice in giving so brief an abstrac~ of the correspondence.
Concluding the report here, we submit the result with some feeling of satisfac·
. ti on that in our humble way we have attempted to benefit the craftsmen by directing
attention to what has transpired in other Grand Lodges, iu communication with ours,
most worthy of their knowledge ; not, however, without a greater feeling of distrust
of the manner in which we have executed it. But with the largest confidence in
your charity, we present our work, knowing that, even if not altogether worthy of
approval, it will not be cast away with the rubbish.
GILBERT B. CLAIBORNE, Chairman.

Which report was ordered to be printed with the proceedings.

Bro. WILLIAM H. HILL, from the special committee to whom was referred the Address of the Grand Master, presented the following report:To the M:. W.-. Grand Lodge of Oalifornia
The committee, to whom was referred the Address of the M. •• W. •• Grand Master,
have had the same under consideration and beg leave respectfully to report:They join most heartily in the congratulations of the Grand Master upon the peace,
harmony, and prosperity which have marked the progress of our beloved Order during the past year- one most eventful in the history of onr country and of the world.
They would acknowledge the Hand of our Great Grand Master above in this, and
they trust that He has still great and glorious work for our Fraternity to do in the
future- that it may be ours to contribute much towards healing the sad breaches
now existing between brethren of the same raee and blood, and to bring together
a.gain as one happy brotherhood, not only the estranged members of our own Fraternity, but the now warring States of our beloved Union, and, with the majesty
of power as well as the kindly accents of brothers, to say" peace, be still," and be
heard and heeded.
They present their congratulations to the Fraternity in this jurisdiction upon the
fact, patent on the face of the address submitted to us, that we have been favored
during the past year with the supervision and rule of a zealous, watchful, and faith·
ful Grand Master, whose services are none the less appreciated because they are so
modestly estimated by himself. It is enough for this to say that both the address
and its author are models of their kind.
With pleasure, also,. do your committee join with the Grand Master in his congratulations and thanks to the brethren in San Francisco for their enterprise and success
in the erection of the beautiful Temple in which we are now assembled. Those
brethren have fully justified the confidence reposed in them by the Grand Lodge and
the Fraternity in this State; and it is our hearty wish that nothing may hinder them
from speedily going on with their good work to perfection. We hope they will make
this Temple as conspicuous and noted, on this Pacific coast, as was that greatest one
of olden time, in the land that gave our Grand Master Solomon birth, and was blessed
with his kingly supervision.
The subject matter of the several decisions upon Masonic law and practice,

alluded to in the Grand Master's address, your committee recommend the reference
of to the Committee on Jurisprudence; and, if not considered an interference with
the more appropriate duty of that committee, the undersigned would say that these
decisions and reasonings of the Grand Master appear to be sound Masonic law and
appropriate deductions therefrom, and that it is to be hoped they will meet the ap.
proval of the Grand Lodge, and thus settle forever those perpetually arising and
perplexing, though often petty questions.
They recommend the reference of so much of the address as refers to the Rep.
resentative Fund and its disposition, to the special committee on that subject; and
so much thereof as relates to Uniformity of Work, to the Committee on Jurisprudence, with a hearty endorsement of the wish expressed that "somebody's
work" may be authoritatively declared to be that of the Grand Lodge, and thus
another most vexatious cause of dispute be removed from the Temple and be consigned to its only proper place among the rubbish.
The suggestions relative to the propriety, and even necessity, of the adoption by

the establishment of Military Lodges, they recommend to be referred to the Commit·
tee on Charters.
Your committee were much gratified at the announcement that the difficulties and
disturbances, whlch at one time threatened the extinction of one of the largest and
hitherto most flourishing Lodges in this city, had wholly disappeared, and that peace
and harmony once more prevailed therein. Brethren 6hould always " dwell together
in unity," only emulous of contributing individually, and as a Lodge, to that result
alone ; and the undersigned do most earnestly trust that all troubles which may here·
after arise in any Lodge, from whatever cause, may have a like peaceful and happy
termination.

Maryland, relative to the appointment of a Masonic chaplain to minister to oick and
wounded Masons in the military hospitals, was but the embodiment of the feelings of
the breth:en ~n this jurisdiction ; and to his most appropriate words as to our duty
and pos1t1on m the fearful struggle through which our country is passing, your committee respond with a. hearty " Amen."

Grand Lodge of California:Your committee, to whom was referred the Annual Report of the Grand Secretary, beg leave to report that, after a careful examination of the same, they recommend the reference of its several subjects to the following committees for their consideration, namely: so much thereof as relates to the issue of dispensations by the
Grand Master to form new lodges, to the Committee on Charters ; so much thereof
as refers to the non-fulfillment of the constitutional requirements, as per Sec. 9, Art.
IV, Part VI, relative to transcripts of trials being forwarded by the officers of subordinate Lodges to the Grand Secretary, with the particular instances of neglect of
said duty alluded to, to the Committee on Grievances; so much thereof as relates
to the issue of special dispensations by the Grand Master, to the Committee on Jurisprudence; and so much thereof as details the monetary transactions of his office, to
the Committee on Finances.
Your committee would recommend all subordinate Lodges to purchase a com·
plete series of the bound proceedings of this Grand Lodge, to be held as the property
of the Lodge for the benefit of their presiding officers; believing that such a course
would obviate the necessity of annually submitting questions for adjudication, which
are often fully explained by former published reports of the Committees on Jurisprudence. By so doing they will establish a basis for Lodge libraries, and to a
great degree reimburse the treasury of this Grand Body for the outlay which has
been required for their publication. Your committee would also suggest the propriety of all Lodges adopting the uniform code of by-Jaws, forthwith, so that a
complete unanimity of legislation shall prevail throughout this jurisdiction.
It is a source of great gratification to the members of this Grand Lodge to see
the fine collection of• Masonic works which now occupy the shelves of our library;
and it is earnestly to be hoped that the zealous and unceasing labors of our Grand
Secretary in that direction, so fortunate for us in the past, will be as successful in
the future. To commend the labors of that able and efficient officer and his assistant, is a pleasing duty; and your committee, as many others have done before, most
willingly bear testimony to the great obligations· which this Grand Lodge owes, for
its present high position among its contemporaries, to the brother who, during eight
years past, has so well discharged the duties of Grand Secretary.
All which is respectfully submitted.

To the M:. W:. Grand Lodge of California: Your committee, to whom was referred the transcript of the proceedings in the
case of JAMES W. ToRNEY, expelled by Mariposa Lodge, No. 24, on the 22d of No·
vember, 1862,having had the same under consideration, reportThat the trial in this case appears to have taken place without the presence of the
accused, and without any testimony having been introduced in his behalf. It is true
that the accused was notified of the time when the commissioners would assemble to
trv the case, but he declined to attend on the ground that he considered their
then meeting irregular, by reason of the failure of the commi~sioners ~o atte~d .the
meeting previous to the one at which the trial took place. Actmg on this convwt10n,

1863.J

87

Grand Lodge of Oalifornia.

nnd supposing that the commissioners had not acquired jurisdiction to try the charges,
he declined to appear, and the proceedings were conducted ex parte.
Whilst your committee would be unwilling to give too much effect to technical objections to the acquiring of jurisdiction over the persons of Masons charged with offences, yet in all cases where they conceive that a brother had lost his opportunity for a
run defence through an honest but mistaken conviction of his legal rights, and the
11ction of the Lodge was not strictly regular, they would be inclined to grant him a
rehearing.
In this case the record shows that, on one of the days appointed for trial, only two
of the commissioners met, and then one hour after the appointed time. The accused
claims to have been present at the time when the commissioners should have met,
hut found no one there to try him. Again, though the accused may have been guilty
of a serious masonic offence, yet the evidence adduced tended rather to convict
him of a different offence than that one charged.
Before concluding this report, your committee cannot avoid condemning the practice which appears to exist, and which is exhibited in this case, for the accused, in
presenting his supposed grievances to the Grand Lodge, to indulge in severe animadversion and harsh strictures against the commissioners-in too many instances borclering on insult. Such communications ought not to be tolerated, and in all instances
Hhould be disregarded and returned to the writers. On a full review of this case,
and in order that ample justice may be done to the accused, your committee recommend the following resolution for adoption :Resolved, That the action of ..lfariposa Lodge, No. 24, in expelling Bro. JAMES W•
ToRNEY from all the rights and privileges of Masonry, on the 22d day of November,
1862, be and the same is hereby reversed; and that the said Lodge be directed to
try the case anew, with power to amend the charges against the accused, if so desired
by the Lodge.
All which is respectfully submitted.
HENRY HARE HARTLEY,
CHAS. L. WIGGIN,
JOHN C. BULL,

The Grand Secretary presented the following report of th~ sp~cial committee of Past Masters, appointed at the last Annual Communication of the
Grand Lodge, on the petitions for the restoration of J. BENSO!'i VAN HAGAN and RrcHARD B. MoYES : To the M.-. W.'. Grand Lodge of Oatifornia:

.
.
Your committee, appointed to examine into and report in detail upon all the facts

Grand Lodge of Oalijornia.

1863.]

91

nnd circumstances connected with the petitions for the restoration of J.B. VAN HA·
<IAN and R. B. MoYEs, respectfully report as.follows :~
As the facts and circumstances connected with the petitions are matters of record
in the Grand Lodge, your committee hnve presumed that it was intended by the refer·
cnce to obtain a statement of the facts and circumstances connected with the duel
between Messrs. MOYES and VAN HAGAN.
In May, 1860, news reached Nevada City of the massacre of ORMSBY, MEREDITH
nnd others, in ~evada Territory, by the Indians, and of future anticipated danger to
the whites. A volunteer company immediately organized at Nevada City. J. B; VAN
!IAGAN was chosen Captain, and R. B. MoYES served as a private in the company. It
proceeded to Virginia City and united with other companies under command of Col.
JACK HAYES. Thence the entire command went out to Pyramid Lake. On the route,
ut William's Station, a skirmish with the Indians occurred. From some contradic·
tion or misunderstanding of orders, the Nevada company took no active part in the
fight. This circumstance created some disaft'ection among the members of the com·
pany, and Mr. MOYES, in conversation with others, did not hesitate to charge, or insin·
nate, cowardice on the part of Mr. VAN lIAGA.N. These remarks and ch.arges, though
not made in the presence of Mr. VAN HAGAN, were afterwards brought to his know·
ledge, and were the immediate cause of the subsequent difficulty.
Subsequently, and while still upon the route, Captain VAN HAGAN reprimanded Mr.
Mons harshly for an alleged breach of discipline, in opening and using, without
orders, a package of stores sent out for the use of the company. This aggravated
the unkind feeling already existing. On the 16th of June, 1860, the company returned
to Nevad!l City. On the evening of that day Messrs. VAN HAGAN and MoYES met in
the street, many members of the company and other citizens of Nevada being
present. A conversation commenced concerning the affair at Williams' Station and
the charges previously made by Mr. MOYES against Mr. VAN HAGAN'S character for
courage. Both were angry. It was finally proposed by Mr. MOYES, and assented to
by Mr. VAN HAGAN, that the dispute should be settled by receiving the statement of
Mr. H. S. BRADLEY, a Lieutenant of the Nevada company, as to the facts of the skir·
mish at William's Station. Mr. BRADLEY came, and made a statement completely ex·
onerating Mr. VAN HAGAN from all blame, and declaring that he had but obeyed the
orders of his superior officers. Mr. MOYES, still dissatisfied, renewed the charges and
imputations previously made by him. Mr. VAN HAGAN replied angrily, using the
harshest epithets. Mr. MoYEs then retired, and the next day sent a peremptory cha!·
lenge to Mr. VAN HAGAN. It was accepted. On the day following the parties and
their seconds left for the place of meeting, on the borders of an adjoining county.
Efforts were made by members of Nevada Lodge, most intimate with the parties, to
prevent a meeting. The Master of that Lodge, however, did not interfere either with
advice or authority. A serie.s of correspondence passed between the seconds, in·
tended to affect an amicable settlement, but it was unavailing ; and on the 20th of
June, 1860, the third day after the challenge passed, the duel took place. Two shots
were exchanged without effect, when the seconds and friends interfered and effected
a reconciliation.
The expulsion of Messrs. VAN HAGAN and MOYES by the several Lodges of which
they were members followed, as of course. The subsequent action, the petitions of
the Lodges recommending their restoration, the reference of that matter to a com·
mittee, and their report at the last session of the Grand Lodge recommending the
restoration of both, are matters of record.
Your committee have endeavored to give in detail, and as briefly as possible, the
circumstances connected with the affair. They are aware that this report, though
necessarily lengthy, is but a meagre outline of the facts. The time elapsed, absence
of parties, and absence or death of others who knew most of the affair, renders a more
nccurate report impossible. They have not found it practicable to comply with the

-

92

[May 14,

Proceedings of the

instruction in the reference, requiring a separate report upon each application, as a
detail of the facts necessarily involves an account of the whole affair, and of the acts
of both the parties. They think it proper, however, to say that, since the several
petitions were filed, Mr. VAN HAGAN has expressed and exhibited an earnest desire
to be restored to the rights and privileges of Masonry; while Mr. MOYfS has con·
cerned himself but little in the matter, and seems to view his own expulsion with
comparative indifference.
As the resolution of the committee to whom the applications for restoration were
referred, is still before the Grand Lodge, this committee have supposed that their
investigation was intended merely as auxiliary to that report, and that they were not
called upon to recommend any disposal of that resolution. They would only add that
the inquiries pursued by that committee were made at a time much nearer the occur·
rence of the events herein narrated, and that their conclusions were derived from the
statements of the parties themselves, and of witnessea most converaant with the facts.
They could determine much more advisedly than the undersigned, whether, under all
the circumstances, the mantle of Masonic charity should be made to cover the errors
of these men.
All which is respectfully submitted.
.ADDISON C. NILES,
WILLIA}{ :McCORMICK,

Your committee, to whom were referred the questions of Bro. WILLIAM H. Hn1,,
in regard to Masons suspended for non-payment of dues, respectfully report as
follows:In regard to the first and main question, they are of opinion that a suspended
Mason, dying while still under sentence of suspension, cannot be restored by any
action subsequent to his death. By his suspension he was deprived of all the right•
and privileges of Masonry ; and, while your committee favor the most liberal c:xerciHe
of charity, they believe that an affirmative answer to the question would open il•
door for such neglect of Masonic duty as would result most disastrously to tltc c:, '" '·
The remaining questions are contingent upon the first ; but, in any event, the
Constitution makes sufficient answer to them in Section 9, Article III, Part III, to
which the committee refer.
All which is respectfully submitted.

Grand Lodge, no Lodge, unless the provision existed in its by-laws at the time of
the adoption of the Constitution, could so amend them as to provide for a separate
ballot for each degree. Yet, believing that such construction would not be in accord·
ance with the intention of the Grand Lodge when that instrument was adopted, and, as
has been ably said by a former committee, also believing" that the fundamental laws
of Masonry respecting its morality should be construed strictly, though always with
charity, but in respect to its government, with liberality, and in the true spirit of its

a Lodge to proffer such an amendment as that proposed by Saint James' Lodge.
They therefore recommend that the proposed amendment to the by-laws of Saint

Bro. JAMES H. LANDER, from the Committee on Charters, presented the
following report:To the M. ·. W.·. Grand Lodge of California:Your committee, to whom were referred the several petitions of Lodges working
under dispensation and praying the issue of charters, respectfully reportThat they have carefully examined the records, petitions, and other papers, in·
eluding those on which the original dispensations were issued, of the following
Lodges, viz.: Mount Carmel, Woodland, Washoe, Gibsonviae, Gilroy, Pilot Hill,
Keystone, and Virginia Oity, and find them essentially in due form.
The committee take pleasure in reporting that the improvement shown and noticed
in the work of the Secretaries of the older Lodges is also manifest in the books and

96

[May 14,

Proceedings of the

papers submitted to it. To quote the language of ou1· predecessors in the last annual
report, "we find that the records of said Lodges present a very creditable appearance, and that their transactions conform to ancient usage and the Constitution of
the Grand Lodge ;" and, to pursue further the report of the previous committee, we
would reiterate their objection, and protest against the haste and hurry which new
r,odges, whether under dispensation or charter, evince. That a new Lodge, estab·
lished in a location, previously deprived of ready accessibility to the privileges of
our Order, should at the outset receive many and frequent requests for admission, is
natural, and it is desirable ; but we fear that too great a wieh exists generally in new
organizations to increase the number of members, to the deterioration of strength
and solidity in the materials. Your committee, in their investigation, also notice a
departure, in one instance, from the recommendation of the committee of the last
year, in this; that a brother took his third degree on the next night after receiving
the second. Although in this case, from explanation given to the committee, no
harm or danger is to be apprehended, yet, as a rule, the hasty advancement of
brethren in the lower degrees is harmful and dangerous, and your committee earnestly deprecate it.
Your committee also would enjoin on Secretaries of Lodges under dispensation to
make their records as full as may be, with a due regard to conciseness, remember·
ing that a clean, fair, and full record will greatly promote the application for a
charter, when made.
Your committee respectfully submit the following resolution, and recommend its
adoption:Resolt>ed, That charters be issued to Mount Carmel Lodge, at Red Dog,Nevada
County; to Washoe Lodge, at Washoe City, Washoe County, Territory of Nevada;
to Gibson1Jille Lodge, at Gibsonville, Sierra County; to Gilroy Lodge, at Gilroy,
Santa Clara County; to Pilot Hill Lodge, at Pilot Hill, El Dorado County ; to Key·
stone Lodge, at Copperopolis, Calaveras County; to Virginia Oity Lodge, at Virginia
City, Storey County, Territory of Nevada; and to Woodland Lodge, at Woodland,
Yolo County; to be numbered in accordance with the dates of their several dispen·
sations.
All which is respectfully submitted.

Bro. GILBERT B. CLAIBORNE, from the special committee to whom was

decease of Bros. GrL:llAN and Gn1n1TH, presented the following report:To (he .'If.-. W.-. Grand Lodge of California

The committee appointed to consider and report upon that part of the Grand
Master's Address which announces the death of the M.-. W.-. CHARLES GILMAN and
the w... HUMPHREY GRIFFITH, submit the following :Our Grand Lodge, having received tidings of the death of the M:. w;., CHARLES
GILMAN, who withdrew from the Craft at Baltimore, in the State of :Maryland, on the
nth day of September, 1861, in order to approach nearer the higher light in the
Eternal East, feels pierced with sharp grief. We knew him lovingly; we have treasured the 11pecimens of work which. he wrought for us ; his name is among the
earliest upon our record. He was Chairman of the Convention which formed our
Grand Lodge. It is an honor, which will grow brighter and grander as the cycles of
time multiply, to have presided at the inauguration of the first American Grand
Lodge of Masons on the Pacific Coast. That honor is his due. Eminent among the
Craft here for his learning and purity of life, he was none the Jess distinguished by
his practical application aud illustration of our principles; and, although the busy
years have swiftly passed away since his form graced our halls, his deeds still exhale
their fragrance. In remembrance of his worth and services, your committee rec om·
mend that it be-Resolved, That we cherish his memory as that of a brother "'ho was chosen by
the Grand Architect, as his instrument, with which to accomplish more good than is
usually allQtteq tQ one Mason.

Resolr1ed, further, That we unite in sympathy with the Grand Lodges of Maryland and New Hampshire, of each of which he had been Grand Master, in constituting
triple pillars to uphold his fame.
Resol'Ved, further, That the Grand Secretary be and is hereby instructed to cause
to be procured, at the cost of this Grand Lodge, a portrait of our deceased brother;
and that a mourning page be printed in our volume of proceedings as a fnrther token
of our affectionate respect.
One year ago an eloquent tongue poured forth silvery strains in words and
thoughts that won persuasive way into our hearts. Bro. HuMPIIRY GRU'YITH, our
Grand Orator as he then was, seems even now to be in our midst. But, no ! His
eloquence is hushed; the silver chord is loosed ; the golden bowl is broken. Two
months since he died in this city. Gifted with talents which ranked him above many
of his associates, generou• and genial in nature, with a grace and simplicity of man·
ner which attached and retained a large circle of devoted friends, his future in life
promised to be one of honor and usefulness. In our Communication we are sadly re·
minded of his death, and the absence of his counsel in the committee, of which he
was chairman, is a loss which the Grand Lodge deeply feels. So worthy of the
honor and esteem of his brethren, your committee reco~mend that it beResolved, That this Grand Lodge will preserve and ever endeavor to keep fresh
in memory the recollection of his many virtues, his worth and services.
Resolved, That the Grand Lodge extend its cordial sympathy to those to whom
he was most dear, who have been so keenly stricken with sorrow.
Resolved, That a mourning page be devoted to his memory in the volume of our
IJroceedings.
All which is respectfully submitted.

"the necessity of a thorough exemplification of the work"; and, 011 the evenin,!!' of

system of work and lectures, any Lodge neglecting or refusing to learn and use

his discretion he shall think proper,) until they shall conform in all things to the regulations of the Grand Lodge in the premises.

Bro. HENRY HARE HARTLEY, from the special committee to whom was
referred the petition of the Trustees of Marysville Lodge, No. 9, presented
the following report: To the M.·. W.·. Grand Lodge of California : Your committee, to whom was referred the petition of the Trustees of Mm·ysvUle
Lodge, No. 9, praying that the Grand Lodge consent to the alienation by said Lodge
of certain interests in a lot in the City of Marysville - heretofore donated to said
I,odge by the Hon. Bro. STEPHEN J. FIELD, with a reversion in favor of the Grand
Lodge -to certain other Masonic bodies in said City of Marysville, or that the Grand
Lodge would relinquish absolutely its reversionary interest therein, having had the
subject under consideration, report as follows: That the conveyance, under which the Grand Lodge holds its reversionary inter·
est in said premises, provides that on the extinction, from any cause, of the Lodge to
which the said lot was originally donated, the same shall revert to said Grand Lodge
"for the uses and benefits of the Fraternity of Masons in said State generally." Your
committee are of opinion that it is very questionable whether the Grand Lodge has
the power absolutely to relinquish its reversionary interest, and there by defeat the
intention of the generous donor thereof. They, however, see no valid objection to
the Grand Lodge consenting that Marysville Lodge may deed to other Masonic
bodies, mentioned in said petition, undivided interests in said property, as the Grand
Lodge would thereby still retain its reversionary right, which, however, in all proba·
bility, may never be called into existence. Thus the object which the said Lodge
has in contemplation may be carried into effect without violating the trust reposed
in the Grand Lodge ; and, to effect this purpose, they propose the adoption of the
following resolution : Resolved, That this Grand Lodge hereby consents that the Trustees of Marysville
Lodge, No. 9, may convey to Yuba Lodge, No. 39, Cor'inthian Lodge, No. 69, and
Washington Royal Arch Chapter, No. 13, or to the Trustees of said bodies, individ·
ually or collectively, such undivided interests in the west half of lot Nq. l, block No.
4, range E, in the City of Marysville, as said Marysville Lodge may deem proper;
and that the Grand Secretary be authorized to attach the consent of the Grand Lodge
thereto to such conveyance, or conveyances, and append thereto the Seal of the
Grand Lodge.
All which is respectfully submitted.

of Masonry, report-

1

Grand Lodge of California.

That, after having examined with due care the record in this case, and heard all
that has been urged in favor of the appellant, they cannot recommend the reversal
of the action of the Lodge. The evidence shows that the accused was guilty of using
exceedingly abusive and violent language towards some of the. brethren, a practice
which cannot be too highly condemned. It has been suggested to the committee

satisfactory on that point; and, as he may at any time hereafter apply to his Lodge
to reverse its action, and being satisfied that it would do so if' assured of his regret
for the transaction, it is deemed best for the present to leave the case as the Lodge
decided it.

Bro. WILLIA.JI: A. D.11.vIEs, from the Committee on Jurisprudence, presented the following report :11:1 the M .., W.·. Grand Lodge of California:-

•

Your committee, to whom was referred that portion of the address of the Grand
Master, in which he states his decisions on certain cases arising under Sec. 5, .Art. III,
Part III, of the Constitution, respectfully report as follows:
In regard to the first decision of the Grand Master, your committee conceive that
it is strictly in accordance with the common sense doctrine that there is a remedy for
every wrong. It must be borne in mind always that under the original organization
of the Fraternity, the Entered Apprentices formed the great body of Masons ; and that
only in modern times have they been placed in their present position in regard to the
body of the Fraternity. So few rights are left to them that not only charity, but justice, demands that those remaining rights receive a liberal construction. No man
should be condemned without a hearing. This would virtually be done did we de·
cide that the brother whose advancement is objected to, can have no knowledge of
the objection and no opportunity of combating it; and your committee apprehend
that "our law condemns no man before it hear what he says." They therefore
recommend that the decision of the Grand Master, made in these words-" In many
cases, therefore, he should be informed of the objection against him and be heard in
his defence" -be and the same is hereby approved.
Upon the second decision your committee believe that the rule-that a man shall
not be twice placed in jeopardy for the same offence -is entirely applicable to Ma·
sonic jurisprudence. If a committee, appointed for the purpose, has properly
attended to it~duty,has investigated the objection made against a brother's advance·
ment, has reported the objection as " not a valid and Masonic one," and the Lodge
has adopted the report, and thus, by a two-third vote, has ratified the finding of
the committee, then the brother who has made the objection, and the minority, acting
with him, should yield their opinion. It amounts, in the opinion of your committee, to
factious opposition on the part of any brother thus to set up his own view against 80
large a majority of his brethren; and, when he has been decided against, to renew the
very same objection. Your committee therefore recommend the approval of the
second decision of the Grand Master given in these words : "It is not competent for
the same or another member to interpose a second objection for the same cause, except on the ground of newly discovered and material evidence, or for acts subsequently committed!'
On the third decision, which relates to the duty of the Master of a Lodge upon the
decision of an objection to advancement, your committee say that, ordinarily, the Master
of the Craft is the proper one to judge of the fitness of the materials of which his
building is to be composed. But, when the Lodge has decided that the applicant is
worthy, and the required proficiency has been attained, the Master should, if not
:absolutely contrary to his obligations, proceed to confer the next degree. Your
<committee would take away no right from the Master of a Lodge which is his by

1863.]

111

Grand Lodge of California.

ancient usage, conferred for the best good of the Craft. They would give no coun·
tenance to the spirit of innovation so prevalent in our free country. They would not
relieve the Master from any responsibility which he of right should assume. He
should not rule his Lodge in a haughty or arbitrary manner, but should, when prop·
er - that is, when no harm can accrue to the Craft therefrom -yield to the decision
of his brethren when constitutionally expressed. They therefore recommend the
approval of the Grand Master's third decision.
All which is respectfully submitted.
WILLIAM .A. DA.VIES,
l

J:I. HOLOOll!l!E RHEES, I

LOUIS ConN'
WILLIAM C. RrOH,
JOSEPH M. HAVENS,

Jfl

Oo'lnmittee.

Which report wa.s concurred in.
Bro. HENRY HARE H.tRTLEY, from the Committee on Grievances, presented the following report :To the M.·. W.·. Grand Lodge of California : Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal of JAns .ALEX. YOELL from
the action of San Jose Lodge, No. 10, suspending him from all the rights and privileges of Masonry, have given the case the most careful and anxious examination
within their power, with a view of doing as far as po;1sible the most ample and com·
plete justice towards the Lodge and the accused.
The transcript of the record in this case is exceedingly voluminous and the time
consumed by the commission on the trial was of unusual duration. All the proceed·
ingsappear to have been conducted in a careful and cautions manner, and ample opportunity seems to have been afforded to the accused, by the aid of testimony and
counsel, to disprove the charges preferred. The nature of the oftence for which the accused was placed upon trial was chiefly for the repeated accusation of his brother
Masons (one of them being no other than the Master of his Lodge) of the moEt
heinous Masonic offences. His defence was, not that those accusations were true,
but that he had been led to give utterance to them under the highest state of mental
excitement, almost bordering upon insanity, induced by statements made to him by
otl1ers, and rumors which had reached him from various sources. Whilst, in view of
the weakness and fallibility of human nature, it is at all times our duty, not only as
men, but as Masons, to throw the broad mantle of charity over offences committed
under high mental excitement, produced by a belief of the truth of any given state.
ment, though the evidence might be false or even partly insufficient, in moments of
calm reflection, to have influenced the judgment; yet that indulgence can only be extended to the moment whilst tl1e passions are under the control and effect of the im·
mediate cause ; and, if time has been given for sober judgment to have resumed its
sway and dominion, a reiteration of the accusations must be deemed an affirmance
of tteir truth, and impose upon the accuser the necessity of proving them, or being
convicted as a traducer. To state the proposition more clearly, we hold that where
a Mason accuses a brother Mason of such offences as were charged by the accused in
this case, one of the following results must inevitably happen, if the peace, harmony,
and dignity of the Craft is to be preserved.
lst. The accuser must retract his charges, as far as possible, as publicly and
widely as made by him, if satisfied of his error or the insufficiency of the proofs to
sustain the accusations.
2d. The accuser, if he declines so to retract, and is still satisfied of the correctness
of his accusations, must immediately prefer the proper charges against the offender,
and convict him of the ofi'ence, or at least show that he had ample and proper
grounds for making the accusations.

112

Proceedings of the

[May 16,

3d. If the accuser declines to adopt either of the above courses, he must submit
to the penalty of being considered as having unjustly and wrongfully traduced the
character of a brother Mason, and there by render himself amenable to the severest
judgment of his Lodge.
In this case, the accused, in numerous instances, and in the grossest manner, insulted
and traduced the character of some of his brother Masons, but, at the trial, wholly
failed to prove the truth of the accusations; and, in fact, did not even attempt so to
do. Upon the principal defence relied upon by him-his alleged mental derange·
ment-we presume the commissioners arrived at the conclusion that a Mason who
could not control his passions within better bounds than the brother accused seemed
to be able to do, was totally unworthy of retention within the precincts of a Masonic Lodge.
Upon a careful review, therefore, of the whole record, we have come to the conclusion that the commissioners acted prudently and wisely, and that their action was
just and proper in the premises; and we report the following resolution, with the
recommendation that it be adopted :Resolved, That the action of San Jose Lodge, No. 10, in suspending JAMES ALEX.
YOELL from all the rights and privileges of Masonry, be and the same is hereby in
all respects confirmed and approved.
All which is respectfully submitted.
HENRY HARE HARTLEY,
CHAS. L. WIGGIN,
JOHN c. BULL,
Committee.

The W.·. THOMAS STARR KING, Grand Orator, then delivered his Annnal
Address as follows ,.:_
MOST WORSHIPFUL GRAND MASTER
AND BRETHREN OF THE GRAND LODGE:ln offering salutation to you, with cordial thanks for the honor and privilege connected with the office and duty which you have entrusted to me, I shall only attempt
briefly, in the discharge of that duty, to note two or three points of harmony and
correspondence between the structure and working of our Order, and the handiwork
of the Almighty in the external world.
We belong to the great Fraternity of Free and Accepted Masons. The implements
of our Craft, however, are no longer for operative toil. We do not now, as part of
our covenant, set fast the Doric pillar, nor release from marble the ornament of the
Corinthian capital. We no longer sketch the complications of Gothic piles, and
cement the buttresses of haughty towers, and cany up, course by course, the aspiring stones of pinnacles. The tools of the Craft are representative now of speculative truth, and speak to the inward eye of laws and duties that make life noble
and character symmetrical and strong. Yet, though we build no structures such as
onr ancient brethren reared, though the temples in which we meet are not the monuments of our own proficiency in the art whose instruments we cherish, we are
builders and preservers in a richer sense ; for our Order itself grows stronger and
more precious with years, and its uses are more varied ~nd beautiful with the lapse
of time.
The Masonic organization is far more remarkable and wonderful than the noblest
edifice it ever added to the landscape of history. Let us pause, brethren, on the
word " organization." That is the great word of the world. The Almighty is the
Organizer. He creates elements in order to mingle and fraternize them in composi-

1863.J

Grand Lodge of California.

113

tion and products. In the original chaos matter was unorganized. The process of
death is dis-organization. All the marvels of beauty, all the victories of life, are
exhibitions and triumphs of organizing force. The most fascinating chapters of
science are those which unveil to us the vast fields which the forces traverse that
sustain the highest forms of life upon the globe.
A crystallized gem is the most attractive form of solid matter, because more
thought and skill are expended in its structure 'than in any other stony combination
of atoms. A flower is of a higher order of charm, for more various and more
suhtile elements are wrought into its composite loveliness ; and then the provisions
for the growth and support of the flower affect us more profoundly still,-the mixture of the air, the various powers hidden in the sun-ray, the alternation of daylight
and gloom, the laws of evaporation and of clouds, and the currents in the air that
carry moisture from zone to zone for the nutriment of vegetation. We soon find in
nature that no element, or force, exists unrelated. It is in harness with other
elements for a common labor, and an interchange of service for a common end.
Organization is the idea which science impresses upon us as the secret of life, health,
power, and beauty in her realm. An organized product can appear only from forces
of nature, which are the movements of the Divine will. Man can arrange, manufacture, weave, forge, adjust, refine; but he cannot organize as nature does. He
can make machines through which the forces of nature will play for cunning ends;
but he cannot conjure the principle of life into any mould of his making. He can start
shuttles that will weave a carpet for the reception room of a palace in one loom; but he
can build no mill, he can start no laboratory, where the warp and woof of the banana
leaf can be plaited. He can tell how the sugar is secreted in the veins of a clover
blossom ; but he cannot make the clover seed. And you might as well ask the wisest
Rcientific man to fashion a world, as to create one of the green needles which a pine
tree produces by the million, or one of the innumerable blades of grass.
But the great glory of organization is when it is revealed in human life. The highest
structure of the creative art is the body of man, representing in its complexity and the
friendly partnership of its powers, the system and co-ordination which society should
attain; and it is a marked epoch in history when a new movement is made which
succeeds in organizing men widely and permanently for noble and beneficent ends.
We are not intended to be separate, private persons, but rather fibres, fingers,
and limbs. The aim of religion is not to perfect us as persons, looking at each of
us apart from others. The Creator does not propose to polish souls like so many
pins,-each one dropping off clean and shiny, with no more organic relations to each
other than pins have on a card. We are made to be rather like the steel, the iron,
and the brass, which are compacted into an engine, where no modest bolt or rivet
is placed so tha1l it does not somehow contribute to the motion, or increase the efficiency of the organism.
In savage life men are slightly organized. A savage tribe is like a heap of sand;
the atoms are distinct; they are aggregated, not combined; no beautiful product
springs from them; and the first wind of disaster blows them away. A half-civilized
nation is but slightly organized, so far as noble purposes and high sentiments are
concerned. Progress is marked by wider, higher, finer developments, issuing from
the combination and co-partnership of souls. There can be no such thing as justice,
until men, in large masses, are rightly related to each other. There can be no prosperity in a community until the majority of its people are so organized that their
minds receive training, and their energies are unfettered. There can be no happiness,
except as the result of proper relations permanently established between the different classes or strata of the social world.
"No man liveth to himself." "Whether one member suffer, all the members suffer
with it; or one member be honored; all the members rejoice with it." "How good and
how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!" When a compacted unity
of living beings is seen, one of the most precious objects for which the world was

114

Proceedings of the

[May 16,

built is attained. A large and well ordered family is such a jewel. A neighborhood
at peace, and free from scandal, is-or, rather I should say, would be-a still more
precious jewel of the same quality. A state, a nation, so constructed that the forces
of all ranks of its inhabitants should be brought into play, and the rights of all ranks
should be saved from pressure, would be a more marvellous and a more inspiring
l!tructure than the material order and harmony of our solid globe.
rt is in the light of this principle that the value and nobleness of ,lfasonry appear.
I say again that no edifice which our ancient brethren reared was equal to the living
structure of which they and we are portions. How often we read, or hear with
pride, that in the building of the first temple, the stones were made ready before t~ey
were brought together; so that there was neither hammer, nor a.....:, nor any tool of iron
heard In the house while it was building! What is that to the growth of our Order
itself? How quiet the process, yet how constant! Who hears the noise of it? Who
sees, or knows, when the sound timber and the approved stones are brought together,
and fitted, and lifted to their place amidst the roar, and strife, and selfishness of the
world? Yet, in thousands of towns and cities of the world, in all its zones, in almost
all communities and tongues of men, this work, in substantial sameness of method
and pledge, is going on. The Temple of Solomon must stand as it was built. It
could not enlarge itself. It could not bud with smaller temples, and then take them
in under a widening roof or a swelling dome. Neither, when some of its pillars
decayed, could it restore its own decrease, as the living cedars of J,ebanon repair
their wastes and renew their leaves. Bnt our conscious temple does all this, and
noiselessly. It fills in its losses ; it enlarges its sweep and sway ; it does it through
men of all conditions, and classes, and races ; and still it stands in its old propor·
tions, though in greater amplitude, symmetrical, mysterious, sublime.
This is the most remarkable social organization of the world. None on the globe,
with half so many elements in its composition, is so old. We are told of late that
excavations made under modern Jerusalem disclose remnants of the old city in va.
rious periods of its history. Portions of the massive masonry of the time of Solomon are uncovered. Above these appear fragments of the work of Zerubbabel. ~n
a higher historic stratum are specimens of workmanship from the age of Herod the,
Great; and still above these, but below the level of the present city, are remains cf
the constructive toil ordered by Justinian. We delight to feel, brethren, that the
past, measured by as many ages, is u11der us; but it is not beneath us in a broken
symmetry, and a dead grandeur, as under Jerusalem. It is rather beneath us y the
roots are beneath a tree, and as the central t'ings are hidden in the trunk. Thef give
power and pith to the structure still. They are part of its present majesty, sources
of its living vigor, prophecies of its future strength.
We should take satisfaction, brethren, nay, a noble pride, in the consciousness of
the age and vastness of our organization. If a stone in St. Peters' could be conscious,
or any portion of the w~ll, or spire, of Strasburg Cathedral, do you not think that it
would rejoice in its position, that it would he exultant over ibi partnership with other
stones in rearing the grandeur of such a pile for such worthy uses? If any fragment
of such an edifice could be conscious, and did not feel any pride, or any privilege, in
its posi.tion and its call, would its indifference be a merit, or a shame rather?. ~ow
shall it be with us? Shall we not feel that there is dignity, that there is privilege,
in being living fibres of an organization wl1ich has passed from one era of the world
to another which is older than the oldest empire of Christendom, which has on its
roll names' that sparkle in history like the sovereign. stars,.and which exists, not '.or
purposes of private aggrandizement, or the selfish JOY of its members, but to give
deeper root to good principles in the world, and to diffuse th" spirit of peace and
order? If a Mason is not grateful and glad over his fellowship, it is because he does
not appreciate the value in the world of the organization of good.
The idea of organization is connected with the idea of order. And here, also,

Masonry reflects t-0 us, or rather illustrates in a higher form, the wisdom breathed by
the Great Architect through nature. It is said that order is heaven's first law. It is
no less true, brethren, that it is earth's first privilege. It is the condition of beauty,
of liberty, and of peace.
Think how the principle of order for all the orbs of the solar system is hidden in
the sun. The tremendous power of his gravitation reaches thousands of millions of
miles, and hampers the self-will-the centrifugal force-of mighty Jupiter, of Uranus
with his staff of moons, of cold, and distant, and invisible Neptune. There's !\
Grand Lodge for you, in which these separate Masters are held in check by the
Most Worshipful Grand Master's power! Nay, they tell us now of a central sun
around which all othersuns, those fixed stars of the firmament, bend and sweep. If
this suggests an argument by analogy in favor of a world congress of Masons, with a
Grand Lodge of Nations, and a Supreme Master, whose power runs over seas and
across continents, girdling the earth like a magnetic stream, I leave it to be discussed
by the Committee on Correspondence, in the next volume of our Grand Secretary's
admirable reports. But, in the case of our planetary system, is it any hardship that
the separate globes are so strictly under rule, and pay obeisance to the sun? Is it
not their chief blessing, their sovereign privilege? What if the order were less strict
and punctual; what if the force in these globes, that chafes under the central rein,
and champs its curb, should be triumphant for a day? ·What if the earth should gain
liberty against the pull of the sun? Beauty from that moment would begin to wither;
fertility would begin to shrivel. The hour of seeming freedom would be the dawn
of anarchy ; for the sun's rule and apparent despotism is only the stern and beneficent
condition of perpetual harmony, bounty, and joy.
Everywhere, order is the great interest. What humanity needs is the fulfillment of
these indications of nature, freedom with order, a proper consciousness of worth in
every breast, a recognition by each man of the worth and claims of every other, and
an acknowledgment by all of a common and controlling law. This idea of order,
fulfilled in the architecture of nature, is committed as a trust to our Fraternity, and
the tiropcr reverence for it is poured out continually through the influence of. our
hallowed bonds.
.
For every country that influence is silently wholesome. In lands where the spirit
of society does not recognise sufficiently the worth of man, but pays too mucll
homage to rank and name, our Order quietly fosters the principle of the equality of
privilege and responsibility under the laws of everlasting justice; and, without being
revolutionary, it upholds the honor of hqman nature, and patiently rebukes despotic
arrogance and aristocratic scorn. In our own country its service is of a different
kind. We need more respect for authority, less self-will, a deeper sense of the
sacredness of law, and education in the habits, manners, and feeling of deference
and loyalty. The rupture of our National Unity, for a time, with its tremendous
costs in treasure, blood, and agony, is in part the revelation, in part the penalty, in
part, perhaps, through the severe beneficence of God, the cure of our chronic insub·
ordination of character to the authority and sanctity·of high principles, which has
unfitted us, all over the land, to handle the sacred responsibilities and delicate
trusts of imperial statesmanship and continental government. Whatever will teach
our people reverence, decorum, respect for others in the utterance and defence of
opinion, submission to constituted authority with dignity and grace, will be medicine
for our trouble, and will prepare for us a better future. I believe that the Order or
Masonry, the quiet efficiency of its organism, the regard for forms it fosters, the love
of order it induces and deepens, the graceful habits of submission it educates, and
the sacredness it pours around organic law and the seats of authority, are a prominent portion of the bonds of civilh1ation in our country, and an immense blessing
when we consider our natural perils.
Brethren, let ns cherish the duties and trusts of our Fraternity for this good infill·

ence that it so naturally and liberally expends. Let us resolve, as part of our duty
to the Creator, the source of order and law, to drink more deeply of the springs,
within our enclosure, whose issue is healing and reviving. In the maintenance of the
bond and customs of order is the pledge of our prosperity, as well as the assurance
of our service. Order has Umits. Let us continue to guard sacredly our limits, to
