gathered within this temple, during the present week, to superintend our general
interests and interpret and apply our law! What harmony has prevailed here, what
decorum of speech, what promptness in duty, what efficiency in protecting and
guarding the common good! A visitor from outside our fello•hip, suddenly brought
in here to look, for a moment, at the representative men thus gathered from all sections of our State domain, a.nd to observe, by one glance, the quiet power embodied
in the assembly, might imagine, if suddenly taken out again, that there could be
something perilous to the public welfare in the association, by secret ties, of so many·
men of such varied ability, working in seclusion from public criticism and without
passion. He would feel secure again by knowing that it is only by keeping rigidly to
the work of fostering the interests of the Order, that the dignity, the calm, the free·
dom from passion, the efficiency, are manifest or possible. Let any other question
be intruded here, and there could be no detriment to public interests; for our harmony would break. Volcanic flame and blackness would burst through the lofty.
and snowy peace. By keeping within our limits alone are we prosperous and orderly ;
and within our limits our prosperity is the welfare of the community, the good of the
State, the strengthening of civilization. Rejoice, brethren, in y 0 ur privilege; wan
off from intrusion the garden of order you have received; and guard the book of
your Constitution with the Tyler's sword.
Organization and Order! Inpreservingthese we are iuharmony with the will and
work of the Sovereign Architect, published in the harmony, dignity, and peace of na~
ture. And one other word must be spoken, so familiar, so precious, to the Masonic
ear and heart. You anticipate what it is- Charity. In nature, which speaks the
wisdom and character of the Invisible Spirit, organization is not for the sake of wis·
dom and skill chiefly-order is not for the sake of law and obedience chiefly-but
all for the sake of Charity. There is harmony and stability that there may be
breadth of bounty, constancy in giving wherever there is need. Within every district of nature there is beneficence to all the need within that district, and then a.
pouring out of alms into a general fund of bounty and cheer.
Every mountain upholds and supports the herbage on its slopes, and sends off rills
to carry dovrn soil to the vales and plains, while they feed herbage there. You can
not find a tree, or plant, or flower, that Jives for itself. The animal world breathes out
gases for the vegetable kingdom, and then the vegetable world exhales or stores up
some elements essential to animal health and vigor. The carbonic acid we breathe
out here and which is poison to us, blown eastward by our west winds, may be
greedily taken up, a few days.hence, by vineyards on the slopes of the Sierra, and
returned to us in the sweetness of the grape. The equator" sends greeting" to the
Arctic zone by the warm gulf-stream that flows near the polar coasts to soften
their winds. The poles return a colder stream and add an embassy of icebergs, too,
to temper the fierce tropic heats. Selfishness is condemned by the still harmonies of
the creation. Perfect order issues out of interwoven service.
Do we ever get tired of the toils and tax of charity? Suppose the sun did. What
does it receive in homage or obedience from the orbs that swing round him, in com·
parison with what he gives-all his light, all his heat, all his vitality for the blessing
of four score worlds I Shall we complain of the demand upon our treasuries, or our
private purses, for the sacred funds of the Masonic Board of Relief? What if the sea
grumbled at the assessment which the mighty sun-the Most Worshipful Grand Master
of the system-levies on hia substance? Every day the sun totichei> its stores with itil

wand of light and says give, give. And it obeys. Evaporation is its tax constantly
demanded, constantly given. Remember, brethren, that every cloud you see, whether

Pour a bucket of it on a hill of corn, or a garden bed, and it kills it. The water

You have been for the second time elected to your high station, and this, the

formed the important duties of your exalted office with skill and fidelity to the best

Proceedings of the

[May 16,

Thirteen years ago, he who now addresses you was installed the first Grand
Master of Masons in California ; and it may not be uninteresting to the younger members of the Fraternity to have their attention called to the wondrous changes which
have marked the progress of our beloved Order since that eventful period. The first
Grand Master assumed his station, surrounded only by the representatives of three
chartered Lodges-all that were at that time within the borders of the State ; and
their authority was derived from three Grand Lodges of different States. You,
Worshipful Brother, are about to be installed for the second time, surrounded by the
representatives of nearly one hundred and fifty Lodges, all whom have received
their charters from the Grand Lodge of California. The emblem of his high office,
with which the first Grand Master was invested at his installation, was of plain silver,
(if not of baser metal) borrowed from a subordinate Lodge, and was worn suspended
by a tape string, or faded ribbon. The jewel which you have worn for the past year,
and with which I am now about to again invest you, is of gold, and the hangings
from which it is suspended are of royal purple, most elaborately fringed and wrought
with bullion and threads of the precious metals- the product of our own great
State. The first Grand Master was installed in a Masonic Hall of humble dimensions,
in an obscure place, with space scarcely sufficient for the accommodation of fifty
members. You, sir, are about to be installed within a temple of ample accommodation for thousands, which, for magnificent proportions and architectural beauty, is
unequalled in any of the States of the Union, and is at this time unsurpassed, if
indeed it be equalled, for its splendor and magnificence, by any Masonic Temple upon
earth. This, among other wondrous changes, has been wrought by the devotion of
the Craft to our noble Order in the short space of thirteen years. Wonderful and
progressive as have been all the institutions of our golden State in that short period,
none, no, not one, has equalled in progressive advancement and in usefulness to the
community in which we live, (save and except the religion of the Saviour of man)
that of the Order of Free and Accepted Masons.
Elected twice to preside over such an Order is an honor of which you have justly
a right to be proud. To him who now addresses and installs you, who for nearly
half a century has been a most devoted and faithful servant of the Order, this is one
of the most gratifying moments of life ; and from the inmost recesses of his heart
does he most gratefully thank the Supreme Architect of the Universe for permitting
him to live to see this day, when, surrounded by hundreds of representatives of
Lodges which had no existence when he was first installed Grand Master and guardian
of our infant Order in this new State, he sees this adolescent Masonic Hercules
which has created all the Lodges and Grand Lodges now giving Masonic laws and
orders to our western coasts.
Bro. STEVENSON then proceeded with the installation of the Grand
Master, who afterwards installed the other Grand Officers.

motion did not prevail.

having reported, orally, in favor of the third accompanying resolution,
relative to the salary of a Grand Lecturer, that, with the other resolutions
appended to the report, was adopted.

Total dues to Rep. Fund ......... $3,044 50. Total payments .............. $4,123 50
It will be seen that to twenty-two Lodges no allowance has been made. Of this
number, eleven, viz.: Nos. 1, 17, 22, 30, 44, 120, 125, 127, 136, 139, and 144, though
their dues are paid and they are represented, are located in this city; one, No. 21, is
not included in the resolution authorizing payment; nine, viz.: Nos. 14, 33, 45, 50, 81,
99, 104, 105, and Washoe, U. D., though their dues are paid, are unrepresented; and
one, No. 43, has neither paid its dues nor is represented.
In 1861, the levy for the Representative Fund was one dollar for each member

Proceedings of the

[May 16,

borne upon the rolls of the Lodges at the da.te of the a.nnual returns ; a.nd the product
wa.s $5,723. Of this amount there remained unexpended, as shown by the Grand
Treasurer's report, the sum of $1,8H 110. In 1862, or rather for the year ending February 28, 1863, the levy was but ha.If that amount, being but fifty cents for each member,
and producing, as has been seen, when all shall be paid, the sum of $S,044 50. This,
ajlded to the.balance in the treasury to the credit of that fund, makes a total now or
to be in hand, for its purposes, of $4,869; from which is to be deducted $66 paid since
the accounts were closed on the first day of March last, to Visalia Lodge, No. 128,
for its representation in 1862-leaving $4,794.. The amount now appropriated for
payment of representatives, as seen in the fore~oing s~atement, is $4,123 60; to which
is to be added $48 50 for the payment of the necessary traveling expenses of the
appointed Grand Oftlcers in attendance at this Communication, who are entitled
to receive such payment; making a total probable expenditure for the year from ,
this fund of $4,172, or theres.bouts. There will consequently still be an overplus in
tJ:ie fund of more than six hundred dollars, after all payments for this year shall
have been made.
If Bil the Lodges were represented at this Communication, the amount required
for the pa.yment of their representatives would be about $4,500, and, in the opinion
o( your committee, the expenses for that purpose will not exceed that amount for
some time to come. The total membership of the Craft in this jurisdiction is about
six thousand, so that, to provide for the payment of the representation in future, a.
levy of seventy-five cents upon each Master Mason borne upon the rolls will meet
the wants of this fund, if the payment of representatives is to be contn:ued. Your committee therefore olfer the following resolution, a.nd recommend that 1t be adopted:Resolved, Tha.t for the year ending March l, 1864, there shall be levied upon the
subordinate Lodges, in addition to the dues prescribed by the Constitution, the sum
of seventy-five c~nts for each member borne upon their respective rolls at the date
of their annual returns-to be assessed for the purpose and in the manner provided
in certain resolutions relative to a representative fund adopted on the sixteenth day
of May, 1861, the same being in lieu of one dollar for each member, as therein
directed.
All which is respectfully submitted.
CHARLES lliRsH,

Proposed Amendments to the. Oonstitution of the

Grand Lodge of Oalifornia.

133

PROPOSED AMENDMENTS
TO THE

CONSTITUTION OF THE GRAND LODGE,

RETURNS

To be Finally Acted upon in October, A. L. 5864.

OF THE

1. To strike out, in the second and third lines of Sec. 2, Art. IV, Part VI, the
words" by due notification, to call a special meeting of his Lodge, as soon as practicable, and there cause to be elected, by ballot, and by a majority of those present,"
and insert in lieu thereof the words" to appoint" ; so that that section will read as
follows:SECTION 2. Upon the presentation of such charges, it shall be the duty of the
Master to appoint not less than seven nor more than nine of its members, who shall
assemble as Commissioners, to hear and determine thereupon, at such time and place,
convenient to the parties, as he shall indicate ; and he shall also summon the accused
to appear and answer thereunto at such time and place; and shall, at the same time,
cause the Secretary to furnish him with a copy of the charges, and to notify the
accuser of the said time and place of trial.
2. To strike out, in· the second line of Sec. 2, Art. IV, Part VI, the words" due
notification," and insert in lieu thereof the word" summons"; so that that section
will read as follows :SECTION 2. Upon the presentation of such charges, it shall be the duty of the Mas·
ter, by summons, to call a special meeting of his Lodge, as soon as practicable, and
there cause to be elected, by ballot, and by a majority of those present, not less
than seven nor more than nine of its members, who shall assemble as Commission·
ers, to hear and determine thereupon, at such time and place, convenient to the par·
ties, as he shall indicate; and he shall also summon the accused to appear and
answer thereunto at such time and place; and shall, at the same time, cause the
Secretary to furnish him with a copy of the charges, and to notify the accuser of the
said time and place of trial.

MASTER MASONS:

ADDITIONAL GENERAL REGULATION,
Adopted, May, A. L. 5868.
The appointed Grand Officers and the chairmen of the several standing commit·
tees sball receive payment for their necessary traveling expenses to and from the
place of meeting of the Grand Lodge, in the same manner as ordered for the repre·
sentatives of Lodges ; but no such officer, chairman, or representative, shall receive
payment in more than one of those capacities; nor shall any such officer, chairman,
or representative, receive any pay who shall already have been paid for such necessary traveling expenses by another Masonic Grand Body.

The Grand Master then delivered his Annual Address to the Grand
Lodge, as follows : BRETHREN OF THE GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA:After a long separation we again meet in Grand Lodge, and it gives me great
pleasure to report that all is well with us, and that, from every portion of our widely
extended jurisdiction, the brethren send up good tidings of peace, harmony, and
prosperity. We all know that we have fallen upon evil times; that our country is
involved in civil war-a war of such magnitude and momentous import as the world
never saw before. Every day we read of the march of great armies, of great battles
fought, and of thousands and tens of thousands slain. We know that the homes of our

[ 11 ]

250

Proceedings qf the

[Oct. 11,

childhood have been made desolate, and are filled with sorrow and mourning, for
their young men have gone forth in beauty and strength, and they come not back
again. The sick and wounded, the maimed and helpless, the widow and orphan, in
every village and hamlet of the land give evidence of the dreadful character of the
contest. We are far removed from the scenes of strife, yet with most intense anxiety
do we watch the progress of events. As citizens, we feel deeply, and perhaps some·
times speak bitterly, but I am happy indeed to say that, as Masons, we have contin·
ued to gather around our altars; that no sound of confusion or strife has there been
heard; and that our brethren appear to have remembered the Ancient Charges, and
have sedulously excluded from the Lodges all disputes and controversies about poli·
tics and political matters," as what never yet conduced to the welfare of the r,odge,
nor ever will."
Verily may we say that our lines have been cast in pleasant places. Since Ma·
sonry first erected her altars upon the shores of the Pactllc, her prosperity bas been
unbroken, the harmony and good order of the Craft undisturbed. In October, 1849,
our first Lodge, California, No. I, was established. In April, 1850, our Grand Lodge
was organized, with three chartered Lodges and two under dispensation, and with a
total membership, probably, not exceeding one hundred. Now, we have upon our
register one hundred and forty.three existing chartered Lodges, and eleven under
dispensation, with a total membership of nearly seven thousand.
The presence to-day, at the opening of the Grand Lodge, of representatives from
almost every Lodge of the jurisdiction, assures us that the fires smoulder not upon
our altars; that the Masons of California and Nevada are still fervent in their zeal
and true to their vows; and that they will be zealous and faithful to the end.
Last year we were called upon to mourn the death of Bro. Hm1.PHREY G.&rFFITH,
a Past Grand Orator of this Grand Lodge. To-day the Grand Orator's chair is vacant.
Bro. THOMAS STARR KING, who should have occupied that chair to-day, has fallen into
that sleep which knows no waking. The memory of his slight, frail form is fresh In
the minds of all, but fresher still the recollection of the glowing beauty of his eloquence as he stood before us here at our last meeting. He died in this city on the
fourth day of March last, at the age of thirty nine years, and it was the desire of his relatives and friends that he should be buried as a Mason. The Grand Lodge assembled
by my order to perform that pious duty, and he was so buried in the beautiful church
which he had reared and dedicated to the service of God, and in which he had hoped
for many years to come to minister to his people. But it was not so to be. The
silver cord was loosed, the golden bowl was broken; the spirit returned to God who
gave it, and in sadness we consigned his body to the earth from whence it came.
He was young in years, but if we measure a life by the work it has accomplished,
then was he old and ripe for the reaper's sickle. :B'ew men have accomplished so
much in a life time as he in a few short years. Very few have left such an impress
of themselves upon the people with whom they came in contact. No man had done
so much as he in moulding the opinions of men upon the Pacific coast, in the present
crisis of our national a:IIltirs. A patriot, in the best sense of that noble word, he
stood out as the foremost man of our State. For his country he lived and labored;
for her he died; and the nation mourned his loss. However much some of us may
have dilfered from him in opinion, we all admired his genius, were led entranced by
his eloquence, and loved him for his goodness and the purity and beauty of his life.
As a Mason, he exemplified in his daily walk among men the beautiful precepts we
teach. He was temperate, brave, prudent, and just; a genial friend, an accomplished scholar, a noble man, and a true Mason. We mourn a good brother gone.
My report of official acts is necessarily very brief, as I have had but little to do.
Eleven dispensations for the formation of new Lodges have been issued and Lodges
established under them, four of which were in Nevada Territory. Three applica·
tions for similar dispensations have been refused.

Sundry questions of Masonic law have been proposed to and decided by me, a few
of which I desire to report for your consideration and decision, that the brethren may
be advised.
First. Do the ancient charges require that an applicant for the mysteries of )fa.
sonry must be physically perfect; and, if not, what degree of dismemberment or
deformity shall exclude him?
Several applications for permission to receive the petitions of those who had
been so unfortunate as to lose a leg, or an arm, or an eye, have been made to me. I
have decided that they could not be received, promising in one case, however, in
which the applicant had lost a leg, below the knee, and had supplied himself with
one of cork, to bring the matter to your attention. For myself, I would say, hold
on to a strict construction of the law. It may work a hardship in particular cases,
but, if we once depart from it, there will be no end to the perplexing questions that
will arise in determining whether this or that particular disability should exclude.
Bro. MACKEY, in bis Masonic Jurisprudence, has collated and discussed the authorities upon this subject, with his usual ability, and concludes his chapter on the qualifications of candidates with this summary-that" the person who desires to be made
a Mason must be a man-no woman, nor eunuch; free born, neither a slave, nor
the son of a bond woman ; a believer in God and a future existence ; of moral conduct, capable of reading and writing; not deformed nor dismembered, but hale and
sound in his physical conformation, having his right limbs as a man ought to have."
Second. Should a Lodge entertain charges for unmasonic conduct against a bro·
tl1er because, for any reason, be has neglected or refused to pay his debts, or has
paid them in the Jepreciated currency of the country?
My own opinion has always been that the Lodge was not the proper place for the
settlement of the business difficulties of its members, or the enforcement of the payment of dsbts; and I have so decided in the cases presented. The civil government
has instituted courts, and appointed judges, and authorized juries, for the express
purpose of determining and protecting the rights of citizens, and enforcing the proper
remedies in cases of wrong. If I owe a brother a debt and refuse to pay him, he
may very properly invoke the aid of the Jaw to compel me to do that which I ought
to have done without compulsion. Exceptional cases may occur, involving such
breach of faith and turpitude of conduct that we ought to notice them, even if
they had been oarried by the parties to the proper tdbnnals for adjudication; but
they are the exceptions, not the rule. Masons should deal honestly with one another,
and with all men, and should pay all they owe; but it does not always follow that
any special moral turpitude attaches to them because they sometimes fail to do this
last; and, however much we may disapprove the act of one who avails himself of
the benefits of the laws, and pays debts, perhaps honestly due hi gold, in legal ten·
ders, I think we may properly leave the aggrieved party to charge the blame, if any,
partly upon himself, that be has been so careless and negligent in the management of
his own business. That which the laws of the land sanction, can hardly be an offense
against any law of Masonry.
Third. I have been asked so often to construe Sec. 4, Art. I, Part V. of the Con·
stitution, that it seems proper to repeat here what I have many times decided, in answer
to particular enquiries-1st. That the Master, or any other officer of a Lodge, may
withdraw therefrom in the same manner as any other member, and that whatever
may be the rule elsewhere, our laws make no distinction: and, 2d. That when a
member of a lodge has paid his dues, and at a stated meeting announced his intention
to withdraw his membership, his membership ceases; and he can become a member
again of that Lodge only by petition and ballot, as tn the case of any other nonaffiliated Mason. It is not competent for the Lodge by vote to reinstate him.
Fourth. There seems to be a good deal of uncertainty as to what should be requir·

Fifth. If a Mason forget his duty to God, his fellow, and himself, and commit suicide, shall he or may he be buried by his Lodge with Masonic honors? Several cases
have occurred, as I am informed, in which suicides have been so buried. It should
not always be so. When a Mason has unfortunately been deprived of that reason
which God has given him to enable him to distinguish between right and wrong, and,
being actually demented, deprives himself of life, I see no reason why he should not
be interred with the usual Masonic honors and ceremonials. .Au insane man cannot
commit a crime, and it would be an utter forgetfulness of that charity which is the
brightest jewel of the Craft, to refuse the Masonic rite of burial, when desired by his
relatives or friends, to one who had only been unfortunate. Not so, however, with
one who wittingly, or in consequence of intemperate habits, destroys the life which
Heaven has given him for useful and beneficent purposes. We would throw the
·mantle of charity over the faults of an erring brother, dead or living, but we should
not lightly overlook his crimes. By all law, human and divine, he who takes his own
life is as guilty as be who takes the life of another. Before God and man he is guilty,
and it is not titting that we, as a society, should holcl ourselves out to the world as
the excusers of such crime.
At our last Annual Communication, I was directed, by resolntions then adopted,

and myself, as a committee for the revision of the work and lectures. The appoint·
ments made, and a statement relative to the labors of that committee, will appear in
the Annual Iteport of the Grand Secretary. It is only necessary here to say that its
members unanimously agreed upon the ritual, as finally adopted, and that the result
of their labors will be exemplified before you, at this Communication, in all the degrees, by the skillful brother who accepted the onerous duties of Grand Lecturer.
Our endeavor was to restore, not to change, and it will be noticed that the few alterations made were principally to correct grammatical errors and incorrect forms of
expression. At the conclusion of our labors we were better satisfied than ever
before tbat the work heretofore adopted and practiced in this jurisdiction was generally true and correct, conforming and adhering to the ancient landmarks and
usages of the Order. ilfter all, however, it is not so important to enquire what particular system should be used, as that we use a uniform one - the same work, the
same lectures, in all the Lodges of our jurisdiction. It is idle to hope that every
Master ·of a Lodge can learn and retain the exact phraseology of the lectures ; but he
can approximate it nearly. Let each one throw aside his prejndices against that
which seems to him to be new, and his predilections in favor of the peculiarities of
the work that was tanght him in the first years of his Masonic life, and seek not to
find here a word too much, and there a word too little, as cause for cavil-not to discover differences, but to find agreements, wherein bis system and our system harmonize-and he will soon learn that there is really no substantial difference; that in all
importa.nt and essential particulars all the systems agree, the same great landmarks
are observed, the same great duties are inculcated, the same great truths are illustrated, and then he will be ready to adopt, and, as far as possible, conform strictly to
our work. Whenever the brethren are ready to do that we shall attain and retain
uniformity. It will be easy then, but until then impossible. I trust that we shall

DEAR Sm AND BROTHER.-! have been requested by the Board of Trustees of the
Masonic Hall Association to lay before you a brief atatement of the present condition
of the Masonic Temple here, and to solicit your advice as to the expediency of pro·
posing to the Grand Lodge, at its Communication in October next. a plan for the
completion of the bnilding and extinguishment of its debt, which, by a tax, not burdensome, will in four or live years at most accomplish that object. make the Grand
Lodge the owner of at least one half the property, and, by reason of the revenueA
thus to be derived, enable it thereafter to free the Lodges from all payments of annual
dues of every kind forever.
I ba.ve not had time to prepare a detailed account of the financial affairs of our
Association, and even if I had, it is hardly necessary for the purposes of this com·
!nunication. Briefly. the capital stock was fixed at $150,000, of which abont $115,000
bas been taken and paid for. In addition to this last sum, $100,000 bas been bor·
rowed at l k per cent. per month, and these two amounts constitute the expenditure
for land, building, and furniture thus far. The highest estim•te we have for the entire completion of the edifice is $35,000, which is, as will be seen, about the amount
of the untaken stock. This amount, and much more, doubtless, would ere now have
been additionally subscribed by the Lodges and Masons here but for the evil times
we have fallen upon. During tbe past two years, the expenditures of all the Lodges
in this city for necessary charity have very greatly exceeded what they ever were
before; and th1rn, instead of the surplus which most of them formerly had at the end
of each year, and which was regularly subscribed for the carrying on this work,
there is perhaps not one which ha.shad more than enough left to pay its Grand Lodge
dues. During the same period, the mania for dealing in mining stocks has seized
upon almost every iudivid11al in the city, and the constant draft for assessments, with
the losses, great and small, which have almost invariably attended these mad speculations, have dried up, for the time, a source of supply to our funus from zealous
·brethren here, which otherwise would have tiowed as freely as before.
Thus, for the present, the building stands nntiuiRhed, anu thus, for the reasons
above given, it is likely to stand for a long time to come, unless the Masons of the
State at large shall take some interest in its completion. It is no exaggeration to
say that, when finished, it will be far the most imposing, most commodious, and most
convenient edifice for Masonic purposes in the world; and it is natural to suppose that
all the Masons of California will feel a just pride in seeing our youthful Grand Lodge
he come the possessor of a Temple dedicated to the lienelicent purposes of our Order.
which will so greatly exceed in magnitude, arcl1itectnral beauty, and spaciousness of
accommodation, any hitherto erected by its elder sisters. Beyond this, it will be seen
that, as a mere investment for revenue, the money necessary for its completion will
be not unprofitably employed. Thus far the expenditure, as has been stated, is about
$21.5,000. The monthly rental, at the present time, unfiniiilied as tbe building is,
amounts to $i17o, being over one per cent. per month; and, with the constant ad·
vance of rents in that portion of the city where it is located, consequent upon the
steady march of trade in that direction, and with the entire building completed and
occupied, it is certain that the rental will amount at least to $2500 per month hereaf·

ter. The completed structure costing, in round numbers, at the highest estimate,
$250,000, the revenue then, as now, will amount to one per cent. per month upon the
capital invested, and, in this city, real estate which pays so much as that, is rarely to
be met with. It is to be remembered, also, that the property is exempt from taxa·
tion, so that its income will suffer no diminution from that cause.
Now the suggestion we would present to you is as follows: If a contribution of
twenty-five cents per month were levied by the Grand Lodge upon all the members
of Lodges in the JUrisdiction, the total of such contributions would amount to some
$18,000 or $20,00 per annum; and this, continued during four or five years at the
farthest, would extinguish the debt, complete the Temple, and, with the stock in it
which it now possesses, would make the Grand Lodge the owner of at least one half
the property. Its revenue then therefrom would amount to a sum more than suffi·
cient to meet all its expenses of eveq kind; and it could abolish all payment of
annual or other dues by the subordinate Lodges, and thus free them from taxation
forever. A little calculation will show that this estimate is not extravagant, for,
while now the interest account (lt per cent. per month on $100,000) absorbs over one
half the present revenue, as the debt is gradually diminished, the excess of earnings
to be added to the sinking fund will be rapidly increased; and thus each year a
greater and still greater amount derived from the rentals, can be added to the sums
proposed to be obtained by the contributions as suggested.
It may he objected that there is no reason why the Masons of the State should be
asked to pay for the accommodation of their brethren in San Francisco. They are
not. Each Lodge in the c.ity pays a regular rent for the ball and other rooms it occupies, as do the tenants of the stores beneath ; and, so, instead of contributing to aid
the brethren here, they will do it to create a property for the Grand Lodge, the revenue from which will enable it to relieve them from all assessments in the future.
This seems to us to be a reasonable propositiou, and one which, if carried into
effect, will not only ensure the safety of, and complete the noblest Masonic Temple
in the world, but will be, in a pecuniary point of view, for the real interest of all the
Lodges in the jurisdiction. We submit this for consideration to you, and to others in
different parts of the State, and would be pleased to have your advice in regard to
it. If you approve it, we would be glad to have you make it known as widely as may
be, so that its scope and purpose may be properly understood before the Grand
Lodge meets; as, unless there should be a tolerable approximation to unanimity in
its favor, it would hardly be advisable to pre8ent it to that body. To have such a
measure passed only by a bare majority, or even with a considerable minority opposed to it, would not be desirable, as it would doubtless cause discord and ill-feeling;
and, unless the Lodges, by their representatives, voluntarily undertake to contribute
as proposed, it would be unwise to undertake its enactment.
A detailed statement of the affairs of the Association, giviog their fullest history,
will be ready for presentation to the Grand Lodge, should it be thought proper to
present this project; and, with the hope that you will give it a fair consideration,
I have the honor to subscribe myself,
Yours truly and fraternally,
ALEX. G. ABELL,
President of the .Masonic Hall Association.
The proposition submitted in tbe foregoing commands my heartiest approval.
The object sought to be accomplished-the speedy completion of the noble structure
thus far reared, and so nearly finished, by the munificent contributions of the
Lodges and Masons of San Francisco-will undoubtedly command the best wishes and
ready co-operation of every member of our Order in the jurisdiction. We all feel a
just pride in the beautiful Temple in which we are uow assembled, for the language
of the President of the Association contains no exaggeration when he says that,
"when finished, it will be far the most imposing, most commodious, and most convenient edifice for Masonic purposes in the world"; and I feel confident that no
brother in the State could willingly contemplate the possibility that so splendid a
monument to Masonic enterprise and skill, might, by some financial mischance,
eventually pass into the hands of strangers. The plan suggested as a means of accomplishing the end desired, appears to me most feasible, being easy of execution,
and involving no burden upon the brethren which would be perceptibly appreciated.
The small tax of twenty·five cents per month proposed, if collected regularly,
would hardly be felt by the poorest among us; and yet the aggregate of those almost
imperceptible contributions, together with the sinking fund now derived from the

rentals of the building, constantly increasing as it would be, in four or five years at
the most, would complete the structure, cancel the indebtedness, and make our.
Grand Lodge the owner of at least one-half the property.
J commend the project to your favorable consideration, not alone because of the
generous interest we should all feel in the happy termination of a work so honorable
to the Craft of our Golden State. Viewed simply as a sound financial measure, it
ought to meet with favor. This almost imperceptible contributioo, for the few years
named, would put the Grand Lodge in possession of an interest in the property,
yielding an annual revenue of $12,000, or $13,000, (probably more in the fntUl'e,)-a

for tl1e future would be cheaply purchased in the way proposed; and I commit the
subject to yon, with the expression of my belief that the honor of the Craft and tl!e
pecuniary interests of the Lodges will both be advanced by yonr lavorable action
upon the proposition as submitted.
In conclusion, let me express the hope that our proceedings at this Communication may be characterized by that harmony and fraternal bearing which should ever
illustrate the intercourse of Masons in their deliberntivc bodies ; and that our legiR·
lation, guided by prudence and wisdom, may be such as will redound to our own
credit, and be promotive of the best interests of our Order.

It is with regret that the undersigned finds it necessa.ry to report that four further
vacancies have ~ccurred_in the numbers of Lodges upon our registry.
. In.Ju~~ last, rnformation ':as received from Rising Sun Lodge,Xo. 153, at Brandy
City, lll oierra County, that, m consequence of the removal of many of its members
from that locality, thus leavmg an insufficient number to successfully carry on its
operations; and in consequence, further, of the destruction of its hall, charter, and
other property by tire, in November last, it had been resolved, on the sixteenth day
of July, 1864, to cease work in that Lodge, and to ask the Grand Lodge to accept a
surrender of the authority under which it had existed. The dues of the Lodge, to
the close of' the last fiscal year, are paid, and all that appears to have remained of
such property as it had-its Record Book and Book of Accounts-have been trans·
mltted to this office, and are herewith submitted.
Three days ago a communication was received from Gilroy Lodge, No. 159,
setting forth that, on the twenty-eighth day of September, 1864, for reasons given in
the record ot a meeting at that date, which are apparently sufficient, that Lodge, in
the manner prescribed by law, had voted to surrender its charter, and to pray the
Grand Lodge to accept its action in that respect. The returns and dues of the
Lodge, for the fiscal year, have been received, and its charter, seal, books, jewels,
papers, &c., have been transmitted to this office.
Yesterday a statement was received from the Master of Butte Lodge, No. 36, giving
information that in consequence of the removal of most of the members of that Lodge
from the place of its location, it had become difficult to procure the attendance of
th~ number required by our laws for the transaction of business; und therefore it bad
been resolved, on the third day of September last, to surrender its charter and pray
the Grnnd Lodge that its organization be declared extinct. The dues of the Lodge
are nearly paid, and the small balance remaining will doubtless be account!Jd for.

MIN B. P.&ENCH, of Washington, D. C., the undersigned has been enabled to perform

wherever our Order has been planted in North America, and whose memory is espe·

diction, as eloquently set forth iu the report of a committee at our last Communication. The undersigned would consider this portion of his report sadly unfinished did
he fail to express his obligations, ln this respect, to Bro. PRENCH. Known to be the

invoked, and the hearty aud zealous readine;ss with which it was afforded will be
seen iu the correspondence herewith submitted. But for Huch assistance, the under·
signed knows not how he could have fulfilled the wishes of the Grand Lodge in this
respect.
4th. Two amendments to the Constitution were proposed at the last Communica·
I.ion, and were ordered to be published in the usual manner for final action at the
present one. See pages 96, \18, an, and 132, printed proceedings of 186J.
The first proposes to change the manner of selecting Commissioners for trials, by
rlirecting that they be nppointed by the Master instead of being elected by the
Lodge:
And the second proposes to change the mode of citation of members of Lodges
to attend special meetings when Commissioners are to be chosen, by directing tbat
they be " summoned " instead of being " notified."
lt is gratifying to be enabled to etate that the recommentlation of the Committee
on By-Laws, at the last Annual Communication, which was concurred in by the
Grand Lodge, has app.areutly hail a very beneficial effect; and that there are now but
three Lodges under our jurisdiction which haYe not adopted the Uniform Code, as
presented some years ago. It is proper, however, again to call the attention of sCY·
cral of the Lodges to the fa0t that their by-Jaws were printed before the adoption
of our last Constitution in 1859, and that they contain a number ofrefereuces to sundry articles and sections in the former one, as well as to certain regulations for trials,
theretofore in use, which arc no longer applicable, thus rentlering them liable to
produce misapprehen~iou and error. Jn this respect many corrections have been
made since the last Communication, and it will be owing to no lack of persistency
on the part of the undersigned if more are not made during the year to eome.
Sundry proposed amendments to the by-laws of chartered Lodges have been
received during the year, all which, with two or three exceptions, (received but
recently,) have been approved by the Grand Master, as they involved only those
cliangcs which, under certain restrictions, are permitted in the C niform Code; and they
are now presented for the action of the Grand Lodge, Accompanying these will
al:io be found copies of the by-laws of the several Lodges acting under dispensation.

In relation to the library, and the receipt of the printed transactions of the other
Grand Lodges with which we are in correspondence, full information will be found in

It will be recollected that, at the last Annual Communication, the Grand Master
stated in his address that, in response to a communication from the Rev. and M.-. W.-.
Bro. J. N. McJmroN, Grand Master of ]\[aryland, asking an appropriation of fifty
dolJa,rs, for the purpose of aiding to secure the services of a ]l[asonic Chaplain in the
hospitals of Washington and its vicinity, he had readily pledged the fraternity here
for that amount; and it will also be remembered that the committee to whom his
address was referred, especiaUy commended his action in that respect, and that the
Grand Lodge concurred in the report of that committee. By an oversight, however,
no appropriation for the purpose was referred to or reported by the Committee on
Finances, as our laws require; and thus there was no lawful authority for transmitting
the amount above named. Upon consultation, however, with the Grand Master, a
few weeks ago, there seemed to be no reason to doubt that it was the intention of
the Grand Lodge to approve his promise and have it carried into effect, and a gold
draft for fifty dollars was accordingly dispatched to Bro. McJ1LTo~; but should this
b~ an error, and the Grand Lodge disapprove tl1e act, the money will at occe be
returned to the Treasury by those who committed the mistake.

Total of del.il;lqMnt dues .A.nglll!t 31, 1864.,. ...•.. $1,692 50 $749 15 ~
Since the date above given, $1,422 25 of the $2,442 2.5 then delinquent, have been
received, and there is little doubt that most, if not all, the remainder will be paid up
before the issue of the published proceedings.
The usual statement of payments up to that period, and of the delinquencies, If
any, then existing, will appear at the end of the printed journal.
The returns from all the Lodges, save two acting under dispensation, have been
received, and those will doubtless be at hand to·day. The regularity which has
characterized the action of the Lodges under our jurisdiction, in this respect, for
several years past, certainly contrasts most favorably for them with the reports we
hear from so many other Grand Lodges relative to the numerous failures of their sub.
ordinates to make returns; and it is earnestly to be hoped that the good reputation
thus earned by our Secretaries will long continue to be deserved.
All which is respectfully submitted.
ALEX. G• .A.BELL, Grand Secretary.

Comprising, thus far, three hundred and forty-six valuable and handsomely bound
volumes, devoted entirely to matters appertaining to Freemasonry.
There 11re, besides, many publications of our sister Grand Lodges still remaining
upon our files unbound; some, because a sufficient number has not yet been received
to make up additional volumes of the average size in the foregoing list, and a few
still for the lack of intermediate numbers to complete a series. This last deficiency,
through the kindness of several of the Grand Secretaries, has been remedied to a considerable extent during the past year; and the undersigned yet has faith that time
and perseverance will furnish a remedy complete. That no exhibition of the latter
means may be lacking on his part, he again presents for the information of his brother
Secretaries, a memorandum of those Grand Lodges whose series of proceedings in
our possession are defective, as follows: MICHIGAN, for 1862. This would complete our files of that Grand Lodge from
1848 to 1864, inclusive.
MINNEsO:rA, for 1861 and 1862. With these our series would be complete from the
organi,zation of that Grand Lodge to and including the year 1863.
Omo, for 1862. This would make our records of that Grand Lodge complete from
its o)'ganization to and including the year 1863.
From South Carolina nothing has been received since 1859; from Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Tennessee, and Virginia, nothing since 1860; and from Mississippi,
nothing since 1861. The reasons for the interruption of communications with the
Grand Lodges of these States are too well known ; and we can only hope for the
speedy termination of a conflict, which, with other peaceful blessings, shall bring
with it a resumption of fraternal correspondence with our brethren of the South. ·
The undersigned is glad to avail himself of'lchis opportunity to publish, on behalf
of our Grand Lodge, his thanks to the Grand Lodge of Maryland and its present efficient Grand Secretary, the R .._ W.'. JACOB H. MEDAIRY, for the five volumes of the
transactions of that b.ody, mentioned in the preceding catalogue - a present all the
more welcome because for several years every effort to supply the deficiencies in
our files from that State had he.en unsuccessful. To the Grand Lodge of Iowa, also,
we are indebted for the third volume of its proceedings, being from 1859 to 1863;
as also to the R. ·. W. ·. Bro. RICHARD VAUX, of Philadelphia, for certain missing numbers of the transactions of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania, which the undersigned
had been unable to o.b.tain from other sour-0es, and which complete our series for
that jurisdiction from 1851 to 18113, inclusive: and to Bro. ANDREW ToRNING, Past
Senior Warden of the Lodge of Harmony, No. 814, New South Wales, the thanks of
the Grand Lodge are. due for a rare copy of Clavel's Histoire Pittoresque de la
Franc-Ma9onnerie.
All which is respectfully submitted.
ALEX. G. ABELL, Grand Secretary.

Bro. GILBERT B. CLAIBORSE, from the Committee on Correspondence,
presented the following report, the reading of which was dispensed with,
the members being furnished with printed copies thereof:To the M." W. ·. Grand Lodge of California : We present the following report, which has been prepared with respect for the
rules which governed the committee last year. Some subjects considered by us
have not received the careful consideration they deserved. Had we given it, we
would now take leave of our position with more satisfaction. Others which might
have been profitably noticed have been passed by. We offer no apology for our
omissions, because the custom is too commou, but console us with the hope that our
successors, whose appointment we must respectfully. ask, will profit by a confess·
ion and avoid our example. In the main we believe we have collected and presented the chief occurrences in Maeonry· which have come to light since the last Commn·
nication.

reasons:"I thought it right to decline being present - first, because my attendance might
have been looked upon as an unauthorized interference in a domestic quarrel, with
which Canada has nothing to do, - and, secondly, because no Southern Brethren
could have an opportunity of giving expression to their feelings. But, although as
your Grand Master, I considered it proper to observe a Masonic neutrality, I convey·
ed the assurance that the Gi·anll Lodge would be exceedingly glad to witness a hap·
py conclusion to this terrible estrangement between men and nrethren belonging to
the same nation - a restoration of ancient good feeling and common brotherhood
and a stop put to the deadly animosity that the force of daily events demonstrates
does really exist, and that she would gladly cooperate towards such a result, if she
could do so with propriety and certainty."
This was approved as prudent and conservative action. The receipt of our vol·

BUNNELL, GEORGE W., said to be a resident of Fair Haven, within the jurisdiction of
a Lodge there, sought his fortunes on the briny deep, a.nd like the Ancient Mariner
sailed
"Alone, alone, all, all alone,
Alone, on the wide, wide sea."
He sailed his vessel out of and back again into the harbor of Xew York, and made it
bis principal port; he was a sea.faring ma.n. In this port he sought knowledge of
the hidden mysteries, and being a worthy man, the vail was drawn aside and dark·
ness became light unto him, because a regulation of the Grand Lodge of New York,
although it declared that no Lodge should initiate, pass, or raise a candidate from
another jurisdiction until he had resided twelve months with them, or had the re·
commendation of the jurisdiction in which he had previously lived, said also the rule
should not apply to the sea-faring or military man, and so they made him a Mason.
GEORGE went back to Fair Haven like a young mother with her first-born to her pa·
rents, sought admittance to a Lodge, and came away grieved and mortified with the
impression that he was refused, and that he had left the reputation behind of having
been il'regularly made. And so it would seem he had occasion to feel, because
some one had probably told him, what is true, that in Connecticut a regulation ex·
ists, which is very general in the jurisdictions now, that residents during a sojourn
elsewhere who receive degrees without permission from the Lodge nearest their
residence shall not be recognized. The sea-faring man told his grief to Bro. JosEPII
D. Ev&Ns, who is the Representative of Connecticut near the Grand Lodge of New
York, who caused it to be communicated to Grand Master HYDE, who laid it before
his Grand Lodge ; and the committee who examined it said that one fact was estab·
Jished by the papers, namely, BUNNELL was not refused admittance as a visitor, but
that he appeared in the ante·room and was advised not to apply on that evening, as
the Lodge was engaged in a. case of discipline, and he withdrew. The case was dismissed, the complainant being non-suited, having failed to make out his case. The

The leading feature of interest is the act granting a dispensation to certain Masons residing in Alexan1lria, Virginia, authorizing them to form a new Lodge. When
the petition was first presented to the Grand Master, he summoned the Ora~ to meet

the Oonstitntion of the Grand Lodge of .the District in the case of applications for

there are no working Lodges in the City of Alexandria, the ~.barters can not be

Federal Union.*
In submitting the application, the Grand Master declared that under ordinary cir·
cumstances such a petition could not have been for a moment entertained in the
jurisdiction, because to grant such a dispensation would have been a clear invasion
of the territory of a sister Grand Lodge, and an act which the Masons of the country have uniformly repudiated ; but that the question presented was, whether the
phsent state of things would justify them in establishing a new precedent in order
to afford brethren of the loyal part of Virginia the i·ights and benefits of the Order.
We employ his own language to show how the question was submitted, and how
clearly, in his own estimation even, he was invited to perform an act without precedent and in opposition to well-established rules in the jurisprudence of .b'reemasonry.
After the subject was discussed the dispensation was directed to issue, and the deter·
mination carried with it-because it is associated in the Address-the opinion of
the Granq. Lodge of the District that the Grand Lodge of Virginia is not loyal to 'the
Federal Government, or politically sound in its ideas of government, and such being the
case, her jurisdictional rights are not to be respected, and therefore that part of Vir·
ginia cut off from communication with its Grand Lodge is territory fairly open to
any and all Grand Lodges, as much so as if it had never enjoyed Masonic privileges.
We have therefore presented to us the strange anomaly of a Grand Lodge constituting itself a tribunal for the consideration of political matters or offenses, and ar·
raigning another upon charges of disloyalty.

This is the first instance we have found where the present war has seriously
brought jurisdictions in conflict, developing a disposition to change the boundaries,
and we do not feel prepared to acknowledge that the Masonic Fraternity can, con1i1tently with its traditions, declare a district of country a territory within the political meaning of the word, or in any other sense, where the sovereignty of a Grand
Lodge is already asserted and exercised. Jealous of the danger which threatened
the unity of the brotherhood, we doubted the policy of granting dispensations for
traveling Lodges, especially with authority to make Masons, because we believed it
would give ground for a charge of hostility on the part of one Grand Lodge to another; that it would be the means by which a great many unworthy persons would
enter; and because, to use a reason urged by Grand Master DRUMMOND, of Maine,
the knowledge acquired of character in camp is not sufficient to enable the Frater·
nity to determine whether the petitioner will be an ornament or a disgrace to us. As
he says again, it requires time to develop character, and the best test of fitness is
that which he bears at home. We have other reasons which fix our convictions and
sustain us in our aspiration for the future welfare of Masonry: we look forward to
the day, which is to come, when governmental differences will be adjusted, and then
the Craft can be calmly and wisely regulated in its duty and relation to political
States and boundaries ; and we have encouraged the hope that then, while mutual
demands and concessions are being made, our organization will or should stand soli·
tary and alone, having safely and honorably passed the fiery ordeal of civil war, itself only conscious of the extent of good it has accomplished, with none to upbraid,
but all to thank us, if we succeed. This happy condition, the best that we can anticipate, will result from the policy, if adhered to, to trust the statesman with the di·
rection of the affairs of State, the churchman with the Church, while we govern our
acts by the general and local laws of our Society. We will then appear with a rec·
ord void of offense, innocent of having violated the rights of others, with no grievances to be redressed or forgiveness to ask. This hope has induced us, wherever
we have had influence, to discourage the practice, which we believe to be wrong, of
a Grand Lodge extending its authority into debateable land and trusting its seal
within the borders of a sister jurisdiction where its existence depends upon the success of arms. We viewed such acts as the beginning of an evil and the inauguration
of a practice which will ultimately cause confusion.
The early territorial ·condition of California, and the existence of the severalsuh·
ordinate Lodges here at that time, organized under authority of Grand Lodges of
older States, is cited in support of the course which is pursued by the Grand Lodge
of the District: we think it inapposite, and very fraternally protest against it in jus·
tice to ourselves and the Grand Lodges generally, for since ours was organized and
supreme authority established we have never invaded another jurisdiction, and none
other has invaded ours, except in accidentally making Masons of persons who belonged to another jurisdiction, and in such cases reparation has invariably been
made when the error was discovered and made known. Our boundary for a while
was undefined and unasserted, but since the day that the Masons assembled in Con·
vention at Sacramento and formed a Grand Lodge with supreme Masonic power and
proclaimed its jurisdiction, it has commanded, received, and reciprocated the re·
spect, comity, and fraternity of all we have had intercourse with, which we pray
may continue ; and we do not think that a Grand Lodge ought ever to tolerate invasion
under any circumstances, or accept any change but such as is made by the State in
the chacn"e of its political boundary, which is the accepted definition of Masonic jurisdictio; of Grand Lodges in the States of America. The authorities on this last
point are abundant, and may be met with in nearly all the reports. Even then the
change should be so plainly established and confirmed, and so patent, that argument

which it Is our duty as Masons to accept. For the same reason, increase of authority

The genius of Preemasonry and we contemplate the powers of Supreme Exec·
utive Bodies- can hardly be urged with good grace to accept an advantage which•
the enforced condition (when arms enter laws are silent) oilers, as giving addi·
tional strength to its temporal interests. When the F'ederal army entered Freder·
icksburg, no true Mason sought the relics consecrated by WASHINGTON as a trophy,
and the same spirit we doubt not animated the true Mason of the Confederate army
when it invaded Pennsylvania. When arms enter, as the Grand Master STANSBUR;
says," the government defacto is that which we must respect" as Masons, even if
it is not our choice, and this is but another form of expression of the establi•hed
doctrine that a Mason must "give no umbrage or ground of political jealousy to the
government for the time being." There can be no doubt in tl1e minds of just men
that the Masons who were attached to the Confederacy, and who remained at Alex·
andria as non-combatants, were bound as citizens by the teachings of the Order to
show no disrespect to the civil or military authority which controlled ; and if their
natures were too earnest, then the true course to pursue was to place themselves
within the jurisdiction of authorities for whom they entertained affection.
From all sources of Masonic information, we learn that our Fraternity as an or·
ganization is essentially inoffensive, faithful entirely to its obligations, to individuals
~nd Government; and even while declaring its faith and affection for the Govern·
ment under which it has for a time prospered, it is as a body respectful to the de
facto successor of its de jure government. And yet a true Mason, in his character
as soldier, while conscientiously assuming duties and responsibilities which set him
at war with others, wlll not parade his Order or bring his Masonic character in con·
fiict with governmental powers, any sooner than the true Christian soldier, in the
practice of his profession of arms, will parade his church; neither will he disregard,
when the clangor of arms and smoke of battle dies away from the stricken field, the
recognized claim which his wounded antagonist has upon him.
Very sensibl<, tbatwe may draw upon us some sharp criticism of our views, possibly
invidious, still we feel that we would have evaded an important question if we said less;
and as this is not an interference with the domestic affairs of the Grand Lodge whose
action we are considering, but an opinion concerning an eccentric act which must
engage the attention of the other Grand Lodges, the committee, ~ndeavoringfa,ithfully
to present the most prominent events of the year connected with the Cratt, do not
deem it proper to keep back or conceal their opinion, which is opposed to the course
of the Grand Lodge of the District of Columbia, in establishing a new Lodge
within the jurisdiction of another Grand Lodge, without consent,- which is ei·
ther an invasion, or a virtual declaration of suspension of Masonic intercourse be·
tween the jurisdictions. Believing that the temporary good which is. conte1;11plat".d
will be far overborne by the alienated sentiment and distrustful feehng which will
grow up between the two antagonistic juriodictions, we no more justify this act of
invasion than that of New York by Hamburg, or Maine by the Provincial Grand
Lodge of New Brunswick, for these were set on foot in time of pea~e, and this is
done in time of war ; \ind to increase the power or extend the authonty of a Grand
Lod"e by the assistance which civil war accidentally gives, reminds us too much of
the :uergetic manner in which the prophet whose shrine is at Mecca spread his reli·
gion.

During this year a subordiate in the Pennsylvania jurisdiction directly communicated to the Grand Lodge of the District its request that the subordinates of the
latter should be informed that all applications made by persons living within its jurisdiction to be made Masons shall be made known to it in P'ennsylvania before the
petition is acted on. The committee to whom the case was referred reported back a
resolution, declaratory of the well known law, that it is unmasonic and improper for
any subordinate Lodge to confer degrees of Masonry upon an applicant who is a
resident within the jurisdiction of another Grnnd Lodge, unless leave has been ob·
tained from the subordinate within whose jurisdiction the applicant resides. The,
committee at the s&me time express an opinion which was approved, and which we
think ought to be understood and practiced, that a Grand Lodge can not in justice
to other Grand Lodges, and in view of its own dignity, entertain_ communications
from a subordinate of another jurisdiction: and we may add, without destroying all
system and violating the rules which regulate representative bodies in their inter·
course with each other.

Our immediate predecessors at the last Communication directed attention to the
existence of the so-called order of " Conservators" as a dangerous orgaD.izatlon. It
was discovered and denounced by the Grand Lodge of Illinois, whereupon upwards
of sixty Masons came forward and signed the following confession and renunciation:
"Ta the M.-. W.·. Grand 1>laster," &c.: "The undersigned, members of and constituting the Conservators' Association of
the State of Illinois, do beg respectfully to state that they believe the purposes of
said Association to be strictly Masonic and loyal to this Grand Lodge, and that we
here make the assertion individually, upon our honor as Master Masons, that we have
never for one moment entertained the idea of violating or evading any edict of this
Grand Lodge, or its constituted authorities, and we repudiate the thought as unwor·
thy of us or our brethren. But it appears to us that the continuance ot said Association would have the effect to create confusion and discord among brethren of this
jurisdiction, owing to its objects being misunderstood; and being desirous of healing
all dissension, and meeting our brethren in the truly Masonic spirit of conciliation and
br(}therly love, we do hereby withdraw from said Association, and do declare it dis·
S(}lved."
We give the brethren as much credit as they deserve for gracefully abandoning
an injudicious plan for the accomplishment of what they b.elieved a just purpose;
but it seems to us that it did not require much wisdom to foresee that such an associ·
ation would breed distrust among the Fraternity, so soon as it was suspected that a
secret organization existed within the body of the Craft, known only to a few, and
whose objects were veiled from their knowledge and withheld from their confidence.
Of course misunderstanding and distrust was natural. v;'hen the Grand Lodge finds
it necessary to declare by resolution that the use of cypher meets with its condem·
nation, that it ls contrary to our obligation as Masons, and a further resolution re·
quires all such as have forgotten their obligation to surrender the evidences" printed
or written in cypher," it is wild work they have been at, we fear, and it is a strange
moral opthalmic epidemic which pervades the jurisdiction. We are startled with
the suspicion that a lineal descendent of Cagliostro has arisen to harass us.
An oration was delivered by the R.·. w.-. Bro. BRUMWELL, Grand Orator, which
we think will win admiration everywhere it is read. In it there is an ingenious allegory of exceeding beauty and literary merit, which rebukes Intolerance and illus·
trates the grace of Charity. It is much too long for insertion here, but we hope that
it will find its way into the Monthly Reviews.

"In that address, the Committee term the Work a National System, and, with true
Masonic modesty, they remarked that they believed it to be in accordance with the
Ancient Landmarks and usages of the Craft.
"This Work, by way of distinction, has been called the' Baltimore Work,' as if it
were distinct and different from other work. Upon this point I will let Bro. CHARLES
W. MooRE, one of the Committee, and who reported the Work, speak for himself
and Convention :"BOSTON, February 15, 1863.
"R. W. Baas.:" Brethren: Your note of the 5th instant came to hand by due course of mail, and
has received as much attention as my other engagements would allow. My answer
must necessarily be brief.
" The ' Baltimore Work' was intended to be a restoration of the English lectu.res,
as modified by Webb. I gave the lectures to the' Committee on the Work,' fresh
from Gleason's instruction. Being a kindred of mine, he took especial pains to prepare me to do so before I left home for the Convention. I also reported verbally and
without notes, every amendment adopted by the Committee to the Convention itself.
These amendments I snbsequently noted down, and have them now in my possession.
They were very slight-mostly verbal and grammatical, and do not affect the general
character of the lectures-and they are also very few. There was no talk in the
Convention about York Work, for the Fraternity of this country then neither knew
nor cared but very little abont Rites. They wanted the old Masonic Work, practiced
by their fathers-and a< it came from England-which, to them, was the home of
Masonry. They wisely rested contentedly here.
Fraternally yours,
CHAS. W. MOORE.
"In commenting subseqnently upon the results attained by the Convention, Bro.
MOORE, in his Magazine, says:"'The system of Work a.nd Lectures adopted may have its imperfections; but it
is believed to be more free from them than any other system in this country, if not in
the world. It is the Ancient York Bite, whjch, in our opinion, is the only true and
legitimate Rite. It is the Rite practiced by our fathers. It is the tree which they
transplanted from their fatherland, and have entrusted to our care. It had begun to
decay. Unfaithful hands had engrafted on it shoots of a foreign growth. These have
been cut off. The decayed brnnches have been restored to their natural health, and
it again stands forth in its primitive verdure and beauty, with its many roots riveted
to the soil, and its broad limbs spread in bold outline to the storm and the sunshine.
The system recommended by the Convention has been very properly termed the
NATIONAL SYSTEM, in the belief that it is destined to become what its name imports.'
"Having shown that this Baltimore Work was and is the Webb and York Work,
sometimes known as the HUTCHINSON Lectures, I will now proceed to show how and
when it was introduced into Illinois.

No unnecessary Jaws ought to exist in Masonry, and the violation of its laws ought
not to be considered technical. The objection which holds here was once before
raised, and an issue was created between the Grand Lodges of Virginia and New
York, whether illegal or clandestinely made Masons, however innocent they may be
of the act, can or ought to be cured in any other way than by remaking? Should
such a case arise in our jurisdiction by inadvertence or oversight, the true and only
course which in our opinion should be pursued would be to heal by remaking, and
that process we believe to have been correctly illustrated in 1813, by the Grand Lodge
in England in the ever-memorable reunion of the so-called modern and ancient Ma·
sons, which restored harmony and caused the affiliation of those two bodies which
were for so long a time separated by pride. It was adopted in 1859 by the M.·. W:.
Jom< W. SiMONS, then Deputy Grand Master, who was commissioned to act, by the
Grand Lodge of New York, in the matter of the adjustment of difficulties with certain
refractory subordinates in that jurisdiction, calling themselves St. John's Grand
Lodge. By his wisdom the errors were avoided which bad. been protested against
more resolutely and decidedly by the Grand Lodge of Virginia, on account of the
unceremonious and hasty method pursued a few years previous in the adjustment of
the difficulties in the same jurisdiction with the Phillips organization. The difficulty
last referred to was one of so great peril, and cloucl3 hovered which seemed so fuught
with disaster, that the most approved and discreet chiefs consented to a questionable
act thA.t good might be. accomplished, anti chey permitted the true rule to be set
aside, and by an immense sweep the Grand J,odge gathered into the fold and healed
and anointed, by resolution, ftocks of c ,a:11lestiue nnd truant Masons ; some of the
latter they had ouce known as true meu, but the former had never worn the
wedding garment in their presence.
We have always thought as the Grand Lodge of Virginia did in the matter, that it
would have been Masonic to have practically healed them by remaking, according to
the English precedent, instead of technically doing so by resolution. However that
may be now, we are willing to rely on the judgment of those distinguished brethren
who closed the breach, and acc,ept their work as the end of controversy; but we are
not willing that it should stand as a precedent on this continent, to be hereafter
referred to as a correct mode of procedure, and obtain as a principle of the common
Jaw of Masonry, without protesting against it. We take occasion by the hand, in
order that the case in Indiana may be brought to the attention and consideration of
our Craft, to express this opinion : that an illegally or clandestinely made Mason
cannot be healed by a resolution, but must be healed by re-making, whether that
re·making be by presenting a petition de novu to a subordinate Lodge in form, as if
he had never known the inside of a Lodge; by application to the Grand Master for a
dispensation to ballot for him; or, as is the custom in some juriodictions where the
local law does not make provision, by presenting himself' before the Grand Master,
who may call to his assistance a sufficient number of brethren to enable him, for good
and satisfactory reasons of his own, to re-make or heal him ; and that is what we call
making a Mason at sight or will.
A resolution was adopted giving power to subordinates to reprimand, suspend, or
expel members for non-payment of dues, but recommending that in c11.ses of inability
that their dues be remitted. There are now two hundred and ninety-three chartered

"BALTHIO!IE, January 28, 1863.

"It is an antique chair of simple pattern, valuable only for its association with the
early history of M.asonry in Mary1and. This relic was originally the property of Jo1rn
Co ATES, M. D., of Easton, Talbot Co., Md., and used by him daily as his favorite seat
during the later years of his life. It was subsequently owned by the intimate friend
and companion of Dr. Coates, JAMES PRICE, Esq., of Talbot, who for more than half
a century filled with great ability the office of Register of Wills in that County. From
the hands of this venerable citizen, it passed into my possession.
"Dr. JOHN COATES was an eminent Chirurgeon and Physician. Little of his history
can be gleaned. He is said to have fitted out a company at Philadelphia during the
Revolution, at his own expense, and served himself, in the Canada campaign under
Arnold. Here he contracted an intimacy with that most remarkable man, A.ARON
BuRR, which continued until the death of Dr. COATES. He was the first Graud Master
of the Grand Lodge of Maryland, and his remains having been exhumed by the Masonic Fraternity, several years subsequent to his demise, were removed with much
ceremony to Christ Church, Easton, where they now lie under a chaste obelisk erected
to his memory by the Order of which he was an illustrious member, and at one time
the head.
"With most agreeable recollection~ of our past friendship, extended through
many years, and a cordial appreciation of its freslineeg and constancy in these sad,
changeful times,
"I am, very sincerely, yours,
" CHRIS. C. COX."

Grand Master McJILTON claims that,
"It may be proper here to state that Bro. JOHN BARNEY, Grand Lecturer nf Ohio,
who t1iught the system of tl1e National Convention of 1843, in several jnrisdictions,
as the National system, was a member of the Convention. He used and tau.u;ht the
system of the Convention as the same that bad been received by him in the year
18B, from the best Masonic experience in the country. It was not, therefore, with·
out good and sufficient reason that Maryland re0eived and used the National system
of the Convention. That system was approved and adopted by the Grand Lodge on
the 24th day of May, 184'.J, which was seven days after the adjournment of the Convention. Consistent with her action in 1843, the Grand Lodge of Maryland, in 1863,
is engaged 111 examining her work with the view of removing any discrepencies that
may have been produced, and of restoring tlle same to the condition in which it was
sent forth as the National system by a National Convention ordered for the purpose."
The Grand Lodge of Missouri has recently been engaged in doing the same thing.
Bro. O'SuLLIV •N being the repository of this work as reported by Bros. CARNEGY and
FosTER, who were sent to Baltimore as Representatives of the Grand Lodge of Mis·.
souri. At this Special Meeting that dangerous and insidious organization self-styled
"ConservatorA of Symbolic Masonry" was thoroughly exposed by the Grand Master,
with the aid of Bro. FENTON, of Michigan, whose Address and Expose he refers to for
facts which are admitted by the Chief Conservator. We unreservedly and cordially
endorse the doctrines, as soundly correct, thus laid down by him, in their general
and special application.
"It is here asserted, as Maryland Masonic doctrine, that no brother or number of
brethren can possess the right officially to organize any association within the body
of Masonry, either in its connexion with a single jurisdiction, or to be associated with
any nnmber, or with all the jurisdictions of the United States. No brother or number
of brethren can possess the right officially to organize such an association in Mary·
land. ·The Grand Lodge of Maryland is the supreme authority within its own juris·
diction, which is bounded by the Jines of the State. No Masonic order can be issued
without its sanction. No Masonic association can be organized within the limits of
its aut.hority, .without its consent.
" It is here further asserted as Maryland Masonic doctrine, that no individual Mason has the right to associate. himself with any unofficially authorized organization,
either within the jurisdiction of Maryland, or within the jurisdiction of any other
Grand Lodge, or purporting to be associated with any or all the jurisdictions of the
United States, of which Maryland is one. Maryland has always held and taught, and
now holds and teaches the doctrine that all unauthorized voluntary associations com·
posed of Masons, are clandestine bodies, and that such bodies a.re utterly and entirely
inconsistent with the genius and spirit of the Masonic institution."
There are about forty Lodges in this jurisdiction.

Among the dispensations granted for new Lodges, one was issued for Pembina in
Dakotah Territory, which is, as he states, the most northern point in the territor; of
the United States, and where a large amount of emigration concen,trates traveling between the oceans. It is situated on the banks of the North Red River, at a point
where the American water takes leave of the land of its fountains, and Bowing directly
north into the British domain, mingles with Lake Winnipeg. Has not the location of
this Lodge an unappreciated significance, which ought to suggest a reflection and remind us of the true purposes of our Fraternlty? How Masonry should take pattern from

the stream which marries the physical geography of the countries as it rushes
a.long iUI bed, ignoring the distinction which peoJJles place upon its waters; the
