We copy the admonition he gives to his Craft; it may be read profitably by ours:
"Brethren, I wish to call your attention to a few matters, not irre~ularities exactly,
bnt inattentions - matters that are often thought of little moment, m themselves, but
that are really important in the aggregate :"1st. Reading of the Constitution of the Grand Lodge, the ancient Charges, and
the old Regulations. These are not accessible to every Mason, but should be in the
possession of every Lodge, and frequently read,• that none may plead ignorance of
the excellent precepts t!iey contain.'
"2d. The proceedings of the Grand Lodge are printed for the instructiou and in·
formation of the Lodges. They are required to be read in every Lodge as soon after
they are received as convenient. In how many Lodges is this done? Every Mason
is required, in his Masonic action, to be governed by and pay obedience to the resolutions and edicts of the Grand Lodge. The printed proceedings are the medium by
which the Craft are authoritatively informed of the resolutions and edicts of the Grand
Lod!!"e· I have been obliged to reprimand two of our Lodges for violation of the res·
olut1ons of the Grand Lodge. The occasion for this unpleasant duty would not have
occurred if the proceedings had been read in open Lodge. " * *
" 3d. Carelessness of Secretaries. This is the most fruitful source of difficulties in
Lodges. Secretaries frequently 'rough out,' as it is termed, the proceedings of the
Lodge on slips or separate sheets of paper, and at some convenient season copy them
in the Record Book. I have found Lodges where the records of seven or eigl1t Com·
munications had not been entered upon the record book. No careful man would thus
conduct his business, and a clerk thus negligent would not long remain in employment. Are not Lodge records as important as buHiness records ? The transactions
of every Communication should be carefully recorded and read before the close of
thP. Lodge. Every petition, dimit, bill, report, communication or other paper relating to the business of' the Lodge, should be promptly filed and securely kept for future
reference.
" 4th. Another evil, and the chief of all, is in allowing the door to stand wide open.
There is too much anxiety to make Masons. It is far preferable, and more advantageous to the interests of the Order, that not one degree be conferred, than to make a
hundred Masons who cannot prove themselves as such afterwards. The privileges of
Masonry are designed only for the select few. If it were otherwise, no attempt at
restriction would be thrown around admissions. I tremble for the good name, the
safety, the perpetuity of the Order, when I hear brethren boasting of the number of
applicants pending in their Lodge. The brethren in olden time had this idea in
view when they enacted the law that but five new brethren could he made at one
time."
A question was submitted to a committee which brought under discussion the au·
thority and powers of their Deputy Grand Master, which was decided of course with
respect to their own Constitution. The question submitted is s11bstantially as follows:
A petition for a dispensation, properly drawn up, signed by the requisite number of
Masons, was forwarded to the Grand Master. The Grand Master being absent from
the State, it was presented to the Deputy, who issued an instrument in the form of a
dispensation to the petitioners. A Lodge was thus formed, and worked, under the
name of Northfield Lodge, for more than a year in good faith, and ignorant of ·any
defect in its authorization until a number of its members forwarded a statement of
facts to the Grand Master, who informed the Lodge that he could not recognize it for
the reason that the Deputy in the jurisdiction had no power to grant a dispensation ; but as he was satisfied the brethren who composed it had acted in good faith,
npon proper application to him, he would grant a dispensati<Jn and heal them. They
very foolishly refused obedience to the Grand Master, in which mistaken course they
were counselled and advised by the Deputy Grand Master.

set aside for the time being certaiu laws, customs or usages, some of which are sub·
ject to the action oft.he Grand Lodge, either to confirm or reverse, to permit or deny.
"The granting of dispensations for new Lodges is elaimed as a prerogative of
the G. M., over wl!ich the Grand Lodge has no control. It is inherent in the G. M.
" 4th. The office of Deputy Grand Master is a modern one, and has no Inherent
powers or privileges connected therewith. A Deputy G. M.canexercise such powers
only as are specially conferred upon him by the particular constitution under whi.ch he
is elected. Nor can the Grand Lodge confer upon the Deputy Grand Master any of
the powers or prerogatives of the Grand Master while the latter is acting. The
truth of this proposition is b11lieved to be self-evident, and needs no other argu·
ment to demonstrate it than this -that if any such powers should be conferred upon
the Deputy. he would, to the extent thereof, become a Master or head; thus creating
two governing powers within the same jurisdiction, whose opposing decisions upon
the same subject could not fail to introduce ' confusion worse confounded' into a Fraternity wherein peace and harmony should ever be the prevailing characteristic.
"Section 64, Title 9, of om· Constitution, specially defines all the powers of the
Deputy Grand Master. All, because none others are conferred by any of our rules
and regulations, and none of any kind by ancient usage. Paragraph third of said section contains all of these which relate to the duties of that otfic~r during the temporary absence of the Grand Master from the jllrisdiction, and sets forth' that in such
case 'he may, with the consent of the Grand, Senior and Junior Wardens, call a
meeting of the Grand Lodge, and exercise such other powers and duties appertaining
to the office of G. M as the interests of the Craft may m their judgment demand.'"
From these propositions it appears
"1st. That the Grand Master only (when the Grand Lodge is not in ses~ion) has
power to graut dispensations, and that a Lodge U. D. is, in a general sense, the crea·
ture of the Grand Master- working by virtue of his authority, and responsible to him
.
for its action.
"2d. That the Deputy Grand Master had no authority to grant a dispensation to
open a Lodge at Northfield or elsewhere, and in doing so he usurped a power to
which he had no right, either in law or custom ; and that, consequently, all the work
done under such dispensation, as Masonic, is null and void.
"It appears, from the facts above recited, that the so-called Lodge at Northfield
continned to \\'Ork as a Lodge after the decision of the Grand Master that they were
irregular and could not be recognized as a Lodge had been communicated to the
members thereof. This was a very grave error, to say the least-it perhaps ought to
he characterized as a crime - and is deserving of the strongest censure, if not severe
punishment. But inasmuch as the brethren of' said Lodge plead in palliation the continued assurance of the Deputy Grand Master, that he had full right and authority for
his action in the premises. and his promises to protect them and sustain their action
upon all which they placed reliance, as commg from what they deemed to be almost the highest Masonic authority in the jurisdiction- aud inasmuch as they disclaim all intention to set at defiance the Grand Master or the Constitution, and as
t~ey now confess their error a_nd profess an entire willingness to submit to the deci·
Hrnns of the Grand Lodge and its Grand Master, and to endure such penalty, if any
as may be inflicted - the committee recommend that the matter be passed ovef
without other action than the expression on the part of the Granu Lodge of its ntter
condemnation of the action of the aforesaid brethren at Northfield."
The committee further recommended that in consideration of the premises, the
Grand Master should heal all persons who had been made Masons in the so-called
T,odge, and that if the good of the Fraternity can be subserved, he be requested to
grant a dispensation to the brethren at Northfield. The action of the Deputy was of
course condemned for violation of the Constitution; but it would not have been so
with us, for ours provides that in the event of the death of the Grand Master, or of
his absence from the State, or his inability from any cause to perform the functions of
his office, the Deputy Grand Master shall aucceed>o and be charged with all its powers

According to the Grand Secretary's tabular statement, there are one hnndred and

the bright and sunny colors of the pallet with which to paint the condition of this
jurisdiction; the best sign for the future is the temperate and hopeful language of
the Grand Master, whose spirit we trust will prevail in his land. The Grand Secretary p:ese~ts a glo?my report of the result of his efforts for the year precedi~g in
seekmg mformat10n of the fate of_ Lodges which have made no report. He states

down " is all that is written. There are eighty-nine in the list, but some of them
seem to be taking the chances of temporary inactivity in hope of resurrection in a
happy day.
The Grand Master says little Masonic business has been before him during the
past year, and yet the usual trials and tribulations of a Grand Master have not been
exempt from his lot. He granted no dispensations for new Lodges, but gave permission to a number which had stopped work on account of the troubles to elect officers
and resume labor, believing that it was for the best interest of the Fraternity to have
all the Lodges in the social chain that possibly could be. It may be long, he says
before all the Lodges can again be at work, longer still before they can pay all thei;
arrearages to the Grand Lodge, and perhaps much longer before they_can fraternize
as they should do-yet patience and perseverence will accomplish much- and in
his opinion it is best both for the Fraternity and country to have them re-instated as
nearly as possible as "they were before these troubles. He suggests that it might be
well to release those which have suffered most, from their pecuniary liability. He
gave permission, upon application to some of the Lodges, to admit to membership
brethren who had been members of Lodges that had ceased working, and from which
they could get no dimits. Application also was made for permission to make a
Mason of a persop. who lived in the jurisdiction of a Lodge where labor had been
~uspendP.d. This he dP.nied, because he did not d.eem the Lodge legally extinct until
1t ~as declared to be so by proper Masonic authority, and because he believed in
peaceable times most of them would resume labor. Taking it for granted that they
will, he claims that no Lodge can act upon the petition of such an applicant without

vlolating the ancient usages of the Craft, and the law of his Grand Lodge. It is a

!Hin accordance with the spirit and letter taught by the Fraternity. We recommend

Aymbolic Masonry," and annex resolutions to this report for consideration in the

Again a volume comes to us from this quarter, laden with valuable and interesting

The Address is clothed in that graceful diction which for several years past has
given repute to the documents emanating from this Grand Lodge. He congratulates ·
them that the jurisdiction is rich in all the elements of Masonic prosperity, and notwithstanding the vicissitudes of former years, those troubles have been happily healed by the magnanimity, forbearance and devotion of the Craft, and the Fraternity of
the State has advanced to a proud and most influential position among the Grand
Lodges of the world. He renewed dispensations for three of the traveling Lodges
~ssociated with the army, and granted a dispensation for another, in addition to those
now in the field; he also gave authority for the creation of nine new Lodges to be
located at home, six of which are for the cities of New York and Brooklyn. He admonishes certain of his Craft, who, on occasions when presentations were made by
Lodges, a.nd members of Lodges, of swords, sashes, and implements of war, had
used language " eminently calculated to weaken the Masonic bonds throughout the
whole of these States," and found it necessary to issue a circular note to all the
Lodges, requesting them that on all such, and on all other like occasions, their members should refrain from pursuing a like course when congregated as Masons. We
freely express our surprise that he did not forbid the application of the Lodge funds
to such purposes -for we have learned to regard the funds of a Lodge as sacred to
charity, - and while a Grand Lodge cannot control it in the dispensation of its funds
when appropriating the same to legitimate purposes, it can prevent it from employ•
ing its means in aid of measnrcs for which Masonry was not organized. The Grand
Lodge of California, by a regulation, once checked a custom which was growing in
our midst, by which the subordinates were diverting their treasures from the true
channels, by purchasing jewels and memorials for brethren who had distinguished
themselves by zeal for the good of our Society. In connection with this subject we
introduce an extract, a portion of which leads on to another important event:"It is of inestimable benefit to both parties in the present civil war, that our Masonic relations should still continue in the same healthful condition as at present. I
may go still further, and say that every honorable means should be used which would
have a tendency to strengthen the fraternal bond between the Masons of the North
and those of the South. Those that are well need no physician. In times of profound peace we can sever our relation with any given jurisdiction without any very
serious effects resulting from it; but in time of war, when the soldier of to-day may
be the prisoner to-morrow, it is peculiarly necessary that there should be no interruption of Masonic harmony. It was with this view that I, as heretofore stated
recommended that our brethren of the North should refrain in our Lodges and at
Lodge meetings, from using language which would be calculated to excite ~cerbity
of feeling on the part of the Masons of the South, and although that act has been
criticised unfavorably in some quarters, still, in view of all the facts, I am more fully
confirmed in the opinion which l then expressed, my only regret bein:.>; that I did not
use much stronger language than I did on the issuing of' the recommen'dation referred
to. ln this connection it is proper to state, that I have looked with some little anxiety upon the action which haR been taken with reference to the establishment of
Lodges in Virginia under the M:. W.". Grand Lodge of' the District of' Columbia as
having.a tendency to complicate our Masonic relations with the South. Such aju'risdictional interference could not have taken place under any other circumstances than
those which result from our present unfortunate political position, which indicates
that we have lost sight, to some extent, of' the great truth that while we are at variance as to matters of politics we have no Masonic controversy, or, at least should
have none, with our brethren at the South. I call your attention to this subject for
the reason that you may deem it your duty to express some opinion, which should be
done in the most fraternal manner, as to the course pursued by the M:. W.·. Grand
Lodge to which I have referred."

The R,•., w;., ELLICOTT EVANS presented, as he has with much credit to his Grand
Lodge for several years past, the Report on Correspondence. The proceedings of

great freedom the act of the Grand Lodge of the District of Columbia in issuing a
dispensation to certain Masons living in Alexandria, Va., to open and hold a Lodge
there, and concludes with what we take to be an appeal to that jurisdiction to recede
from its position. His argument against the act is based upon two principles: first,
that Masonry has no jurisdiction over political offences; and, second, that every
Grand Lodge is absolutely independent of every other, except that they are as much
bound toward each other by the common law of Masonry, as sovereign Nationalities
are bound toward each other by the law of Nations; or to give his own language,
they are "subject only to such jurisdiction upon Masonic subjects as is analageus to
the rights claimed by civilized States under the law of Nations, to judge of the con·
duct of independent sovereign powers." The Grand J,odge concurred in the sentiments expressed by the Committee, and adopted a resolution approving the positions
and conclusions. The .M.·. w.-. Jom1 W, J,Ewis, Jr., is appointed chairman, to sue·
ceed the R:. w.·. ELLICOTT Ev ANS.

of our Fraternity.
Grand Master DAVID C. SKERRITT, in his Address for 1863, gives us the assurance
of continued prosperity, but refers to practices by the District Deputies to which he
strongly objects. Some of them have granted dispensations to confer degrees too
freely. He declares it is a power be has invariably declined to exercise, even in
cases where the parties have entered the military service of the country-cases too
to which he would most favorably incline, if he could be induced under any· circumstances to depart from his rule, which is to require the individual to apply in the
usual form to a Lodge, and after the report of a committee and unanimous ballot,
then to grant a privileg~ to the candidate to receive the degrees at one meeting. He
urges the necessity of strict scrutiny into the moral character of applicants for admission.
The Chairman of the Committee of Correspondence, Bro. SAM. C. PERKINS, who
succeeds Bro. RICHARD VAUX, now Junior Grand Warden, presents a review of the
proceedings of twenty-three Grand Lodges, and among them we find ours for 1863
noticed. He takes, we think, a very just view of one branch of the duties of a committee, which is to gather such details and facts as may be profitable to the brethren
of his jurisdiction for their deliberate personal consideration, and also expresses a
purpose, which he earnestly hopes his Grand Lodge will sanction, to effect a regular
interchange of printed documents between Pennsylvania and all recognized Grand
Lodges in foreign states, in addition to those on thi; Continent. He is laudably emu·
lous of the influence l\lld reputation which New York has so justly gained by its able
and indefatigable labor in that behalf, which make its reports so valuable and inter·
eating as books of reference.
The invitation to take " a position in the procession on the ground·" at the conse·
cration of the National Soldiers' Cemetery at Gettysburg, in November, 1863, was
declined for the following reason, which will be readily understood by every intelli·
gent Mason :"It would be unusual. and contrary to the principles of our Order, which seeke
no popularity by public display, to appear in procession on any occasion whatever,
unless called upon to perform the ancient ceremonies devolving upon us as Free and
Accepted Masons; and as such are not contemplated on the present occasion, they
feel reluctantly compelled to decline the honor which, under otter circumstances
they would have cheerfully and witt1 pride accepted."

SYL.v~STER LUTHER, Past Grand Officers. We referred in our last report to a seeming
colhs10n between the Grand Lodge and a neighbor, entrusting its solution to our successors wh.en the facts were presented; the difficulty was with Connecticut, and is
thus explamed. The subordinate jurisdiction of a Rhode Jslaud and Connecticut
Lodge adjoin each other ; the Secretary of the latter, by an error that is now admitted, returned the names of five members of the former Lodge in the list of suspended
Masons, which was published in the Heports of the Grand Lodge of Connecticut. The
circumstance was officially brought to the notice of Grand Master BAI.LOU, who, when
his attention was directed, immediately caused investil!'ation. The Grand Lodge or
Connecticut, upon suggestion of the facts, very courteously passed a resolution ex·
pressing regret that the error had occurred, and also a readiness to do all in its power
to set the brethren right before the world. Occasion was taken by the executive of
Rhode Island, during the investigation, to declare the doctrine now conceded, that a
Lodge in one jurisdiction does not possess the right to confer the degrees of Masonry
on a citizen of another, without express permission being first given. The dispensations issued during the year were for conferring degrees, and most of these were for
the benefit of persons in the service of the United States. Such has been my distrust,
he declares, that the motives of the petitioners were mercenary, that the Masters of
the Lodges were cautioned to be particular in that respect. Two decisions were
made by him which were approved; first, to restore a Mason suspended for an indefinite time, the ballot must be unanimous, and the petition for restoration follow the
s~me course. as '.s presc.ribed for a petition for initiation. The rule in our jurisdiction
differs; notice IS reqmred to be given at a stated meeting, when at the next, two
thirds of the votes of the members present may annul a sentence of suspension pronounced by itself. Another decision was rendered, to the effect that a petition from
a person in the military service, not a citizen of bat stationed in the State, cannot be
entertained without permission of the Lodge under whose jurisdiction he last resided,
or of the Grand Master of the State of which he is a citizen.
The Monument Association reported that they had caused to be completed the
monument to the memory of THOMAS SMITH WEBB, who was Grand Master of this jurisdiction. It is erected in the North Burial Ground in Providence, and a fund is created out of surplus money remaining on hand after the completion of the monument,
which is ordered to be invested so that the income arising from it will be applied
toward keeping it in repair.

At the Communication of the Grand Lodge of Rhode Island in August, 1862, the

follows:"ADDRESS TO THE MASONS OF SOUTH CAROLINA.
"WISDOM, UNION, STRENGTH.

1864.]

Grand Lodge of California.

323

"BRETHREN: The Grand Lodge- anxious for your prosperity, and desirous that,
as members of the great mystic family, you should preserve in unfaded brightness the
light of Masonry which has been entrusted to your keeping -did heretofore address
au encyclical letter of advice and admonition. In the last Grand Communication,
moved by like feeling, it made request of me to direct another letter unto the same
purpose.
"I republish and reaffirm the former letter for your guidance in all respects therein
set forth; as to other general doctrines, my brethren, the Masters of Lodges will admonish you; it is your duty, and should be your pleasure, to hearken diligently and
observe their precepts. Special matters remain concerning which I have to charge
you. Walk circumspectly in the present evil time, ever mindful of solemn undertakings on your part in the presence of Almighty God ; be faithful in observance thereof towards all and singular the brethren, whether these be met in Lodges dedicate,
or only known to yon by divers means, in darkness or light; in health or sickness;
in wealth or want; in peril or safety ; in prison, escape, or freedom; in charity or
evil-mindedness; armed or unarmed; friend or seeming foe, and as to these, most
certainly as towards brethren, when masonically met on, by or with all due and regular intercommunication and intelligence. You have registered words which cannot
be unspoken or recalled, antedating as they will survive all disturbance among men
and turmoils in state; words which in fullest force and meaning should be ever present unto you in thought, utterance and deed. Time with its affairs will soon to every
one be past. We are at labor for a short while only in the work of Him who hath no
respect for persons, building us, if meet, into another and an enduring temple ; if
vouchsafed unto us to be so edified, it will never be regret to remember any good deed
done in the name of a common Master and Father to whatsoever brother, even him
whom the profane would call an enemy. If we do good to those who love us and do
good unto us, what more do we than other men? I charge every one of you, in the
name of our supreme and universal Master, tn be mindful how you are bound in certain duties whereunto you have called Him to witness your obligations and performance who will hereafter judge. I charge you, in His great name and in view of His
final day, suffer not the disputes and broils of men to impair the harmony which has
existed and will exist throughout the Fraternity; for whether or not you put to
shame the teachings of our Craft, they cannot be annulled ; nor despite evil members
who may pain us, can the body of our faithful brotherhood be annihilated or destroyed, or even so much as paralyzed.
" Let us not hear among us that there is war, that strife and dissension prevail; as
Masons it concerns us not.
"Speak no ill of your brethren; if you have aught against one, suffer not your anger to get the mastery of your troth. If any, deeming that ·their personal desires of
advancement or gain have been hindered by a brother, clamor unto you, h~ed them
not when they speak apart; consider that it were nnmasonic and unmanly to take
amends by backbiting and slandering; hearken not to such, nor be covinous, joining
together and comp lotting whereby brethren unheard and undefended may be injured.
There are such among you; of such make no further observance than to shun their
errors. Except unto themselves, blame them not for speaking, nor blame those of

whom it is spoken; listen not to the one, not repeat to the other; Jet the great
Searcher of Hearts alone decide on right or wrong. Judge not when but one accuses
and the other is absent. You do gravest wrong as men not even called Masons,
should yon act on partial judgments severally formed. Nevertheless, should this
wrong be done unto you, forgive even when misjudged, forgive as yon hope to be
forgiven. Above all things, give no cause of offence ; see that your brother has no
just complaint against you; walk erect and upright, in fact as well as appearance,
Masons. Remember wherein to be zealous, to give aid, counsel, protection; lend attentive ear, preserve a faithful breast, having withal a ready and true heart. If it be
ill to speak evil, by how much more is it to do evil.
"It would be useless to write unto you save to remind you of these things, and
but for my office-sake I should not warn or counsel or commend ; for speaking without vain humility, I best know how much I have of error and regret, how much I have
to learn and listen; I was constrained to write, and that not as one having authority
of himself, but such as was placed in his hands to write doctrine approved among us
at all times.
"I laud and honor you, brethren, for many things, and chiefly forasmuch as you
have been diligent in your work of faith, hope and charity. You have been and are
constant in well-doing ; some among us have gone astray, but even these wandered
from our fold, and erred not within its sacred bounds; their condemnation is of themselves and not of' us. You may say without boastfulness that you have fulfilled your
undertakings in your Lodges unto all whencesoever coming in our common name.
So continue, and not for praise of men, but looking forward to the time when your
example will confirm future good deeds in good or evil days, and also looking forward beyond all times to the well done of our Master who is in Heaven.
" And may the Supreme Grand Architect of the Universe ever have yon in his holy
keeping. May brotherly love prevail, and every moral and social virtue cement you
in the bonds of peace and fellowship.
"DAVID RAMSAY, Grand Master of Masons."
W ASRINGTON.
There are only nine chartered Lodges in this Territory, sustained by two hundred
and seventy-two Masons. Numerically it ranks low on the list of Grand Lodges, little
in advance of Nebraska and Colorado. It is six years old. In spirit and intelligence,
order and system, it is entitled to rank high on the list with its sisters. The declaration so often made by Grand Masters that quality and not quantity is necessary in
rearing the enduring monuments of the Craft is signally illustrated in the healthy
growth and propserous condition of our Northern neighbor. We will not institute
comparisons which, while they would be complimentary to this young household,
would detract from others; nevertheless we can take pleasure in assuring them that
their reports, such as they have sent us of the Communication held at Olympia, in
December, 1862, stimulates the aspiration that at some future day, not remote, the
Grand Lodges of the Western slope will divide the honors and influence of Masonry
on this Continent with their sisters of the Eastern.
The M.'. W.'. DANIEL BAGLEY postponed the day of the Communication fixed by
their Constitution for September, which accounts for their meeting at an unusual
time, for the reason that many members were absent at the mines, and the good of
the Craft required him to act in an extreme case. He submitted the act of questionable authority for consideration, in which he was sustained, but care was taken to
" deny the right of the Grand Master to change the time of any future Annual Communication, except in the manner provided by the Craft." Neither himself nor Deputy were present, and the M.·. W.·. JAMES BILES, Past Grand Master, presided, and
the R.·. W.·. THOMAS M. REED, Grand Secretary, read the Address.
The Address is terse, thoroughly a business paper, and submits many matters of
local interest for consideration. No new Lodges were formed during the year. Several rulings were made, among them the following: - that a Master Mason can be
elected and serve as Master of a Lodge, without having served as Warden; -a specific nnm ber of months' residence is not required of an applicant for the mysteries of
Masonry, but upon satisfactory evidence of suitable qualifications, he can receive
them. He advised the Grand Lodge to define more clearly tbe effect of striking a
brother's name from the roll of membership for non-payment of dues. These ques·

The Report on Correspondence, presented by the Grand Secretary, reviews the
proceedings of twenty-one jnrisdictions, and among them ours for 1862. Although
he apologetfoalJy claims to have been acting for seven months past as a practical
miner, it is evident that in the present, when he prepared bis report. he was the
practical Mason, having very thoroughly examined the volumes which he reviews.
He is pleasantly critical in his notice of the Report on Correspondence presented by
onr M.·. W.·. Bro. BELCHER while Chairman. He erects his crest because he con·

that our Bro." takes frequent occasion to give it a sly dig under the fifth rib," which
causes him to express the hope that "the Bro. is not at all envious." We assure him
that he can encourage that hope with a safe prospect that it will end in fruition, for
Bro. BELOHER'S nature cannot possibly accommodate so much of that ugly ingredient
as to entertain it for all, nor even so little as the subject mentioned might provoke.
An expression of opinion concerning the ritual which runs counter to phrases
preferred and set in the memory of others, very generally arouses discussion. Our
Bro. of Washington unwarily illustrates this, and is led into a defence of Bro. RoB
MORRIS, as if he thought an attack was about to be made upon him; and gives him
much credit for his "great zeal" in harmonizing differences; in which we do not, by
any means, join. The disposition manifested to defend the Chief Conservator, adds
to the suspicion expressed in the report which preceded this, that an Association of
which the Grand Lodges were intended to be kept in ignorance was secretly working
under our feet on this coast, to undermine and snare us. We believe that our Com·
mittee of 1862, with us, will give the Chief Conservator credit for being learned,
energetic, untiring, zealous-and all of these qualities have been exhibited by him
to the honor of the Craft- but latterly a dark cloud seems to have arisen 'before bis
vision which may veil the Sbekinab of Masonry from his sight. The questionable
zeal of his house is eating him up. Bro. REED'S attainments and familiarity with
jurisprudence, displayed with ability in bis report, satisfies us that be will agree that
a Grand Lodge is supreme Masonic authority in its jurisdiction, and an attempt to
seduce and mislead young and uninformed brethren, or dazzle and flatter older and
thoughtless, thus alienating them from the Grand Lodge and their duty to it, ought
to be discountenanced and.rebuked by every Craftsman, whose voice or pen is clothed
with authority sufficient to give his opinion superior weight and consideration. We
have no doubt that the effect of this Association is as we have stated, although we
know that the intent is disclaimed by th<>se who have aided in organizing it. He
takes issue with the Committee of' 1862 in the opinion expressed that " our landmarks
are not written," b<"cause, as he says, some of our landmarks are written.

WISCONSIN.
The Report of the Communication held at Milwaukee, ninth June, 1863, presents
the jurisdiction in a prosperous condition. The Address and reports generally are
characterized by directness of purpose in pursuing the interests of the Fraternity,
which affords the best guarantee of continued harmony. We discover nothing from
the pages of the volume by which to trace the march of the Cons~rvators, unless it be
the failure of a committee to report upon the Missouri Resolutions, which were committed. The Grand Master makes no allusion to that association, which we rather
looked for because the north-western jurisdictions seem to have been especially selected for attack; he reiterates his warning against the danger which threatens from
the admission of those who do not fill the standard by which they should be judged,
and expresses his fear that in some inetances the Lodges have departed from the customs of the fathers in the heedlessness with which they have admitted candidates to
a participation in the knowledge of our mysteries ; he granted seven dispensations
for new Lodges, also gave an opinion upon a question which was submitted to him,
to the effect that a Lodge cannot entertain the petition of a candidate who has been
rejected by a Lodge having concurrent jurisdiction with it, which was approved in
Communication ; and in addition it was decided that no Lodge shall receive a candi·
date in either of the degrees who has been rejected in any other Lodge, without the
nnanimons consent of the Lodge which rejected him. The Jaws of our jurisdiction
require the applicant to declare in his petition that he has not, within the preceding
twelve months, been rejected by any Lodge of 1''. & A. Masons, and Lodges having
concurrent jurisdiction are reqnired to give notice to each other immediately of all
applications made for degrees or membership. The object of this is evidently that
the Lodges of the class mentioned may have an opportunity of warning each other
against the approach of unworthy or objectionable persons. The rule in Wisconsin
is carried to the extreme extent.
Bro. G. W. WASHBURN presented the Report on Correspondence, and thinks it
strange that out of thirty-seven American Lodges, proceedings of fifteen only have
been placed in the hands of the Committee. We think it strange that our volume
does not appear in the list. The New York circular letter of 1859, relating to the dif·
ficnlty with Hamburg concerning jurisJictional rights, is incorporated in the report,
and the following resolutions on the subject were presented and adopted:" Regol,ved, That the Grand Lodge of Wisconsin earnestly/rotest against the attempt of any Grand Lodge to exercise its Masonic power an authority within the
territorial jurisdiction of another Grand Lodge.

The following resolutions, with our report, are respectfully submitted for consid·
eration to the Grand Lodge:-

Resol'Ved, That the Association, self-styled "Conservators of symbolic Masonry,"
of which Ron. MORRIS assumes to be" Chief Conservator," is an organized and dangerous league, subversive of the established principles and ground work, which
threatens to make innovation in the body of Masonry.
Resolved, Further, that it is the duty of every Mason to discountenance all who
aid, support or maintain the said Association or its purposes as imposters and dissenters from the original plan ; and the Grand Lodge here by declares that any Mason
within its jurisdiction who willfully adheres to, aids or supports the said Association,
shall be deemed guilty of Masonic crime, and upon proof thereof shall be subject to
reprimand, suspension or expulsion by the Fraternity; provided, that any who may
have been ignorantly and innocently led into error may be purged of the same by
renouncing in open Lodge all connection with the said Association, its teaching,
objects and design.

Bro. JAMES PULLMAN, from the special committee to whom was referred
the subject of the loss sustained by this Grand Lodge in the decease of its
late Grand Orator, presented the following report:-

To the M." W." Grand Lodge of California : Your committee, to whom has been confided the duty of preparing resolutions
expressive of the feelings of this body on the occasion of the death of our late Wor·
shipful brother, the REV. THOMAS STARR KING, beg leave to present the following
report:Bro. KING was born in New York, December 16, 1824. His boyhood was spent in
Portsmouth, N. H., and in Charlestown, Mass. He was preparing to enter college,
when the sudden death of his father left the family in a measure dependent upon his
services for support. From the age of twelve to twenty, he was employed either as
a clerk or schoolmaster, devoting his leisure hours to theological studies. His active
labors in the ministry commenced in 1846, when he was settled over his father's for·
mer parish in Charlestown. He arrived in San Francisco, April 28, 1860. He was
initiated as an Entered Apprentice Mason in Oriental Lodge, No. 144, July 27, 1861;
passed to the degree of Fellow Craft on the tenth, and raised to the degree of Master
Mason on the seventeenth of the following month. .At the .Annual Communication of

[Oct. 12,

this Grand Lodge in May, 1862, he was appointed Grand Orator, and at the Annnal
Communication of the following year, he was again appointed to the same office.the highest compliment the Grand Master could bestow. This office he held at the
time of his death, March 4. 1864.
Within these dates, which embrace a period of less than forty years, the task of
self-training was done and the duties of a noble life were performed. The maturity
of Bro. KING's intellect in bis earliest years was remarkable. The boy soon acted
the part of a man, assuming and fully meeting filial and fraternal trusts, whilst dili·
gently fitting himself for yet greater usefulness. Although thus burdened at the
outset of life with responsibilities which generally prove fatal to youthful ambition,
"his zeal and aptness for learning," writes one of his oldest friends, "his mercurial
alertness of intellect, had curried him at a bound over roads slowly plodded by the
heavy feet of men clogged with easy resources."
From the beginning of his career as a public man to the date of his decease, there
wa.~ no pause in the growth of bis power and r~pntation. He was a close thinker,
acute and •Ubtile in analysis, logical and cogent in argument. He bad a natural
aptitude for large ideas and deep sentiments. It bas been truly said that " throughout his career, in sermon and in lecture, his strong tendency to view everything in
its principles was always prominent; and, as a popularizer ofidea.q removed from ordinary apprehension,- secreted, indeed, from general view, in the jargon of metaphysics,- he was, perhaps, without an equal in the country." We may attribute chielly
to the possession of this endowment, his unexampled successes in the lecture room,
which proved to be the field of his finest intellectual triumphs.
Bro. KING'S moral and spiritual qualities were not detached from bis mind, but
pervaded it. Whomsoever be met he unconsciously enriched. Courageous in tbe
expression of his views, his courage was tempered by an admirable dhmretion and
sense of the becoming. His charity and benevolence were as wide as his knowledge
of' men; he moved and acted as a man among men; his piety, deep and unpretending, found its best illustration in the quality of his life ; and his sympathies, broad as
his bounteous uatnre, extended to the meanest of his kind.
A distrust of his abilities as an extemporaneous speaker seems to have prevented
any attempt at their exercise until he had taken up bis residence among us. It was
therefore reserved to the people of this coast t.o witness Bro. KING'S proudest
achievements as an 01·ator, as well as the display of those other gifts before con·
cealed - executive capacity, organizing ability, and power over men. He had the
rarn felicity of communicating himself in everything he said and did. To that person~l!ty, 1lrawing its value aud its influence from purity and sincerity of purpose 80 aJ!JenG mmtally and morally, so creative iu its use of material, so quick of sight,
"o ardent and so magnetic - we must look for the secret of his splendid oratory.
The worth ol' his servic~s in our city and State in behalf of public institutiorcs and
benevolent enterprises cannot be estimated. "He was a vast power which any
struggling good work could command."
lt1 the first and ouly oration which he was permitted to deliver before this Grand
Lodge, we may perceive the high estimate which Bro. KING placed upon a connection
with our fraternity ; we may also derive in~truction from the lessons it conveys and
the pure spirit which it brea•hes. In the full spee<J of a career, victorious, benefi·
cent, and without stain, he was arrested by death" Resigned he f»ll~ s11periot to the dart
'fhaL quenched its rage in Calitbrnla's heart.''

May we who remain emulate his virtues, cherish his peace-giving yirinciples, and,

meet, whether prepared or unprepared therefor, that for such opinions at least, we
are specially responsible, not to each other -not even to this Fraternity, hut to Him
who alone has the decision of all such questions, and who will mete out full justice
to all, for He ever does all things well. I would never forget, then, when I think of
my deceased brother, as I do not when I look upon the R. •. W:·. Senior Grand Warden
in the WEST, (Bro. Louis CoHN,} who differs so widely from us both,- that we who
are living are all passing to that same tribunal whose ordeal our brother has already
undergone. And I would also remember that however widely we may dilfer in our
theology, and argue thereon even with that earnestness which is but too apt to en·
gender bitterness of feeling and want of charity in action, we cannot alfect in any
way the decision of our Great Grand Master above. I thank God, sir, that whatever
you or I, or a thousand of imperfect, fallible men may think or say as to what that
final decision should be, there goes up to His tribunal nothing so imperfect to change
the fiat of the Omniscient Judge. The decrees of all the great ones of earth can
never pass beyond the portals of the grave. They leave no mark on the boundless
ocean of eternity. We may except from this indeed, those prayers of the poor and
needy and suffering which do reach the ears of the Lord God of Sabaoth, and call
down blessings, rich because unspeakable and eternal, on the head of him, who, re·
membering the command of the Redeemer, did unto the least of His brethren what
he would have done t-0 Him, had he appeared in the flesh, and asked the charity.
And, Most Worshipful Grand Master, may you and I, and all who hear me; have as
much interest in such prayers from as many grateful hearts, in our time of need, as,
I trust, he had, whose departure from our midst we mourn so sadly to-day. On him
came the blessing of the Psalmist, for he was emphatically "the man who provided
for the sick and needy; and the Lord delivered him in his time of trouble."
Pardon me, Most Worshipful Grand Master, for saying so much about questions
on the merits of which we differed, white" our brother was yet alive." I would not
that even that difterence should cause the least jar in the concord of sorrow which
we all feel at our loss in the death of our esteemed brother. Gladly do I bring my
meed of praise,- my chaplet of living•laurels,-to lay upon his tomb, as a M.1.N, a
PHILA.:KTHROPIST, and a good M.1.soN. How illustrious, in all these, was his career!
It was brief, but brilliant, and he has left behind him a halo of glory, such as few can
equal, and none excel. In years he was my junior ; so was he as a Mason, as a min·
ister, a.nd even as a politician. Yet I feel to-day, that with perhaps a single excep·
tion, he was my senior in them all, and entitled to rank me in the regards and esteem
of our fellows and brethren. No man is perfect. He who is dead was no exception
to this universe.I rule. But viewed as a whole, his character was singularly bright
and attractive. .And why? Because he was eloquent? Because he was foremost in
his advocacy of all the great questions that now agitate the community and our whole
country to the very centre? Because his name and praise were on every lip, and
crowds, in church, and hall, and forum, ever delighted to do him honor? Because
the public press, the organ and exponent of the feelings of the people, almost ex·
hausted the language of eulogy itself in his praise? Perhaps so,-and that we should,
therefore, call him one of the great and honored of the heroes of earth, and water
his lowly bier and open grave with our tears. I would detract not one word from all
these high and far sounding eulogies-for in this the distant shores of the .Atlantic
respond in perfect harmony with those of the Pacific, where his honored dust sleeps
in peace,- and few men could deserve more of what has been said and written than
did our Worshipful Grand Orator ; but in my humble estimation his best eulogy was
this,- that the warmest tears were shed, and his loss was most bitterly regretted
and lamented by the poor, the oppressed, and the lowly, who ever found in him a
sympathizer and a friend, whose help ended not in words, but in the substantials
which made glad the hearts of the sorrowful and the friendless. His heart was
never closed; his hand was always wide open ; his purse, like the widow's cruse,

ever full, when the poor, God's messengers, made their appeal to him for help. .And
where is the worthy applicant who can rise and say that he was ever sent empty
away? In this he showed himself indeed to be the true Mason; for though young in
the study, if not the practice of her ritual, it was his creed too that was proved in
his practice ;-that Masonry regards not the outward a.ppearance or standing, but
looks only to the better qualities of the inner man. No prouder monument could he
ask-none better could his children cherish, and pass the remembrance thereof to
their children also, than this, that his memory is kept ever green within, as the lineaments of his well remembered features adorn the walls of almost every house in this
city, and upon this Pacific coast, where dwell those who have in time past been
known and treated only as the friendless, the outcast, the down trodden, and the op·
pressed. He was their true and constant friend. His eloquence was often heard in
defence of their rights, and he lived to see the dawning of that day, for the advent
of which he prayed, and hoped, when the Brotherhood of man shall be universally
acknowledged.
And who more than our departed brother helped on the patriotic work of saving
our beloved conntry in her hour of danger, when traitors, nursed in her bosom and
living upon her bounty, sought to stab her to death, and make our UNION a by-word
and a hissing among the nations of the earth! The danger was great, but the patri·
otism of' the people was found equal to the emergency. Nations and Kings, friendly
and unfriendly, stand amazed at the exhibition of strength and power which our
Government is manifesting in her grappling with internal foes, and her bold defiance
of foreign sympathisers and would-be helpers of her enemies. The end is sure, and
peace, prosperity, and harmony, though mayhap long delayed, will once more visit
and bless our bleeding and distracted country. And when the history of this war
shall be fully and accurately written, and all the actors in this mighty drama shall
have measured out to them the praise or blame which shall be their just due, who
will stand higher on the roll of merit than he whose living words of eloquence and
patriotism rang far and wide over our slumbering State, and, moving true men to a
Aense of their danger and their duty, saved us from secession and the horrors of that
civil war which has laid destitute so many of our sister commonwealths at the East?
'fhe blazing torch of the Highland Chieftains was no more efficacious in rousing up
their followers to gird on their armor and rush to the rescue, than were the trumpet·
tones of our brother, when he called, not on North or South, on East or West, hut on
AMERICA.NS, to do and dare, and, if needs be, die for their country. In the mourning
page, which in our minutes shall testify our regard for our friend and brother, forget
not to speak of him as a PATRIOT, in word and deed, whom all true Americans
delight to honor.
As a man of ELOQUENCE, does it need that I should speak one word of praise ?
Who has not heard him and been charmed as he listened ? Whether he was culling
the beautiful flowers of modern literature ; or, throwing himself into scenes of the
past, made them the living, pleasing realities of the present; or, striking the higher,
nobler chord of his country's demands, roused all his auditors to the same enthusi·
ustic resolves and lion-hearted determination ; it was ever the same. Men never
tired of listening to the charms of that silver-toned eloquence. The words were ever
tl1e best, and tlte manner unrivalled. He spake for your Masonic Relief ~'und, and
your treasury overflowed; for the Sunday and Public Schools, and tbe children
almost worshipped him ; for the sfok and wounded soldiers, and the thousands of
dollars which came from purses that opened as if by magic while he made his appeal, carried consolation, and relief, and joy, and life, to hundreds on the battle-fields
of the Potomac, the Tennessee, and the Mississippi; for the colored man, and while
opposition blushed at ite injustice, the life-long serf stood up in all his manhood of
liberty ; for his country, and the lukewarm became patriots indeed. What a facile
pen he wielded! And how well he !mew how to give life to the written word by the

Bnt few topics are presented in this Address which require reference to the committees of the Grand Lodge. The beautiful tribute •paid to the memory of our late
brother THOMAS S'!'ARR KING, Grand Orator of the Fraternity, has already received
a cordial response in the report of the special committee heretofore appointed, and
ita unanimous adoption by the Grand Lodge.
We recommend that so much of the Address as refers to the questions of Masonic
law presented to and passed upon by the Grand Master, and also, that so much
thereof as relates to certain action in the case of non-affiliated Ma.sons, be referred
to the Committee on Jurisprudence.
We concur in the remarks of the Grand Master as to the impropriety of burying
suicides with Masonic honors; and, to remove the embarrassing decision of particular cases from both the sympathy and action of the local Lodges, we snggest the
passage of a standing resolution, prohibiting such honors in all cases except those
mentioned hy the Grand Master. J,et the tear of sympathy be dropped, and the
grave be filled in silence, feeling the impressiveness of the solemn warning; bnt let
it not be said that Masons especially honor an act that has justly received the condemnation of all civili:z:ed and enlightened communities. That there may be some
rule of action on this subject, we suggest a reference of this portion of the Address,
also, to the Committee on Jurisprudence.
We recommend that the action of the Grand Master and the committee appointed
by him for the examination and revision of the Work and Lectures, in accordance
with the resolutions adopted by this Grand Lodge at its last Annual Communication,
and also the appointment by him of a Grand Lecturer and Deputies be approved ;
and that the work in the three degrees, as exemplified by the Grand Lecturer at this
Communication, in all its parts, be also approved, and made obligatory on all the
subordinate Lodges within this jurisdiction. Your committee append a resolution
to that e1fect to this report, and recommend its adoption by the Grand Lodge.
The subject of the proposed assessment upon the members of the fraternity, of
twenty.five cents per month for a limited period, for the purpose of completing this
Masonic Temple and ultimately making it in great part the property of the Grand
:i;;odge, which has received the approval and endorsement of the Grand Master, pre·
sentS several very grave questions and difficulties which should receive most careflll
examination and open discnssion before adopting or rejecting so important a proposition. One of these grave questions that will meet us at the threshold is, has the
Grand Lodge the power to do what is asked? and behind even an affirmative answer
to this, lies a still more pressing if not important inquiry - would it be expedient,
if lawful, at this time, when Masons and all good men have so much to do in the way
of charity to poor and distressed brothers, and when, on account of the pressure of
the times, from the war and other causes, hundreds of good Masons can scarcely
meet their necessary family expenses and the regular, imperative demands of their
I,odges, to impose this additional burden upon them? Would it not be well to wait
until the skies about us are somewhat brighter than at present, and when there
is a probability of a surplus, rather than the certainty of a vacuum in our purses 'I
The report of the San Francisco Board of Relief, presented at this session, shows
that during the past year, the brethren of this city, large hearted and bountifully
liberal as we know them to be, had demands upon them which exceeded the funds
provided for their good work. So, as we are credibly informed, is the case with
the Sacramento Board; and so, doubtless, can the individual members and particu·
iar Lodges say for themselves. We cannot hope or believe there will be less of this
"greatest work" of Masonry in the year to come, or for several years at least. We
have hardly received, as yet, the first instalment of the sick and distressed, the
maimed, halt and blind, that this terrible civil war will throw upon our hands, and
who must be cared for, if Masons divide their last dollar with them. Your committee suggest these things, not because they are opposed to the completion and adorn[ 98]

1864.]

ment of the Masonic Temple, as its founders and architects intend and propose.

To the M.·. W.·. Grand L01lge of Oalifornia :In the matter of the burial, with Masonic honors, of Masons who commit sui~ide,
referred to in tile Address of the Grand Master, the Committee on Jurisprudence
report as follows: . It .is diffie~lt to co~ceive that any man in liis right mind could be guilty of destroy·
mg lus own hfe. It 1s probably true that one who commits suicide has p1·eviously
become, by some meaus, demented. Self-preservation is the first law of nature. A
very high authority declares that" no man ever yet liated his own flesh." This be·
ing true, a man must in some way have lost tile rigl!t use of his mental powers before
he can lift a hand against his own life. Reason may be dethroned, either by the visi·
tations of God, or by indulgence in licentious and vicious habits. If the hand of God
has been laid upon a brother, recalling the reason which He had given, and, while
thus demented, he shall take his life, we think he may properly receive the honors
paid by our Order to the dead. But if, forgetting the first perfect point of his en·
trance and the virtue by which it is exemplified, and which it is designed to enforce·
if, neglecting his solemn obligations and that prudence which should characteriz;
every bro~her i~ his conduct in the Lodge and when abroad in the world, he, by indulgence m drmk or other habits which are calculated to enervate the mind 1 loses
his reason, and, while thus out of his mind, destroys his.own life, we think he is not
entitled to and should not receive the burial rites of the Order.
We therefore recommend that the sentiments of the Grand Master's address on
this subject be approved.

The Committee on Grievances, to whom was referred the transcript of the pro·
ceedings in the case of Bro. JOHN W. FITZHUGH, sentenced by La Grange Lodge,
.No. 99, to be reprimanded, having had the same under consideration, report as fol·
lows:[ 101 ]

340

Proceedinglf qf the

[Oct. 13,

It appears from the proceedings, that the brother was accused of unmasonic con·
duct, in paying off a security debt in United States legal tender notes, commonly
called greenbacks. The evidence in the record is signally defective in substanti·
a ting tl:e charge. Not only does it fail to prove the allegation, but, on the contrary,
the proof was conclusive that the payment was not made by or with the procure·
ment of the accused, but solely by another party to the transaction equally bound
to the payment of the debt as the brother accused. Had it been even so, that he
had thus made the payment, we are of opinion that that fact alone would not have
rendered him amenable to a charge of unmasonic conduct before his Lodge. These
notes have been issued under authority oflaw, and have been declared in this State, by
the highest legal tribunal, to be a valid tender in discharge of debts; and, though it
doubtless is a great hardship to creditors to be compelled to receive their just dues in
depreciated currency, we are not prepared to say that their offer is a Masonic offense.
In this ca.se, particularly, the parties to the obligation solicited an extension of time,
promising payment in coin, which was not acceded to.
'l'here is another error apparent on the face of this record which we call especial
attention to, as it alone would have necessitated a reversal of the judgment of the
I,odge. Nine Commissioners appear to !1ave been elected ; seven only acted, and
the decision was arrive(! at by only four. Under the Constitution, Sec. 7, Art. III,
Part VI, a majority of the Commissioners are required to pass judgment, and that ma·
jority was held by the Grand Master-see p. 381, vol. IV, of the Proceedings of this
Grand Lodge~to mean a majority of all the Commissioners elected.
On a full review, therefore, of this case, we are of opinion that the action of the
Lodge was erroneous in its conception and action, and we recommend the adoption
of the following resolution: Resolved, That the action of La Grnnge Lodge, No. 99, in deciding to reprimand
Hro. JouN W. FITZl!liGH, be and the same is hereby reversed, and the Lodge directed
to enter on its records a dismissal of the charges against that brother.
All which is respectfully submitted.
HENRY H. HARTLEY'
JAMES L. ENGLISH,

To the lrf. ·. W. •• Grand Lodge of California : Your Committee on Grievances, having had under consideration the appeal of
Bro. GEORGE W. WALKER from the action of lone Lodge, No. 80, expelling him from
all the rights and privileges of Masonry, report as follows:The accusation against the brother in this case was for unmasonio conduct in
"gambling," and being connected with "games." There is no specification attached
to the charge, detailing whether the accused was in the frequent practice of such of·
fences, or whether it had occurred but on one occasion. On the trial, the brother
pleaded not guilty to the charge of "unmasonic conduct," but admitted the charge
of gambling and being connected with gambling games, and claimed that, in so
acting, he bad not, as he understood it, violated the constitution, by-laws, or regula·
tions of the Order. No witnesses were produced at the hearing, and on the admission of the brother, he was found guilty, by a vote of four to three, and sentenced to
expulsion. '.l'he brother, in a communication to the committee, (the sincerity of
which they had no reason to doubt,) states that the offence was committed but on
one occasion, and then under excitement and in utter ignoronce that he was violating any Masonic duty ; that it had not since been repeated by him, and will not be in
the future ; and that he experiences sincere regret for his error on that occasion.
The brother manifestly labored under a serious error when he considered that gamb·
ling was not a Masonic offence. A very slight examination of the ancient regula·
tions of the Order, or a conversation with any intelligent Mason, would have apprized
him that this offence is one strictly forbidden by Masonry, upon all moral and social
grounds; and is an evil in all its effects and consequences which cannot be too greatly
deprecated.* In view, however, of the fact that the commissioners were far from
unanimous in their judgement as to the guilt of the accused, and in the hope that the
action thus far taken by the Lodge will operate as a sufficient caution to the brother
not to be guilty of a similar Masonic otfence in the future, your committee report the
subjoined resolution, and recommend its adoption:
Resolved, That the action of Ione Lodge, No. 80, in expelling Bro. GEORGE W.
WALKER, be, and the same is hereby reversed, and that said Lodge be ordere<f to
cause that brother to be reprimanded in open Lodge by the Master thereof, at a spe·
cial communication to be called for that purpose.
All which is resp ectfUlly submitted.
HENRY H. HARTLEY,
JAMES L. ENGLISH,
SAMUEL c. WRIGHT,
Oommittee'•
WM. H. PETERSON,
FREDERICK F. BARSS,

To the M:. W:. Grand Lodge of Otilifornia :-

In reference to that portion of the Grand Master's address which treats of the
question ~hether a Masonic Lodge is a proper place for brethren to settle their differences Ill bus~ess transactions, and whether, if a brother pays debts owing to
another brot.her, m the depreciated currency of the country, he is liable to a charge
for unm~somc conduct, the Committee on Jurisprudence report as follows : This is one of those questions which we think ought to be determined by the clroums~nces. We agree with the Grand Master, that the courts of the country are
es~bhshed for the purpose of settling differences which may arise in business transact10ns between men. A man does not cease to be a citizen when he becomes a
Maso~. All his d.uties and rights as a citizen are retained. Masonic Lodges are
established and exi~t f~r other and different purposes, and were we to open the door
of the Lo?ge and mv1te Masons to make it the tribunal before which to try their
business disputes, the real purposes of the fraternity would be forever rendered im·
possible. It ls true, however, that circumstances may arise, in the course of transactions between Masons, of such a character that one or the other would be liable to
a charge for violation of Masonic obligations; and of such circumstances and their
bearin! ~pon the par~cular case to which they are sought to be made applicable, the
co~1ss1oners must Judge, subject to the revision of this Grand Lodge on appeal.
It1s 1mposslb'.e to establ~sh any certain rule. We have seen already, in the reports
of the Committee on Grievances, that cases arise and are duly tried, in which the
proof was of such a nature that the able committee who considered them found no
violation of tbe obligations of the brother charged; and yet, we apprehend that
ano:her case might arise in which the same committee would feel themselves con·
stramed to affirm 11 judgment of conviction.
We recommend that no action be had in the premises.
All which is respectfully submitted.
Hmn1Y H. RHEES,
WILLIAM C. RICH,

would be willing to state.

1b fhe M. ·. W. ·• Grand :i~odge of California : In .the matter of the proposition to amend the Constitution, submitted by Bro.
JAKES ANDERSON, and referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence, we respectfully
report our belief that its adoption will be of great advantage to the fraternity, and
will much facilitate the business of the commissioners for trials. Many times the
commissioners find themselves at a loss on points of Masonic jurisprudence, and
need to have the authori1;ative decision of some one more versed than themselves in
matters of law. The proposition, as we understand it, places the Master in the position
of judge, who decides th<! law, but has no voice, in the Jury room when the questions
of law and fact are considered with relation to each other; and the Secretary occupies the position of clerk of the court, while the commissioners are the jury.
We recommend the adoption of the amendment.
All which is respectfully submitted.

his intention to withdraw from membership, his membership ceases, and he can be·

It is not competent for his Lodge by, vote to reinstate him.''

~ the M.·. W.·. Grand Lodge of California :

Your committee, to whom was referred the resolution proposing a remission of
the dues of lfiram Lodge, No 43, to the Representative Fund, for the past three
years, have considered the same and report as follows:The only reason assigned for the proposed remission is, that the Lodge has had no
representative at the communications of the Grand Lodge, during the period named.
This, so far from being a valid excuse for the violation of Sec. 4, Art. II, Part III, of
the Constitution, relative to the payment of dues, is but an additional violation of the
law, as, in Sec. 3, Art. II, Part III, of that instrument, it is declared that each char·
tered Lodge shall be represented at every Communication.
Your committee are of the opinion that the law relative to the collection of dues
should, in thls case, be rigidly enforced, in accordance with the recommendation
contained in a report from the Committee on Jurisprudence, presented yesterday;
and they recommend, therefore, that the resolution be not adopted.
All which is respectfully submitted.

Bro. JAMES L. ENGLISH, from the Committee on Grievances, presented
the following reports: To the M.·. W>. Grand Lodge of California :Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal of Bro. Is.u.o M. WALTER from
the action of Plumas Lodge, No. 60, in suspending him from all the rights and priv·
ileges of Masonry, have had the same under consideration, and respectfully report as
foUows:The charge is unmasonic conduct, with two specifications. The brother was
found not guilty as to the rncond specification aml guilty as to the first: This speci·
flcation is that the accused refused to make a deed for property sold to a brother,
according to his agreement. The testimony shows that Bro. W ALTBR offered to make
a deed for all he sold; so that the question between the brethren was as to what was
the a"'reement between tliem. This question should have been referred to the courts
of th; country, and not have been brought before a Masonic Lodge for adjudication.
Lodges cannot undertake to settle all the legal questions that may arise between
brethren from their bm1iness transactions. Brethren may honestly differ as to the
terms of an agreement, althongh one or the other must be wrong ; and it would not
be consistent with Masonic justice to punish for such difference of opinion. To
warrant an appeal to Musonie censure, the case must involve a wilful and deliberate
disregard of moral and Masonic duty, and nn intention knowingly and wilfully to
chent and defraud a brother. Nothing of the kind appears in this case; and your
committee therefore recommend the adoption of the following resolution: Resoltied, That the action of Plumas Lodge, No. GO, in suspending Bro. ISAAC M.
WALTJm from all tlic rights and privileges of Masonry, be and the same iB hereby
reversed and set aside.
All which is respectfully submitted.

Bro. HENRY HARE HARTLEY, from the same committee, presented the
following reports : 1b Che M. •. W. ·• Grand Lodge of California:-·
Your Committee on Grievances, to whom was referred the appeal of Bro. S. C.
GARD!ifER from a judgment of Mount Moriah Lodge, No. 44, expelling him from all
the rights and privileges of Masonry, having duly examined and considered the same,
report as follows
Great doubt exists in their minds as to the sufficiency of the evidence adduced
upon the trial to support the judgment. The difficulty between the accuser and accused arose as to a transaction in the sale and purchase of mining stocks, a class of
business which unfortunately bas been carried on in our community for some time
past with the greatest recklessness, and a lack of good faith in too many instances
almost bordering upon fraud. This feeling has progressed to sucl1 an extent that
men who, in any other business, would he strictly and most scrupulously honest and
upright in their dealings, would consider everything fair in their transactions regarding mining stocks. It is true that this general unhealthy state of morals in this respect, is no justification or sufficient excuse for the uec of improper practices be·
tween Ma.sons ; yet a "common error" is always allowed to be urged in palliation.
The accused in this case has presented to the committee an application in the nature
of a motion for a new trial, on the ground of newly discovered evidence. The motion
is supported by his affidavit, showing the relevancy of the testimony, and the reasons
why he could not obtain it upon the trial had ; and your committee are satisfied that
the evidence is material, and that if it had been produced, it would have sensibly
af!ected the judgment of the commissioners. Under these circumstances, they think
the accused should have such new trial, and an opportunity of obtaining and presenting the testimony he desires; and they therefore recommend the adoption of the

To the M. •. W. ·. Grand Lodge of California :Your Committee on Grievances, to whom was referred the appeal of Bro. GEORGE
EHMAN from the action of Hermann Lodge, No.127, in expelling him from all the
rights and privileges of Masonry, having had the same under consideration, report as
follows:They have carefully examined the testimony in this case and find that the accused
was convicted upon the evidence solely of one who, by her own statements, was pai·ticeps criminis, without any corroborating circumstances; and that this only witness,
apart from the gross immorality and viciousness of her conduct, contradicted herself
in several particulars, and plainly exhibited herself as totally unworthy of credit.
In all cases where the guilt of the accused is sought to be established by the naked
testimony of but one witness, unsupported by any corroborating circumstances, and
any doubt exists as to the probity or integrity of the witness, it is held safer, to avoid
the possibility of imposition or the introduction of false testimony, to hold the evi·
deuce insufficient aud the charge not proven. Believing that the testimony upon
which this conviction was had, was entirely unworthy of credit and such as ought
not, unsupported, to have been acted upon, your committee recommend the adoption
of the following resolution: Resolved, That the action of Hermann Lodge. No. 127, in expelling Bro. GEORGE
EHMAN from all the rights and privileges of Masonry, be and the same is hereby
reversed and set aside.
All which is respectfully submitted.
HENRY H. HARTLEY,
JAMES L. ENGLISH,

Bro. HEMRY H. RHEES, from the Committee on Jurisprudence, presented the following reports:To the M. ·. W. ·. Grand Lodge of Califoniia : -In the Address of the M.·. W.·. Grand Master the following question is submitted
for adjudication:"Do the ancient charges require that the applicant for the mysteries of Masonry
must be physically perfect, and, if not, what degree of dismemberment or deformity
shall exclude ?"
This having been referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence, we have given to
it such careful consideration as we were able, and respectfully report as follows:We had supposed this matter to be res adjudicata, but our researches have shown
that wide diversity of opinion exists among the wise and learned of the Craft, so
that in whatever way we might decide the question, we should be compelled to diffor
with those for whose Masonic learning and experience we have the highest respect.
We are resolved, then, to the foundation-the landmarks and ancient charges.
What do these say in regard to the qualifications of one who desires to enter the
doors of the Lodge and become a brother among us?
The XVIII Landmark, as given by Bro. MACKEY in his late publication, the " Manual of the Lodge," is in these words:-" Every candidate for initiation must be a
man, freeborn, and of lawful age."
In the ancient charges, given in the same work, professedly from the compilation
made by ANDERSON and DESAGULIERS, and submitted to the Grand Lodge of England
in 1721, and by that body approved in 1722, we find this regulation:-" No Master
should take an apprentice unless he has sufficient employment for him, and unless he
be a perfect youth, having no maim or defect in his body, that may render him incapable of learning the art of serving his Master's Lord, and of being made a brother,
and then a Fellow Craft, in due time."
Do these, taken together, form a part of the body of Masonry, in which we are
agreed that no mau or body of men can make innovations'/ We think they do.
'rliey were not for the first time established in 1721. They were simply gathered out
of the rubbish which the lapse of' ages had accumulated, and placed in the form in
which we now have them, that they might be preserved for the bchoof of Masons in
all time.
'l'he question to be determined is as to the proper interpretation of the language
used in the landmark and charge quoted. Shall we take the ultra view of MACKEY,
as expressed in his "Principles of Masonic Law," pp. 1G6, 167, nnd require absolute
perfection? Is it possible that our fathers used terms which, if strictly interpreted
npon the rule laid down by Bro. MACKEY, would have proven the death of the fraternity? Where, out of the" celestial Lodge above," is the perfection for which he
contends to be found? Bro. ADELL, some years ago, very well answered the sublimated argument of that learned Masonic jurist, in relation to the sense in which the
word "perfect" was to be understood ;-and to those who are curious on this sub·
ject we recommend a reference to his Report on Correspondence, page 87, et seq.,
proceedings .of this Grand Lodge in 1855.

( 12!> ]

364

[Oct. 16,

Proceedings ef the

But shall we accept the other extreme and admit under this regulation, as has
sometimes been done, those who are blind, have lost an arm or leg, are deaf, or hav•
some similar disability? We do not so understand the meaning of the law. In Bro,
MAOKEY's " Masonic Jurisprudence "we find this quotation from the constitutions of
926 :-"A candidate must be without blemish, and have the full and proper use of
his limbs, for a maimed man can do' the craft no good;" and, in the charges of 1686,
this language is found-" That he that be made be able in all degrees, that is, free
born; of a good kindred, true, and no bondsman; and that he have his right limbs
as a man ought to have."
These questions are made from charges, which were in existence, as we are told,
before the compilation of A:snERSON ; and were doubtless known to him, and served
as a basis of the charges as approved by the Grand Lodge in 1722. Taking the three
together, we apprehend that they explain each other, and they must be so inter•
preted as to give every part its proper effect. The several clauses must be taken
together. We are not authorized to take one word or two, or an entire clause, and,
separating it from the rest, base onr interpretation of the whole law upon ~hat .on_e
word or clause. Taking the rule as given by ANJJERSON, as a whole, we thmk it is
capable of such an interpretation as that every part ~ha!.! have due effect, and. ten.d
to the best good of the fraternity. "A young man m his nonage, an old man 1n hJS
dotage," could not be called, masonically, "a perfect youth." One who had lost any
of those members, or any of those senses which are brought into use and required by
the necessities of the work of the Lodge, would have such "maim or defect in his
body as to render him incapable of learning the art;" and he could not be said to
"have hls right limbs as a man ought to have." In the instance mentioned by the
Grand Master, of a man who had lost his foot and had an artificial one, which served
every pUl'pose of locomotion, we apprehend that he had not his right limbs. He is
a cripple, a maim, is disabled. So if a man has a stiff' knee, has lost a hand, is de·
prived of either of the human senses which are important to Masons, he cannot he
made a Mason, for reasons which we may not express in words, hut which will at
once occur to every brother.
'While we cannot agree with Bro. MACKEY that " absolute physical perfection is
required," in his sense of perfectness, we believe that it is a violation of Masonic
usage to admit any man who is incapable of complying literally with what is required
of him in passing through the ceremonies of each degree. Nothing bnt the question
of physical qualifications was submitted to this committee, hut we have concluded
to append the quotation of the Grand Master, made from M ACKEY's Jurisprudence,
with an addition for which we are indebted to the late M.'. W.-. PHILIP C. TUCKER,
of Vermont; aud, as now reported, we recommend its adoption as the rule in this
jurisdiction :
"The pel'son who desires to be made a Mason must be a man; no. wom~n nor
eunuch; freeborn. neither a slave nor the son of a bondw?man; a b~l!ever m God
and a future existence ; of moral conduct; c:ipa?le of r.eadmg and wr,1tmg; i;ot d~·
formed or dismembered, but hale and sound m his physical conf~rmat1on, havmg his
right limbs as a man ought to have ; and be able to conform lit,erally to what the
several degrees respectively require of him."
All which is respectfnl!y submitted.
