Your committee, to whom was referred that portion of the report of the special
committee on the Grand Master's Address, relative to levying a tax of twenty-five
cents per month on each member of the Order in this State, to be used for· the purpose of extinguishing the debt due upon the Masonic Temple, and thereby making
the Grand Lodge the owner of at last one half of that property, have carefully considered the proposition and submit the following:They unanimously recommend that the Grand Lodge levy the tax, making the
several subordinate Lodges responsible for its monthly collection from their respective members, and its prompt transmission to the Grand Secretary. They make this
recommendation, believing that a tax so light cannot be considered burdensome or
onorous, especially if the officers entrusted with its collection do not allow amounts
to accumulate against members. If paid monthly, it will, at the expiration of the
time when its object shall have been accomplished, be lightly remembered by the
contributors. Its result will be in some sort the purchase of an annuity for the Grand
Lodge, although paid by the fraternity in the manner of an insnrance premium,
which will make this body self-sustaining, and ensure to all its subordinates exemption
from taxation forever. In older communities and more settled forms of society, it is
considered a privilege to be allowed by the governments to make such investments for
individual purposes; and for an Order like Masonry it would he certainly a great
desideratum. Many a noble charity is maintained through the foresight of benevolent individuals by means of like investments, and their names have been affectionately cherished for their practical skill in devising the means to carry out such
objects. We pay too much attention to the immediate. Our progressive character
is so fast that we are too prone to forget the future-only living for ourselves and to
provide for our present wants. Let us stop a moment and think for the time to come.
A small consideration, a trifling sum, will make us remembered by those w'ho come
after us, with the same gratitude and veneration which we, practical as we are, ac·
cord to those who have founded institutions of learning, and preserved our laws and
organizations amid anarchy and confusion. By small contributions, almost unknown
and unfelt in communities, the most noble objects of Christian charity and benevoence are made successful and are continually maintained. Cannot we cheerfully
submit to so inconsiderable an assessment for so noble and useful an object - one
17
[ 129 ]

[Oct. lii,

Proceedings if the

368

from which we shall all derive great benefit, and which will leave a splendid inheri·
ta.nee for our successors? Let us• remember that, though we to-day constitute the
Grand Lodge, it will be a. Grand Lodge when none of us can be present. Will not
the foresight and generosity of this day be cherished by those who succeed us 1
Would not we be gratified could we have been the recipients of such an annuity? Can
the expediency of the proposed measure be questioned, or can there be objection to
it based upon other than reasons of parsimony? Nine-tenths of the members of the
fraternity are in the habit of daily expending a larger sum than is required monthly
for this purpose, and that for uses which, if this que~tion was brought to their imme·
diate notice, they could easily forego. By this exemption from taxation, San 1''rancisco
alone would be spared more than three thousand dollars per annum to devote to one
of her most renowned charities- her Masonic Board of Relief; and in like manner
would the other subordinate Lodges be enabled to exercise greater and more extensive charities than their means now permit. That the object sought by this measure
can be obtained we have no doubt. The property is situated in the best business por·
tion of the city, and, if we are to judge from past experience, it will continue greatly
to appreciate in value. It affords a revenue, at the present rates of rental, of about
twenty-five thousand dollars per year; is not subject to taxation ; and is built of the
best materials and in the most durable form consistent with the requirements of such
a structure.
It has cost, up to the present time, about two hundred and fifteen thousand dol·
lars, and is encumbered for one hundred thousand, which is the debt proposed to be
liquidated by the carrying out of the measure under consideration. It will cost'. ac·
cording to the highest estimate, thirty-five thousand dollars more to complete it malting its total cost two hundred and fifty thousand dollars ; and will no doubt, in
its finished state, pay at least one per cent. per month nett upon the investment.
The expenses of the Grand Lodge, for all purposes, are about twelve thousan~
dollars per annum, and they are not likely to increase above that sum ; and hence it
will be seen that the revenue to be derived from the investment will meet all the
probable expenses of the Grand Lodge hereafter. We express the hope that the
proposition will receive careful attention, and that it will be adopted by sue~ a
majority as will ensure its being carried out with that unanimity and harmony which
should be the prominent characteristics of our Order; and we therefore append the
following resolutions, and recommend their adoption:Resolved, That in addition to the amounts at present levied upon the subordinate
Lodges in this State, there shall be levied the sum of twenty-five cents per month
for each Master Mason borne upon their rolls, the amount of which levies shall belong to and be called the "Masonic Hall Fund ; " and that it shall be the duty of
the several Lodges to collect the same monthly and transmit the amount so collected
to the Grand Secretary on the first days of January, .April, July, and October, of
each year, beginning with the first day of January, 1865.
.Resolve!}., That the Grand Secretary be and hereby is directed to invest the mon·
ies, so received, in the stock of the" Masonic Hall Association of the City of San
J<'rancisco," by having them immediately applied to the liquidation of the debt due
upon the Masonic Temple, and for no other purpose.
All which is respectfully submitted.
CHARLES MARSH,

were not satisfied that he had. Our sixth Regulation, for good and familiar reasons,
prohibits any communication on the part of our Lodges and Craftsmen with those
who acknowledge allegiance to that Grand Lodge, whilst it continues in its present
antagonistic attitude toward the American Grand Lodges. We see no good reason
why Bro. FRENCKHAUSEN, if he is worthy, may not be permitted to affiliate with a
Lodge in our jurisdiction whenever he can satisfy the brethren, who compose it, that
he has regularly dimitted from '\he Lodge under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge
of Hamburg, of which he was a member; and that he disclaims and renounces any
allegiance thereto, and is ready and willing to support and maintain the laws which
govern the Lodge with which he 1iroposes to affiliate. Indeed, under such circum·
stances, we would be inclined to consider favorably an application from the Grand
Master of Hamburg himself-he being penitent.
All which is respectfully submitted.
GILBERT ll. CLAIBORNE,}

The facts ln the case are, that JAMl!S ALF.X. YoELL was suspended by San Jose
Lodge, No.10, from all the rights and privileges of Masonry, which sentence was
affirmed, on appeal, by this Grand Lodge; and Mr. YoELL now applies to this Grand
Lodge to be restored to his rights and privileges as a llfoson, without any application
having been made to San Jose J,odge, No. 10, or any action whatever having been
had by tl1at Lodge In reference to his restoration. The question then arises, will the
Grand Lodge, under such clrcu!Dlltances, considei,the application and restore the
applicant? That the Grand Lodge possesses the power to do so there is no question.
But the subordinate Lodge equally has that power, in caseR of suspension, whilst at the
same time the members of the subordinate Lodge possess opportunities for determili·
ing the propriety of the restoration which it is impossible for the Grnnd J,odge to
have. As a general rule, the restoring power will not be exercised by tlie Grand
Lodge, even in cases of expulsion, where the power of restoration resides solely !11
the Grand I,odge, except upon the application of the subordinate J,odge in which the
original trial was had. That being the rule in case of expulsion, a fortiori it should
be the rule in cases of suspension. Your commit'tee therefore recommend that the
application, as made, be denied, and that they be discharged from the further con·
sideration of the subject.
All which is respectfully submitted.

'1.'o the M. ·. W. ·. Grand Lodge of California :Your committee, to whom was referred the complaint of Bro. Jo1!N JlfUNRO, respecting certain action of the w... J\faHter of Crockett Lodge, No. 13!!, having had the
same under consideration report as follows:The difficulty in tl1is case appears to have arisen from an impression on the part
of the Master of the J,odge that it wll.S necessary for a brother again to sign the bylaws thereof, on his restoration to membership after suspension for non-payment of
dues. Your committee are of opinion that, although tl1is appears to have been the
cnstom of the Lodge in question, the requirement cannot be found in the Constitution
or General Regulations of our Grand Lodge, or in any general usage of the Order.
When a brother, who has been suspended for non-payment of dues, pays up all his arrearages, he thereby becomes restored to all the former privileges enjoyed by him
in Ms Lodge, and it is unnecessary that he should again go through the form of signing its by-laws. The Master, therefore, in this case erred in judgment in holding
that he would not recognize the brother as a member of the Lodge till he lla<l once
more so signed. Whilst, however, the Master thus erred, we by no means intend to
justify the conduct of the brother in the Lodge, on hearing the ruling of the Master.
It is at all times the duty of a Mason respectfully to snbmit to the decision of the
Master whilst in open Lodge, no matter what may be his own opinion as to the correctness of the Master's rulings. The peace and harmony of the Lod1<e uepenu;;
upon implicit obedience to the orders of the presiUing officer whilst the Lodge is
open- there being always the right of appeal to the Grand Lodge or Grand Master from any erroneous decision which he may declare. In this case, the brother
undertook to dispute the decision of the Master, aml that too to such an unwarrantable extent, that the }faster found himself compelled to cause him to be forcibly
ejected from the Lodge room. Iu view, therefore, of all the circumstances of this
case, your committee recommend the adoption of the following resolution:. Resolved, That it is the duty of the Master of Crockett J,odge, No. 139, to recogmze Bro. l\luNno as a member of said Lodge, in good standing; and that said brother
be reprimanded in open Lodge, by the Master thereof', for insubordination and disobe·
dience to the orders of said Master, whilst the J,odge was in session.
All which is respectfully submitted.
HE.>mY H. HARTLEY,
JAMES L. ENGLISH,
8.A.MUEL C. WRronT,
Oornrn'iltee.
WrLLIAllI H. PETERSON,

'lb the M. •. W.·. Grand Lodge of Oalifoi·nia :Your committee, to whom was referred the memorial of Yolo Lodge, No. 81,
presenting certain charges against Grafton J,odge, No. Hl, having had the same
under consideration, report as follows:
The statements set forth in the memorial show that a member of said Grafton
Lodge (one of its officers) was, during.the past year, stricken with paralysis and be'
came entirely dependent for his support and that of his family upon the charities of
his brethren and fellow men; that the officers and members of said Lodge were
aware of his condition and neglected and refused to take any steps towards his
relief; and that, nnder these circumstances, Yolo Lodge, being situated near the residence of the. brother, made provision for his relief and attended to his necessities.
Subsequently, Yolo Lodge applied to Grafton Lodge to repay to it the amount so
advanced, and also to provide for the wants of the brother in the future, both of which
requests appear to have been denied. The question then for consideration is-ctm
this Grand Lodge, on such a state of facts, take any, and if any, what notice of the
action of Grafton Lodge in the premises? Your committee are aware that Masonic
authorities are somewhat contradictory upon this point; but, upon a full considera-~
tion of the subject, they are of opinion that it would be an unfortunate proposition
to establish, that a Masonic J,odge, devoted, as it should be, to charitable objects
and the assistance of the distressed, could with impunity sulfer its members to want
for the necessaries of life, and thus bring discredit upon the whole traternity. Act·
ing under this view, your committee recommend the adoption of the following reso-

lntlon: -

of Bro. P. L. Di:sTON, Junior Warden of said Lodge, be and the same is here by strongly
condemned by this Grand Lodge; and tbat, if it shall appear to the Grand Master
that said Lodge continues in such course of conduct, after due notification of the
action of this Grand Lodge, he be and hereby is requested to arrest the charter of ;
said Lodge, or take such other action in the premises as he may deem expedient.
All which is respectfully submitted.

Bro. GILBERT B. CLAIBORNE1 from the special committee to whom, upon

the following report: 1b the M. ·. W.-. Grand Lodge of Catifornia : -

The special committee, to whom was referred the appeal of JESSE MORRILL from
the decision of Union Lodge, No. 58, report as follows:In this case the otfence charged-gross unmasonic conduct-is of the highest
order in Masonry. There are two specifications: the first, that the appellant cheated
and defrauded a Masonic cemetery association of a certain sum of money which he
had received and should have paid over; and the second, that he wilfully cheated
and defrauded a brother for whom he was acting as agent, by collecting a certain
sum of money and appropriating the same to his own use. Your committee so far
as the evidence goes, digcover none of that essence of crime-the intent to defraudwhich would complete it, but there is, on the contrary, somewhat that might have
gone to mitigate the punishment adjudged. It is in evidence that the accused, after
the charges against him were reported to have been tiled with the Lodge, and before
they were served, discharged his obligations to the cemetery association, which,
although tardy, was considered satisfactory by them. To the second specification,
and ~n fact to each, his plea is poverty, or in other words, that the money was used
by him ~t a time when h~s necessities were so great that his moral strength weakened
under c1reumstances wluch were to him irresistible. Your committee have charity
for the weakness and infirmity of human nature, and, while they cannot omit words
of ~ondemnation as~~ the act of an agent in malappropriating, or diverting from
~heir p~oper and leg1t1i;iatc c!Jannel, any funds received by hinI in a fiduciary capac·
1ty, which should be pard over to'thosc for whom they were intended, or guarded as a
sacred trust, ready at all times for the purpose for which they were devoted, they
submit the following resolution, and recommend its adoption:_
·

All which reports were concurred in, and the recommendations therein
contained were thus ordered by the Grand Lodge.

from all the rights and privileges of Masonry, be and the same is hereby modified·
and it is hereby ordered that said MORRILL be and remain suspended until such tim:

It will be seen that to forty.five Lodges no allowance has been made. Of these,
thirteen- being Nos. 1, 17, 22, 30, 44, 120, 125, 127, 136, 139, 144, 166, and 169- are
located in this city; two-Nos. 21and98-were represented by brethren now re·
siding in San Francisco; seven-Nos. 9, 13, 16, 19, 25, 28, and 102-were represented by brethren who received pay in other capacities; one-No. 57, -was unrepresented after the first day; fifteen-Nos. 45, 46, 50, 52, 75, 76, 79, 93, 104, 141, 143, 147,
157, 165, and 168-had paid their dues, but were not represented; three-No. 43,
and Alpine and Elk GrO'!Je, U. D. - had neither paid dues nor were represented; and
four-Nos. 36, 152, 163, and 159,- had surrendered their charters. It is proper also
to note that to the representative of Lodge No. 108, but half the regular allow·
ance was made, as it is not his intention to return to his former place of abode,
In 1861, the levy for the representative fund was one dollar for each member upon
the rolls of the Lodges, which produced more than was required; in 1862, the tax
was reduced to fifty cents for each member, which was found to be iustl1Iicient; and
iu 1863, the assessment was fixed at seventy.five cents, wl1ich, as nearly as is .convenient, has been found to be the necessary taxation for the purpose indicated. Your
committee, therefore, append a resolution fixing that as the rate for the ensuing year.
The resolution of 1861, authorizing the payment of representatives, declares" that
no delegate shall receive such payment who shall not have remained during the
entii'e Communication, unless excused by the Grand Lodge."
*An error in addition occurred
for dues to the Rep. Fund, as reported by the Committee on Returns, at page 346 ante. The amount, instead of $4,930 25, ,..
there stated, should be, as above, $5,080 25; and the total dues there carried out, in•tead of
$14,677 25, should be $14,777 25.

Proceeaing.g ef tlie

[Oct. 17,

nication," if it means any thing, means from the first day to the last, inclusive; and
so considering it, yonr committee had, at first, made no allowance for those Lodges
whose representatives were not present on the first day of this Communication. But
their good natnre was strongly attacked by the many reasons assigned for failure in
attendance on that day; and it was urged, moreover, that in 1862, the resolution was
relaxed in this respect by the action of the Grand Lodge, so that the representatives
of the eleventh hour, even, received each his penny. The committee, therefore, as
will be observed, have made allowances to several representatives who did not ap·
pear until tlie second or third day; but they do not believe that this is in accord·
ance either with the language or intent of the resolution upon the subject, and they
have only yielded thus far at this time, because the Grand Lodge has once consented
to the same course of action. That this may not become a precedent, and that the
law in this matter may be sufficiently plain, explicit, and imperative hereafter, they
submit a resolution in addition to the one before mentioned, and recommend the
adoption of both, as follows :Resolted, That, for the ensuing fiscal year, there shall be levied upon the Lodges
under this jurisdiction, in addition to the dues prescribed by tlie Constitution, the
sum of seventy-five cents for each member bo!'ne upon their respective rolls at the
date of their annual returns, for account of tl1e Representative Fund ; which assess·
ment shall be paid at the same time and in the same manner as is prescribed for the
payment of the regular annual dues.
Resol'IJed, That hereafter no Grand Officer, Chairman of a Standing Committee,
or representative of a J,odge, shall receive payment for his necessary traveling expenses in attending a Communication of the Grand Lodge, who shall not have been
in attendance from the first to the last day, inclusive, of such Communication, unless
excused by special action of the Grand Lodge.
All which is respectfully submitted.
WILLIAM A. DAVIES, i
